Get a policy for your spouse too, even if they don't earn an income, because replacing childcare and household work is expensive. Term at your age is cheap, so lock it in while you're healthy.
just tell me the fastest way to get +100 points in 30 days. no lectures

The only lever that moves that fast is utilization. Pay your card balances down to under 10 percent of their limits before the statement closing date, not the due date, and your score can jump significantly within one billing cycle. If your report has errors, dispute them now, since bureaus have about 30 days to investigate. Anyone promising 100 points in 30 days beyond that is selling something shady.
My brother inherited the same amount as me and wants me to go in with him on opening a restaurant. 100k each. I love him but I'm nervous.

Your nerves are justified: restaurants have high failure rates, thin margins, and mixing family with business partnerships strains a lot of relationships. If you're seriously considering it, insist on a detailed business plan, a written operating agreement with a lawyer, and only invest what you could lose entirely without damaging your finances. Many people put in a smaller amount, or offer support without being an owner. Protecting your money can also protect the relationship.
how much should a beginner buy

Start with an amount you'd honestly be okay losing completely, which for most people is a few hundred dollars or a small percentage of their investments, and only after the emergency fund and retirement contributions are taken care of. Buying a fixed amount every month through dollar-cost averaging takes the stress out of timing. Learn how it all works before you scale up.
Can I pay my car loan with a credit card to get the points?

Most auto lenders don't accept credit cards directly, and the workarounds usually charge fees of around 2.5 to 3 percent that wipe out the rewards. If the payment ends up sitting on the card and you carry a balance, you'd be paying credit card interest of 20 percent or more on a car loan. It's not worth it. Pay the loan from your checking account and earn points on everyday spending you can clear each month.
We're retired and our kids keep needing help. How much is too much?

A good guardrail is to fund help only from money beyond what your retirement plan needs, because you can't borrow your way through retirement but they have decades of earning ahead. Set an annual family-support budget and treat requests within that limit. Meeting with a fee-only financial planner can show you exactly how much you can safely spare.
My parents keep all their money in cash at home because they don't trust banks after what happened in their country. How do I talk to them?

Start by respecting why they feel that way, since their distrust likely came from real experience. Explain gently that cash at home is exposed to theft, fire, and inflation, and that US bank deposits are insured by the FDIC up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, for each account ownership category. Suggest moving just a portion first, maybe into a high-yield account they can see growing, so trust builds gradually. Visiting a bank together or meeting a trusted advisor can help a lot.
My church member runs an investment club promising 30% returns for 'kingdom building.' Feels wrong to question him.

Asking questions isn't disrespectful, and an honest leader will welcome them. Affinity fraud, where scammers target their own religious or community groups, is a well-documented problem precisely because trust replaces checking. Ask whether he's registered with the SEC or your state, where the money is held, and whether you can see audited statements. If he answers with faith or pressure instead of paperwork, keep your money out, however much you like him.
Is it worth paying $997 for a course on starting a print-on-demand business?

Almost certainly not, because nearly everything those courses teach is available free on YouTube, Reddit and Printful's or Printify's own guides. Print-on-demand margins are thin, so spending $1,000 up front means you might need hundreds of sales just to break even. Start with the free material and open a shop for little or no money. Only pay for education later if you hit a specific problem you can't solve yourself.
I got denied for a credit card. Will applying for 5 more today help me find one that approves me?

Please don't, because each application usually triggers a hard inquiry, and a cluster of them makes you look riskier and can sink your score further. Your denial letter must explain the reasons, so read it and fix the main issue first. Use prequalification tools on issuer websites, which only do soft pulls, to see where you're likely to be approved. A secured card is a near-certain approval if your credit is thin or damaged.
My parents are elderly and I'm their main helper. Can I just take money from their account to pay myself back for stuff I bought them?

Don't do that informally, even if you're owed it. Without the proper authority, it can look like financial exploitation and cause real legal and family trouble. If you have power of attorney, keep receipts and a clear log of every reimbursement. If you don't, talk to an elder law attorney about setting one up, plus a caregiver agreement if you're spending a lot of time or money on their care.
Is it worth getting the extended warranty on a $900 laptop for $180?

Usually no. Extended warranties are priced so the store profits, and most electronics either fail early under the manufacturer warranty or last past the extended period. Check whether your credit card already extends warranties automatically, since many do. If you're genuinely clumsy, accidental damage coverage might be worth it, but for ordinary breakdowns you're better off putting that $180 into savings.
Co-signing my brother's car loan — will it affect my credit?

Yes, the full loan shows up on your report as your debt, and any late payment he makes will hit your score exactly as if you'd missed it. It also counts toward your debt-to-income ratio, which can make it harder for you to get your own loan or mortgage later. Only co-sign if you could comfortably make every payment yourself if he couldn't. If you do go ahead, set up account alerts so you know immediately if a payment is missed.
Thinking of putting my card debt on a crypto bet to double it and pay it off. Thoughts?

Please don't, because you'd be taking on more risk exactly when you can least afford to lose. Crypto can drop 50% in weeks, and if it does, you'll still owe the full card balance plus interest with less money to pay it. Guaranteed returns from paying off a 25% card beat speculative bets. Put whatever you were going to gamble toward the debt, and if it feels overwhelming, a nonprofit credit counselor can help you build a realistic plan.
I'm 19 and want to learn crypto day trading with leverage on Bybit. Tips?

My main tip is to skip the leverage. Most retail leveraged traders lose money, and with 10x or more a normal 10% swing can liquidate your whole position in minutes. If you want to learn, trade small spot amounts with no leverage and keep a journal of every trade to see whether you actually have an edge. Honestly, at 19 the bigger win is putting steady money into an index fund and letting compounding work for decades.
heard about the rule of 55. what is it

If you leave your job in or after the calendar year you turn 55, you can take withdrawals from that employer's 401k without the 10% early-withdrawal penalty, though you still owe income tax. It applies only to the 401k at the job you left, not old 401ks or IRAs, so rolling that money into an IRA would actually cost you the benefit. Some plans have quirks about partial withdrawals, so confirm with your plan administrator before relying on it.
Can I buy a house with student loans?

Yes, plenty of people do. Lenders look at your debt-to-income ratio, which generally needs to stay under about 43 to 45 percent including the new mortgage. If you're on an income-driven repayment plan, make sure your lender counts the actual payment correctly. Try to keep your student loans current and your credit utilization low in the months before you apply.
My brother wants to borrow $30k from my inheritance for his business. I want to help but I'm nervous.

Listen to that nervousness, because family loans for businesses go unpaid often and can strain the relationship badly. Only lend an amount you'd be at peace never getting back, and think of it as a gift in your own head even if you call it a loan. If you do it, put it in writing with repayment terms, and have him show you a real business plan first.
I got a text offering $300/day for liking YouTube videos. Then they want me to deposit money to unlock bigger tasks. Legit?

That's a well-known task scam: they pay you small amounts at first to build trust, then get you to deposit money you'll never get back. Real jobs never ask you to pay to earn more. Stop responding, don't send any money, and if you've already shared bank details, contact your bank right away.
My uncle wants me to invest in his friend's private company that's 'about to go public.' Minimum is $25k. Says it's a sure thing.

Treat the words 'sure thing' as a warning, especially next to 'about to go public,' a classic pre-IPO scam line. Ask for the offering documents, check whether the offering is registered or filed with the SEC, and have a securities attorney or fee-only adviser look at it before any money moves. Even legitimate private investments can lock up your money for years or go to zero, so never put in more than you could lose entirely.
Should I buy a fixer-upper to save money?

Only if you have the cash, skills and patience to match. Renovations almost always cost more and take longer than planned, so budget 20 to 30 percent over your estimates. Get a thorough inspection plus contractor quotes before you buy, because some problems, like foundation, sewer lines or electrical work, can wipe out any savings. A cosmetic fixer can be a good deal, while a structural one rarely is for a first-time buyer.
My mom keeps asking me for money and it keeps wiping out my emergency fund. I feel guilty saying no.

That's a hard spot, and feeling guilty means you care about her, but your emergency fund protects you, and if it's gone you won't be able to help anyone when a real crisis hits. Set a separate, specific amount you're comfortable giving each month and tell her that's what's available, which is kinder and clearer than saying yes until you're tapped out. If her requests stem from ongoing money trouble, pointing her toward a nonprofit credit counselor could help her more than cash.
I'm 45 and behind on retirement. Is crypto my best shot at catching up?

It's tempting, but betting on crypto to catch up can just as easily set you back further, and you have less time to recover from a crash. The more reliable levers are maxing out your 401k, including the extra catch-up contributions allowed at 50, plus an IRA and cutting expenses where you can. A fee-only financial planner can map out a realistic catch-up plan. Crypto can be a small side position at most, not the plan.
Thinking about using a 0% balance transfer credit card to pay off my student loan and save on interest. Smart hack?

It's riskier than it looks. Transfer fees usually run 3–5%, many cards won't even let you pay a loan this way, and if you don't pay the full balance before the promo ends, you'll be facing 20%+ interest on what's left. If the loan is federal, you'd also permanently lose income-driven repayment and forgiveness options. Unless it's a small balance you're certain you can clear within the promo window, skip it.
should a 70 year old be in index funds or is that too risky

Index funds themselves aren't the problem, since the real question at 70 is how much is in stock index funds versus bond index funds and cash. Many retirees keep something like 30 to 60 percent in stocks for growth that keeps up with inflation, with the rest in bonds and cash to cover several years of withdrawals. The right mix depends on income sources like Social Security, health, and how much you'll be withdrawing. A fee-only fiduciary planner can help you set an allocation you can stick with.
Should I waive the inspection contingency to win a bidding war?

That's a risky move, because you're giving up your way out if the house turns out to have a $30,000 foundation or roof problem. If you need to compete, safer options are a pre-offer inspection or an informational-only inspection where you agree not to nitpick small items. A larger earnest money deposit also helps. Losing a bidding war stings, but buying a money pit is worse.
I'm 24, just got my first real job. Want a BMW, can technically afford the $650 payment. Any reason not to?

Being technically able to afford it isn't the same as it being a smart buy. A $650 payment plus premium insurance and pricey BMW maintenance could easily run you $900 or more a month. Early in your career, that money could build an emergency fund and get your retirement savings going, which compounds massively at your age. Consider a reliable car around $300 a month, and get the BMW later when it's a smaller slice of a bigger income.
Is putting less than 20% down a mistake?

Not necessarily. Plenty of people buy with 3 to 10 percent down and do fine. The tradeoff is private mortgage insurance and a bigger loan, so your monthly payment goes up. What matters more is keeping a healthy emergency fund after closing, because putting every dollar into a 20 percent down payment and having nothing left over is the riskier move.
I run a small landscaping business. Can I pay my nephew in cash under the table so neither of us deals with taxes?

Don't do that. It's tax evasion for both of you, and it leaves your business exposed if he gets hurt on a job, since he wouldn't be covered by workers' comp. Paying him properly is easier than it sounds and comes with benefits: his wages are a deductible business expense for you. If your business is a sole proprietorship and he's an independent contractor, you just file a 1099-NEC once you pay him $600 or more. A payroll service can handle actual employee wages cheaply, and it keeps you on the right side of the IRS.
my score is 790. is there any point trying to get it higher?

Not really. Most lenders give their best rates and terms to anyone above about 760, so going from 790 to 840 rarely saves you anything. Keep doing what you're doing, and spend your energy on savings and investing instead of chasing points.
I'm retired, 67, and my advisor wants me selling options on my portfolio for income. Is that normal?

Some advisors do use conservative strategies like covered calls for income, so it isn't automatically a red flag. Still, ask exactly which strategy they're proposing, what the worst-case loss looks like, and how they're paid for it, since options can generate extra fees and commissions. Make sure your advisor is a fiduciary, and get a second opinion from a fee-only planner if anything feels unclear. At 67, protecting your principal matters more than squeezing out extra income.
Can I borrow against my house to buy into a high-yield note offering 14%? Spread seems like free money.

It's not free money, because you'd be putting your house on the line for a return that's only high because the note is risky. Private notes paying 14% often default or turn out to be fraud, and you'd still owe the loan either way. Before doing anything like this, get a fee-only fiduciary advisor to look at it, and I'd strongly lean toward no.
Should I take out private loans or federal loans for my sophomore year? Private one offered a lower rate.

Max out federal loans first, since they come with income-driven repayment, deferment, forbearance and forgiveness options that private loans almost never match. A slightly lower advertised private rate is often variable or reserved for borrowers with excellent credit or a strong cosigner. Only turn to private loans for whatever gap remains after federal aid, scholarships and work-study.
Teacher here, district says no negotiation on the salary schedule. Am I stuck?

Mostly on base pay, but make sure you're placed correctly on the schedule. Ask that all your prior teaching years and any graduate credits or degrees be counted, since that's often where real money gets missed. Stipends for coaching, clubs or hard-to-staff subjects are worth asking about too. Your union rep can tell you exactly what's negotiable.
Offer letter says salary is non-negotiable. Do I believe them?

Sometimes it's true, especially at government jobs, unionized roles or companies with strict pay bands. Even then, you can often negotiate level placement, start date, a signing bonus, PTO or relocation support. A polite question like "I understand base is fixed, is there flexibility elsewhere in the package?" carries basically no risk. If the answer is a firm no, decide on the offer as it stands.
Market just dropped 15% this month. Should I sell my index funds and buy back in when it recovers?

Hold steady, because that strategy sounds smart but rarely works. You'd need to be right twice, on when to sell and when to buy back, and some of the market's best days often come right after its worst ones, so people who sell usually miss the rebound. If your timeline is long, keep your regular contributions going, since you're now buying at a discount. If this drop is genuinely keeping you up at night, consider a more conservative mix after things settle rather than selling in a panic.
I want to max out a backdoor Roth. Anything that can go wrong?

The big trap is the pro-rata rule. If you hold any pre-tax money in a traditional, SEP, or SIMPLE IRA, part of your conversion becomes taxable, so roll that money into your 401k first if your plan allows it. Make the nondeductible contribution, convert promptly, and file Form 8606 every year to document your basis. It's very doable on your own, but if you have old IRA balances lying around, a quick check with a CPA is worth it.
My kid is 15 and we have literally $0 saved for college. Is it too late to even bother?

It's not too late, and starting now still makes a real difference. Every dollar you save is a dollar less borrowed, and in many states a 529 contribution earns a state tax deduction even when the money gets spent within a few years. With only three years to go, keep the money in conservative investments rather than chasing growth. Just as important, sit down with your teen now to look at net price calculators, in-state public schools, community college transfer paths, and merit scholarships, because those choices will matter more than any investment return.
I'm 25. Should I even care about inflation or just invest and forget it?

At 25, the best inflation hedge you have is time in the market. Over long periods, diversified stock index funds have historically outpaced inflation by a wide margin. Build an emergency fund first, capture any employer 401(k) match, then automate contributions into a low-cost total market or target-date fund. You can mostly ignore the inflation headlines and let compounding do the work.
Interest rates are high. Should I buy now and just refinance later when they drop?

Only buy if the payment works at today's rate, because a future refinance is a hope rather than a plan. Rates might not fall for years, and refinancing costs around 2 to 5 percent of the loan in closing costs. You'd also need enough equity and good credit at that time to qualify. If the house fits your budget now, a later drop is a bonus. If it only fits after a refinance that hasn't happened, that's a red flag.
Divorce is final and my ex is still on the mortgage. How do I get them off?

A divorce decree doesn't remove anyone from a mortgage, because only the lender can do that. Usually the person keeping the house has to refinance into their own name, or the home has to be sold. Some lenders allow an assumption or release, so ask your servicer. Coordinate with your divorce attorney so the refinance timing matches what the decree requires, and until it's done, both of you are legally on the hook.
can i use a 0% balance transfer card to buy stocks and pocket the gains

Technically yes, but it's a risky way to borrow to invest. If the market falls during the promo period, you still owe the full amount, plus the transfer fee, which is usually 3 to 5%. Once the promo ends, the rate often jumps above 20%. Stocks can easily drop more than that over 12 to 18 months. Invest money you already have, not borrowed money with a deadline.
Got a $15k bonus-ish windfall from a lawsuit settlement. Crypto or index funds? Need an answer fast, market's moving.

Urgency is the enemy here, because no market move is worth making a rushed decision with a lump sum. Index funds are the sounder core choice, and if you want crypto at all, keep it to a small amount you could watch drop 70% without flinching. Also check whether any part of the settlement is taxable before you invest it, so you aren't caught short in April.
Thinking of using my 401k to pay off my $20k in student loans all at once. Freedom!

I'd strongly advise against it. Withdrawing early usually means income tax plus a 10% penalty, so you could lose a third or more of the money, and you also give up years of compound growth. Unless your loans carry a very high rate, a structured repayment plan with extra payments will get you to freedom without gutting your retirement. If the payments are what's crushing you, an income-driven plan is a far cheaper fix.
do i need a credit score if i plan to pay cash for everything forever

You can live without credit, but a score affects more than borrowing. Landlords, insurers, utilities and sometimes employers check credit, and a thin file can mean higher deposits, worse insurance rates, or a harder time renting. A single no-fee card used for one small bill on autopay costs you nothing and keeps a strong score ready for emergencies. You can stay cash-first in every way that matters and still keep that option open.
Is VOO or VTI better?

Both are excellent, ultra-cheap Vanguard funds, so you can't go badly wrong with either. VOO tracks the S&P 500 large companies, while VTI covers the whole US market, including mid and small caps, and the two have performed very similarly over time. Pick one, set up automatic contributions, and stop worrying about the difference.
Quick one: is student loan interest tax deductible?

Yes, you can deduct up to $2,500 of student loan interest a year, and you don't need to itemize to claim it. The deduction phases out at higher incomes, and you can't claim it if you file married filing separately. Your servicer sends a Form 1098-E showing the interest you paid, usually once it passes $600, and you can still claim smaller amounts from your own records.
got a $1,200 tax refund. part of me wants to finally treat myself. bad idea?

Not a bad idea if you do it on purpose, so give yourself a set amount, maybe $100 to $200, and enjoy it guilt-free. Put the bulk toward an emergency fund if you don't have one, or toward high-interest debt if you do, because that's what stops the next surprise bill from wrecking you. A split like that keeps you motivated without wasting the windfall.
My parents want me to take private loans for grad school instead of federal Grad PLUS because the rate is lower. Thoughts?

A lower rate is tempting, but federal grad loans come with income-driven repayment, PSLF eligibility, deferment and discharge if you die or become disabled, and private loans usually offer none of that. Grad school outcomes are uncertain, and those protections are valuable insurance if your income comes in lower than expected. Compare the actual rate difference across the whole loan. Lean federal unless you're very confident about your career path and income, and remember that federal borrowing limits for grad school have been changing, so confirm what's currently available for your program.
do index funds pay dividends or do i only make money if i sell

Most stock index funds do pay dividends, typically quarterly, from the companies they hold. The S&P 500 has yielded around 1.5 percent recently. You can set them to automatically reinvest, which is what most long-term investors do to keep compounding. Your other gain comes from the share price rising over time, which you realize when you eventually sell.
Is an SBA 7(a) loan worth the paperwork or should I go with an online lender that approves in 24 hours?

If you can wait a few weeks, the SBA 7(a) is almost always the better deal, with rates usually several points lower and terms up to 10 years for working capital. Fast online lenders charge for speed, often with effective APRs of 30% to 60% or higher and daily or weekly repayments that strain cash flow. Use a quick lender only for a short, specific gap where you know exactly how you'll pay it back, and read the true APR before you sign.
I'm 61 and terrified after watching my individual stocks drop 30% this year. Should I sell everything and go to cash?

Hold off on selling everything in a panic, because locking in losses at the bottom is one of the most expensive mistakes people make near retirement. A 30% drop does show your portfolio is too concentrated and too risky for your age, though. A gradual move into diversified index funds and some bonds makes sense. Since retirement is close, this is a good time to sit down with a fee-only fiduciary advisor who can build a plan around when you'll actually need the money.
index funds or stocks. one sentence answer.
Index funds for nearly all of your money, because they're cheap and diversified and they beat most stock pickers over time, with individual stocks only as a small side bet if you want one.
My wife wants index funds, I want to pick tech stocks. We're fighting about it. 31 and 29, $60k to invest.

A compromise that works for many couples is to put most of the money, say 85 to 90 percent, in a total market index fund and let you manage a smaller tech portion of $6,000 to $9,000. Agree up front that if your picks trail the index after three years, that money goes into the index too. Your wife's approach is the statistically stronger one, and an index fund already gives you heavy tech exposure through Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia.
is the rule of 55 real

Yes. If you leave your employer in or after the calendar year you turn 55, you can take penalty-free withdrawals from that employer's 401(k) or 403(b), though you still owe income tax. It only applies to the plan at the job you're leaving, not to IRAs or old 401(k)s, so some people roll old plans into their current one before separating, and you should confirm the details with your plan administrator before making that move.
quick q: negotiate over email or phone?

Do the actual conversation by phone or video, because tone builds goodwill and you get immediate signals about their flexibility. Then confirm everything you agreed to in a follow-up email so there's a written record. If you get nervous live, it's fine to send your counter by email first and talk through it afterward. Nothing is final until it's in the written offer.
I'm 55 and nervous. Should I move my 401k entirely to cash until inflation calms down?

Going to all cash usually backfires, because cash is exactly what inflation erodes and it's very hard to time when to get back in. At 55 it does make sense to have a balanced allocation, with a chunk in bonds and stable funds so a downturn doesn't derail you. Rebalancing to a mix that fits your retirement date is better than an all-or-nothing move, and a fee-only fiduciary advisor can help you set that number.
Recruiter keeps asking for my number before they'll tell me the range. How do I dodge this?

Turn the question back to them, with something like "I'd love to understand the budgeted range for this role first so we can see if we're aligned." Many states now require salary ranges in job postings, so it's fair to ask for it. If they truly won't budge, give a researched range with your target near the bottom of it, not a single number. Never anchor low just to keep the process moving.
I'm 67, retired, house paid off. A guy at church says a reverse mortgage is free money. Is it?

It isn't free money. It's a loan against your home that grows over time and usually gets repaid when you sell, move out for good, or pass away, which can leave much less equity for you or your heirs. A reverse mortgage can make sense for some retirees, but the fees are high and the terms are complicated. Federally insured HECM loans require you to meet with a HUD-approved counselor first, and that meeting is worth taking seriously before you sign anything. Bring a family member or a fee-only financial planner who isn't selling you the loan.
A guy messaged me saying I won a foreign lottery and just need to pay a $500 processing fee to release my $1.2 million. Legit?

That's a scam, 100 percent. Real lotteries never ask winners to pay fees upfront, and you can't win a lottery you never entered. Don't send money, gift cards, or personal information, and block the sender. You can report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
Should I take a HELOC on my house to buy bitcoin? Everyone says it's going to a million.

No. Borrowing against your home to buy something that has fallen 70% or more several times puts your house at risk for a speculative bet, and loan payments come due whatever bitcoin does. If you want some crypto exposure, buy a small amount with spare cash you could lose without it hurting you.
My employer has an accidental death policy and a cancer policy option. Worth adding?

Generally skip both. Accidental death only pays if you die in an accident, which is far less likely than dying of illness, so solid term life coverage does the job better. Cancer policies cover just one disease and tend to pay out little relative to premiums. Put that money toward a good disability policy, a bigger emergency fund, or your HSA instead.
Someone texted me about a 'gold-backed' investment paying 18% yearly, insured. Insured by who though?

That's exactly the right question, and the answer is usually nobody real. Investment returns aren't insured the way bank deposits are, so an 'insured 18%' claim is a red flag on its own, especially coming from an unsolicited text. Don't reply or click links, and delete it.
I'm a freelance graphic designer and my income swings a lot month to month. Does that change how much I should save?

Yes, aim higher, typically six to twelve months of essential expenses, because irregular income means a slow stretch and an emergency can hit at the same time. It also helps to pay yourself a steady 'salary' from a separate business account, so good months fill the buffer and lean months draw from it. Don't forget to set aside money for quarterly estimated taxes separately so it never gets confused with your emergency cash.
Is staking basically a free savings account? The APY is way better than my bank.

It isn't a savings account. Your rewards are paid in a token whose price can fall far more than the yield you earn, so 6% APY on a coin that drops 40% still leaves you well down. There are also lockup periods, platform risk, and no FDIC insurance. Staking can make sense for crypto you already plan to hold long term, but money you need to keep safe belongs in a high-yield savings account or Treasury bills.
ARM or fixed? quick answer pls

For most people, fixed, because your payment can never rise. An ARM only makes sense if you're quite sure you'll sell or refinance before the fixed period ends and you could still handle the payment if rates rose to the cap. If you're unsure about either of those, the predictability of a fixed rate is worth paying for.
I'm 25 with $15k in student loans and $3k saved. A guy on YouTube says real estate wholesaling needs no money and I could make $10k per deal. Worth pursuing?

Wholesaling is real, but it's a hard sales job and much harder than YouTube makes it look. Deals are slow and competitive, and some states now regulate or restrict it. Don't buy a pricey mentorship to start: check your state's rules, learn for free, and keep building your savings and paying down the loans while you test whether you can find even one deal.
My grandson wants $10k to invest in crypto, says he'll double it and pay me back. I'm 74 on a fixed income.

Please don't lend this, because crypto can drop sharply and fast, and on a fixed income you can't easily replace $10k. 'I'll double it' is a promise no one can actually make with a volatile investment. Encourage him to start with his own money and small amounts, and if anyone is pressuring you, a trusted family member or financial advisor can help you hold the line.
quick q: crypto as my early retirement fund? yes or no

No as a core holding, and maybe as a small slice. Early retirement depends on assets you can reliably draw from for decades, and crypto's 70 to 80% drawdowns could force you to sell at the worst possible time. If you want exposure, keep it to around 5% or less, money you can afford to lose. Build the actual retirement base on diversified index funds.
Lending dad money to avoid foreclosure. He's 3 months behind. Do it?

Before lending anything, he should contact his mortgage servicer right away to ask about loss mitigation options like a repayment plan, forbearance, or a loan modification. He should also reach out to a HUD-approved housing counselor, which is free. Your money alone may only delay the problem if his income can't cover the payment going forward. If you do help, consider paying the servicer directly as part of a plan that actually fixes the shortfall.
Just inherited 80k. My buddy says I should take 10k to Vegas, play big, and maybe double it. Dumb or nah?

Dumb, honestly. The expected result of betting $10k in a casino is losing a chunk of it, and "maybe double it" is the same coin flip as "maybe lose it." Put the money in a high-yield savings account while you decide, pay off any high-interest debt, and talk to a fee-only planner about investing the rest. If you want a Vegas trip, budget a few hundred for fun and treat it as the cost of entertainment.
Rent is just throwing money away, right? I'm 24 and want to buy ASAP.

Not quite. Rent buys you housing and flexibility, while owning has its own unrecoverable costs like mortgage interest, property taxes, insurance, maintenance and the 6 to 10 percent it can cost to buy and later sell. At 24, buying makes sense mainly if you expect to stay put at least five years and can cover a down payment and closing costs while keeping an emergency fund. If not, renting while you invest the difference is often the stronger move.
A company online says they can cut my debt in half for a fee. Sounds great?

Be very careful, because many debt settlement companies charge hefty fees, tell you to stop paying your creditors, and leave you with damaged credit, late fees and sometimes lawsuits, all with no guaranteed results. It's illegal for them to charge fees before they actually settle a debt, so any upfront fee is a red flag. Start with a nonprofit credit counselor affiliated with the NFCC, who can review your situation for free or cheaply and tell you whether a debt management plan, settlement or even bankruptcy makes sense. Check the company with your state attorney general and the CFPB before handing anyone money.
how do i get rich fast

There's no fast route that doesn't carry a serious risk of getting poorer fast. The approach that actually works is boring: raise your income through skills or a better job, spend less than you earn, and put the difference into low-cost index funds for years. Most of the speed comes from increasing what you earn, not from chasing returns.
I'm 24 and want to open a coffee cart. Should I just max out my credit cards to buy the equipment? I have about 30k in available credit.

I'd avoid that, because card APRs above 20% can sink a small cart before it finds its footing, and missed payments would wreck your credit right when you need it for future financing. Look into a microloan through Kiva, which is interest-free, or the SBA Microloan program, and consider buying used equipment to cut your startup costs. If you do use a card, choose one with a 0% intro APR and have a realistic plan to pay it off before the promo ends.
Someone emailed saying my mortgage servicer changed and I need to wire my payment to a new account. Legit?

Treat it as a likely scam until you verify it. Don't use any phone number or link in that email. Call your current servicer using the number on an old statement or their official website. Real servicing transfers come with written notice from both the old and new servicer, and legitimate servicers almost never ask you to wire money. Wire fraud in real estate is common and very hard to reverse, so slow down.
My mortgage got sold to a new company and they want me to pay through a new link they emailed. Legit?

Be careful, because servicing transfers are a common setup for payment scams. A real transfer comes with written notices from both your old and new servicer, usually around 15 days before the switch. Don't click the emailed link. Call your current servicer at the number on your statement to confirm the transfer, then log in only through the official site.
there's a hard inquiry on my report from a car dealer i never applied with. big deal?

One inquiry only costs a few points, but an unauthorized pull is worth taking seriously because it can mean someone tried to open credit in your name. Contact the dealer and ask why they pulled your credit, then dispute the inquiry with the bureau that shows it. If you can't get a clear answer, check all three reports for other strange activity and consider freezing your credit, which is free at each bureau.
My brother-in-law wants family to invest in his friend's oil well venture, projecting 25% annual returns. Everyone's in. Feel weird saying no.

Feeling pressure because everyone's in is exactly how affinity fraud spreads, and even legitimate private oil and gas deals are high-risk and illiquid, often losing money entirely. Before anything else, ask for the offering documents, check whether the deal is registered or properly filed with the SEC or your state, and have an independent attorney or advisor review it. It's perfectly reasonable to tell family your money is committed elsewhere, and if you do invest, only put in an amount you could lose without it hurting your relationships.
I'm self-employed and my income swings a lot month to month. Is 3 months enough?

Probably not; with variable income, six to twelve months of expenses is a safer target. Calculate based on your bare-bones monthly costs, and remember to keep your tax savings in a separate account so your emergency fund doesn't quietly become your quarterly estimated payment fund. In good months, send a fixed percentage of income to savings before paying yourself, so the strong months cover the lean ones.
I already took two MCAs and now a third company is offering me one to cover the payments. Should I?

Please don't, because stacking MCAs to pay off other MCAs is a debt spiral that sinks a lot of small businesses. Talk to a business attorney or a nonprofit small business counselor now about restructuring or negotiating the existing advances. Some lenders also offer consolidation loans at much lower rates, so it's worth getting an honest look at your numbers this week.
Is $1 million enough to retire early?

It depends almost entirely on what you spend, not the headline number. At a safe early-retirement withdrawal rate of around 3.5%, $1 million supports roughly $35k a year, which is plenty in some places and tight in others, especially once you add health insurance before 65. Track your real annual spending first, then multiply by 25 to 30 to get a target that fits your life.
my friend makes like $500 a day scalping SPY, he says he'll trade my money for a cut. good?

I'd pass. Handing your money to a friend to trade is risky legally and financially, and claims of steady daily profits are rarely what they seem without audited records. If he loses your money, you have little recourse, and it can damage the friendship too. Keep control of your own funds and invest through a regulated account in your own name.
best side hustle for fast cash this week, rent is short

Gig apps like DoorDash, Instacart or TaskRabbit are your fastest bet, and most offer instant cash-out for a small fee once you're approved, though approval can take a few days. Selling things you don't need on Facebook Marketplace can bring in cash within a day or two. Also call your landlord now to ask for a short extension, since that often works better than scrambling. Avoid payday loans and cash advance apps if you can, because the fees can trap you in a cycle.
Should I sign up for a buy now pay later plan for groceries? It's interest free.

Using BNPL for groceries is a warning sign that your budget has a gap, and it's easy to stack several plans and lose track of payments, which leads to late fees. It's better to look at SNAP eligibility, food pantries and cheaper staples to close that gap directly. If you do use it once in a pinch, keep it to a single plan and set reminders for every payment date.
pay off loans or invest? 4.5% rate, 24 yo

Do both, in a specific order. First, get any employer 401(k) match, because that's an instant return you can't beat, and build a few months of emergency savings. After that, a 4.5% loan sits in the gray zone where extra payments and investing are both reasonable, so split the extra money if you can't decide. Paying down the loan is a guaranteed 4.5% return, while investing probably earns more over decades but comes with real volatility.
I want to file an insurance claim for a stolen bike but I'll say it was worth more than I paid so I actually get something after the deductible. Everyone does it.

Inflating a claim is insurance fraud, and it can lead to denial, policy cancellation, and even criminal charges, so it's not worth the risk for a bike. Claim the actual value with receipts or comparable listings. If the bike's value barely clears your deductible, consider not filing, since small claims can raise your premiums for years.
What's a good salary range to give when they ask on the first call?

If you can, deflect by asking what range they've budgeted, since many states now require employers to disclose it anyway. If you have to answer, give a range whose bottom end is a number you'd genuinely be happy with, because employers tend to anchor on the low end. Research Levels.fyi, Glassdoor, or BLS data for your title and location first so the range is defensible.
Advisor wants to sell me a variable annuity inside my IRA. 2.5% annual fees. He says it's protection. Should I sign?

I'd hold off. An IRA is already tax-deferred, so the annuity's main tax benefit is wasted, and 2.5% a year in fees can eat a big chunk of your retirement over time, plus these products often carry surrender charges that lock you in for years. Ask him in writing whether he's acting as a fiduciary and how he's paid on this sale, then get a second opinion from a fee-only fiduciary advisor before signing anything.
My insurance denied my MRI as 'not medically necessary.' Do I just pay it?

Don't pay yet, because denials like this are frequently overturned on appeal. Ask your doctor's office to submit a letter of medical necessity or request a peer-to-peer review with the insurer's doctor. File a formal internal appeal before the deadline in your denial letter. If that fails, you generally have the right to an independent external review. Keep copies of everything, and call the provider to ask them to hold the bill while the appeal is pending.
Got an email saying I'm pre-approved for a $250k business grant, just need to pay a $1,500 processing fee. Legit?

That's a scam. Real grants never ask you to pay a fee to receive them, and nobody gets pre-approved for a grant they didn't apply for. Don't send money or personal information, and report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov. To find legitimate grants, check grants.gov, your state's economic development office, and your local Small Business Development Center.
I'm a nurse and a coworker wants me to co-invest in her sports betting syndicate, she claims a 40% annual return with an algorithm. Is it worth a small amount?

I'd pass. Claims of a consistent 40% from a betting algorithm don't hold up, because sportsbooks limit or ban bettors who win steadily, and unregistered 'syndicates' that pool other people's money can be illegal. There's also little you could do if the money disappears. If you have spare cash to grow, a retirement account like a 403(b) with an employer match is a far better 'return'.
ugh just tell me yes or no, is 1% weekly return on a gold trading platform ok
No. That works out to more than 67% a year, and gold doesn't move like that reliably, so the platform is almost certainly a scam. Keep your money out.
I'm 28, single, no kids. My employer keeps pushing life insurance during open enrollment. Do I actually need it?

If nobody depends on your income and you don't have co-signed debt like private student loans, you probably don't need life insurance right now. The free basic coverage most employers include, often one times your salary, is plenty to cover final expenses. Revisit it when you get a partner, a mortgage or kids. That's when term life becomes genuinely important.
My husband died last month and I found a life insurance policy in his papers. I don't know where to start and I'm overwhelmed.

I'm so sorry for your loss, and this part is more manageable than it looks right now. Call the insurance company listed on the policy, tell them you're the beneficiary filing a death claim, and they'll send you a claim form. They'll also need a certified copy of the death certificate, so order several from the funeral home or vital records office because you'll need them elsewhere too. Payouts usually arrive within a few weeks, and there's no rush to decide what to do with the money, so parking it in a high-yield savings account while you grieve is perfectly fine.
I want to withdraw my IRA, hold it 50 days, then put it back. Basically a free short-term loan right?

Technically you can do a 60-day rollover, but it's riskier than it sounds. If you miss the deadline by even a day, the whole amount becomes taxable and possibly penalized, and you're limited to one indirect IRA rollover per 12 months. Any tax withheld also has to be replaced out of pocket to avoid it being taxed. If you need short-term cash, a personal loan or a 401(k) loan is usually a safer route than betting your IRA on a deadline.
is buying weekly calls before earnings a good play

Usually not. Options get pricier before earnings because everyone expects a big move, and right after the announcement that extra value collapses (this is called IV crush). You can be right about the direction and still lose money if the move is smaller than the market priced in. If you want to trade earnings, keep it small and look at how big the expected move is before you buy.
my friend says use a crypto loan instead of selling so i avoid taxes. good idea?

It can work for large, sophisticated holders, but it's risky. If your crypto's price drops, the loan can be margin-called and your coins liquidated automatically, often at the worst moment. Lending platforms have also collapsed and taken customers' collateral with them. If taxes are your concern, talk to a CPA about strategies like spreading sales across tax years, which is usually far safer.
My dad died and left me $600k in his traditional IRA. Can I just cash it out and buy a house?

I'm sorry about your dad. You can cash it out, but the entire withdrawal counts as taxable income in the year you take it, so pulling $600k at once could push you into the top tax bracket and cost you a fortune. As a non-spouse beneficiary you generally have to empty an inherited IRA within 10 years, which lets you spread withdrawals out and keep your tax bill much lower. Please talk to a CPA before touching it, since the rules have quirks, including possible annual withdrawal requirements, and mistakes are expensive.
Should I take out a personal loan to lend my sister money for her business?

No, borrowing to lend means you're on the hook for the payments whether her business succeeds or not, and most new small businesses struggle in their first few years. If she needs startup capital, she should look at SBA microloans, small business lenders, or a solid business plan she can pitch to investors. If you still want to support her, only put in cash you already have and could afford to lose.
My 16 year old wants to start day trading with his savings. Can he even do that? Should I let him?

He can't open his own brokerage account until 18, so it would have to be a custodial account you control, and most brokers don't allow margin or options in those. A better approach is to let him paper trade for a few months to see how he'd really do, and maybe put a small amount, say a few hundred dollars, in a custodial account to buy actual stocks or an index fund. If he has earned income, a custodial Roth IRA is one of the best financial gifts you can give a teenager, and it teaches patience instead of gambling.
The flood insurance quote is $1800/yr and we've lived here 15 years without a flood. Skip it?

Fifteen dry years isn't as reassuring as it feels, because flood maps change and storms are getting more intense. A single flood can cause tens of thousands in damage that homeowners insurance won't cover. Look at your FEMA flood zone and elevation, and get a quote from a private flood insurer as well as NFIP, since private prices can be much lower. If you have a federally backed mortgage in a high-risk zone, you may be required to carry it anyway.
I'm down $14k on calls that expire Friday. I'm thinking of taking a HELOC to average down so I can make it back. Thoughts?

Please don't do this, because borrowing against your house to double down on expiring options turns a painful loss into one that could threaten your home. Options don't recover the way stocks sometimes do; if the move doesn't happen by Friday, the extra money disappears too. Take the loss, step away from trading for a few weeks, and if you feel pulled to chase it back, talk to a fee-only financial planner or a gambling helpline like 1-800-GAMBLER, which handles trading compulsions too.
Thinking about taking a 401k loan to build my emergency fund faster. Thoughts?

That's backwards and risky, because if you leave or lose your job, the loan can come due quickly and turn into taxable income plus penalties if you can't repay it. You'd also be losing market growth on that money. Build the fund the slow way from your paycheck, and temporarily reducing contributions above your employer match is a safer way to free up cash.
My dad is 67 and wants to move half his retirement savings into crypto because he's worried about inflation. How do I talk him out of it?

Point out that crypto has been a poor inflation hedge in practice: in 2022, while inflation ran hot, Bitcoin fell roughly 65%. A drop that size on half his savings, at an age when he has little time to recover, could seriously damage his retirement. Suggest he talk to a fee-only fiduciary advisor about inflation-aware options like TIPS, I bonds, or a diversified stock allocation. If he insists on crypto, a small position of a few percent at most is a far safer compromise.
what's the expected value of a powerball ticket

For a typical $2 Powerball ticket the expected value is well under $2, often around 60 to 90 cents after you factor in taxes, the lump-sum discount, and the chance of splitting the jackpot. Even huge jackpots rarely push it above break-even once those factors are counted. Mathematically, you lose money on every ticket over time.
lender says I'm approved for $650k but I make $140k. that seems like a lot??

Your instinct is right. Lenders approve what they think you can technically repay, not what leaves room for savings, kids, car repairs, or a job loss. A common sanity check is keeping total housing costs, including taxes and insurance, under about 28% of gross income, which for you is roughly $3,300 a month. Build your own budget around your actual take-home pay and treat the approval as a ceiling, not a target.
I'm retired, 74, and my bank's adviser wants me to put $150k into an indexed annuity with a 'bonus' of 10%. Is it a good deal?

That bonus usually comes with long surrender periods, often 7-10 years, and caps that limit how much of the market's gains you actually receive, so it's rarely as generous as it sounds. At 74, tying up $150k for a decade with steep penalties for early withdrawal deserves real scrutiny. Ask for the surrender schedule, the cap and participation rates, and the adviser's commission, all in writing. Then get a second opinion from a fee-only fiduciary who isn't selling you anything.
Theta. What is it. Short answer pls.

Theta is how much value an option loses each day just from time passing, with everything else unchanged. It hurts option buyers and helps sellers, and it speeds up sharply in the final few weeks before expiration. That's why cheap short-dated options so often shrink to zero.
Can I use 529 money for my kid's private elementary school?

Under federal law, yes, up to $10,000 per year per student for K-12 tuition. But not every state follows that rule, and some will claw back the state tax deduction you took if you use the money this way, so check your state plan before withdrawing. Also remember that every dollar spent now is a dollar that won't have years to grow for college.
My employer offers accident insurance, cancer insurance, and hospital indemnity add-ons. Should I get them?

Usually skip them. These narrow policies pay only in specific situations, and as a group they pay out much less than they collect in premiums. A better plan is a solid health plan, an emergency fund big enough to cover your out-of-pocket maximum, and long-term disability coverage. The exception is a high-deductible plan with no savings to cover the deductible, where hospital indemnity can bridge that gap for a while. Even then, putting that money into an HSA is often the better move.
Lost $4k on puts today, my stomach hurts. Should I double down tomorrow to average down?

Take a breath and don't make tomorrow's decision while you feel like this. Averaging down on options is far riskier than averaging down on stock, because time decay works against you and the position can expire worthless. Look at the trade with a clear head: if your original reason for it is broken, accept the loss. If it still holds, there's no need to add more risk. Taking a day off from trading after a big loss is a smart move, not a weak one.
Moving in with my boyfriend. Should we combine car insurance?

Often yes. Many insurers let unmarried partners at the same address share a policy, and multi-car and bundling discounts can save you real money. The tradeoff is that both driving records affect the rate, and if you break up, splitting the policy is a hassle. Get quotes both ways. Either way, tell your insurers you're living together, since they usually expect household drivers to be listed.
I'm 23 with $8k in credit card debt. Should my side hustle money go to debt or investing?

Put it on the debt. Credit cards usually charge 20% or more, so paying them off is a guaranteed return no investment can reliably match. Keep a small cushion of $1,000 or so in savings so a surprise expense doesn't send you back to the cards, then send everything else at the highest-rate card first. If your day job offers a 401(k) match, still contribute enough to get it, since that's free money. Once the cards are clear, switch that side hustle cash to investing.
I keep seeing ads for courses that teach you to make six figures from 'AI side hustles.' Are any of these worth buying?

Most of them are recycled hype whose real business model is selling the course to you, often with fake income screenshots and urgency timers. The genuinely useful skills, like using AI tools for writing, design or automation, can be learned free from YouTube, official tool documentation and practice. If you do pay for something, choose a modest course with a refund policy and real reviews off the seller's site, and ignore anything promising a specific income.
Inflation is eating my savings alive. Should I just pull everything out of the bank and buy gold bars?

Going all-in on gold swaps one risk for another, because gold can sit flat or fall for years and pays no income while it does. A better move is to keep a few months of expenses in a high-yield savings account or money market fund, then put long-term money into a diversified mix like a broad stock index fund plus some inflation-protected bonds. If you want gold, a small slice of 5 to 10 percent through a low-cost ETF is plenty and saves you the storage and resale hassle of physical bars.
Is bankruptcy ever the right call for credit card debt or is it always a disaster?

It's sometimes the right call, especially when your debt is more than about half your yearly income and can't realistically be repaid within five years. Chapter 7 can wipe out credit card debt entirely, and while your credit takes a serious hit, many people rebuild to a decent score within a few years, often faster than they would by struggling with unpayable minimums. Many bankruptcy attorneys offer free consultations, so get a professional opinion before deciding either way.
is it dumb to retire early if i'm single with no kids and no backup

Not dumb, but you do need a sturdier safety net because nobody else is your backup. That means a bigger cash buffer, solid health insurance, a lower withdrawal rate around 3 to 3.5%, and probably umbrella and disability coverage while you're still working. Put estate documents in place, including a healthcare proxy and power of attorney. It's very doable with that extra margin built in.
quick: whats the 401k limit this year

For 2025, you can contribute $23,500 to a 401k. If you're 50 or older, you can add a $7,500 catch-up, and people aged 60 to 63 get a bigger catch-up of $11,250. Employer contributions don't count toward your $23,500.
quick q, do I owe taxes if I traded crypto but didn't cash out to dollars?

In the US, yes. Swapping one crypto for another is a taxable event, so trading ETH for SOL counts as selling ETH at its current value even if dollars never touched your bank. Download the transaction history from every exchange you used, and consider crypto tax software or a CPA if you made a lot of trades. Reporting it correctly now is much cheaper than dealing with the IRS later.
I'm 19 and my dad asked to borrow $2,000 from my college savings. I don't know how to say no.

That money is set aside for your education, and pulling from it could leave you short when tuition or books are due. You can say no respectfully, like 'I need this for school, but I'm happy to help in other ways if I can.' If it's a real emergency for him, a trusted adult or a counselor at your school might help you navigate the conversation.
what withdrawal rate if i retire at 35

For a 50-to-60-year horizon, around 3 to 3.5% is a common conservative target, which means saving about 30 times your annual spending. If you can flex your spending down in bad years or earn some income, you can lean toward the higher end. Starting conservatively is much easier than recovering from running low at 60.
won $2,500 on a scratch-off. do I have to pay taxes on that??

Yes. In the US, gambling winnings are taxable income no matter the size, though the lottery usually only withholds automatically on larger prizes. Set aside roughly 20 to 25 percent to be safe and report it on your return. You can deduct gambling losses only if you itemize and have records, so keep your losing tickets if you buy a lot of them.
Should I consolidate my federal loans?

It depends on what kind of loans you have. Consolidating into a Direct Consolidation Loan makes sense if you have older FFEL or Perkins loans and want PSLF or certain income-driven plans, or if you'd like one payment instead of several. Your rate becomes a weighted average rounded up slightly, so it won't save you interest, and in some cases it can reset your progress toward forgiveness. Check how it would affect your qualifying payment count on studentaid.gov before you apply.
My buddy says I should put my whole IRA into one AI stock because it's about to explode. It's a Roth so gains are tax free. Smart?

Tax-free gains only help if there are gains, and a single stock can drop 70 percent and never recover, which in a Roth means that contribution room is gone forever. Your retirement account should be broadly diversified, like a total market or target-date fund. If you really believe in the stock, cap it at a small slice, say 5 percent, that you could afford to lose entirely.
Can I deduct my gambling losses?

Only if you itemize deductions, and only up to the amount of gambling winnings you report. You can't use losses to create a net loss against other income. Keep detailed records such as dates, amounts, locations, and win/loss statements from casinos. Rules shifted with recent tax law changes, so confirm the current treatment with a tax preparer.
Okay so I'm 52, recently divorced, and every account was in my ex's name. I basically have no credit of my own. Where do I even start at my age?

Age doesn't matter here, and plenty of people rebuild after a divorce, so you're in a solid position to start fresh. Open a secured card or a no-fee starter card from the bank you already use, keep the balance small, and pay it in full every month. A credit-builder loan from a credit union is a good second account that adds an installment loan to your mix. Pull your reports at AnnualCreditReport.com to confirm no joint debts from the marriage are still showing up on yours, and if any are, ask a family law attorney how to get your name removed.
I've lost $11k day trading this year and my wife doesn't know. I think I can win it back by March.

Please stop trading and tell your wife. The plan to win it back by a deadline is the mindset that usually turns an $11k loss into a $30k one, because it pushes you into bigger, riskier bets. Hiding money from a partner tends to do more damage than the loss itself. If the urge to keep trading feels hard to control, gambling support lines like 1-800-GAMBLER in the US handle trading compulsions too, and a couples or financial counselor can help with the conversation.
Wife and I got 200k from her parents. We disagree on what to do. She wants to pay off the house, I want to invest.

Both instincts are reasonable, and the right answer depends partly on your mortgage rate and partly on how much peace of mind matters to you two. If the rate is above roughly 6%, paying it down looks strong; if it's 3 to 4%, investing likely wins mathematically, but owning your home outright has real emotional value. Many couples split it, paying down a chunk while investing the rest after topping up emergency savings. Since it's from her parents, also be aware that inheritances can be considered separate property, which is worth a quick conversation with each other.
Is it true that checking my own credit score lowers it?

No, checking your own score or report is a soft inquiry and has zero effect on your score. Only hard inquiries, which happen when a lender pulls your credit because you applied for a card, loan or mortgage, can knock off a few points. You can check as often as you like through your bank, a card issuer, or a free service, and keeping an eye on it is actually a smart habit.
What's an ARM and should I get one to afford more house?

An adjustable-rate mortgage starts with a fixed rate, often for five or seven years, then resets periodically based on market rates. That means your payment could rise substantially. Using an ARM to stretch into a bigger house is risky, because you're betting that rates fall or your income rises before the reset. If you consider one, make sure you could afford the payment at the loan's maximum rate cap. Most people buying a long-term home are safer with a fixed rate.
I'm 67, living on Social Security, about $1,300 a month. Medications eat a lot. Any help?

Look into Extra Help, the Medicare Part D Low-Income Subsidy, because at that income you may qualify and it can sharply cut your prescription costs. Also contact your State Health Insurance Assistance Program, or SHIP, for free one-on-one help reviewing your plan and checking for a Medicare Savings Program that covers your premiums. Ask your doctor or pharmacist about generics and manufacturer assistance programs too, since these can save hundreds a year.
My deductible is $5000 and I have a weird mole. Should I just wait and see if it goes away to avoid the bill?

Get it checked, and don't let the deductible talk you out of it. Most plans cover preventive visits, and a skin check or a quick dermatologist look often costs far less than you'd fear, especially if you call ahead and ask for the cash or negotiated price. Melanoma caught early is very treatable and much cheaper to deal with than melanoma caught late. If cost is a real barrier, many community health centers and dermatology clinics offer low-cost screening events.
I'm 16, can I trade options?

Not on your own. You need to be 18 to open a brokerage account, and options approval usually takes extra experience on top of that. A custodial account is a great way to start investing now, though custodial accounts generally can't trade options. Use these couple of years to learn with a paper trading account and to build a habit of investing in broad index funds, which will put you way ahead of most adults.
Need cash fast. Is betting my rent money on a sure-thing game tonight a bad idea? The odds are super favorable.

Yes, it's a bad idea. Sure things don't exist in sports, and heavily favored teams lose often enough that the odds pay you very little for taking a huge risk. Losing rent money creates a much bigger problem than the one you're trying to solve. If you're short, call your landlord now about a short delay or a payment plan, and look into local emergency rental assistance, which many cities offer.
renting with a dog is a nightmare, thinking of buying just for that

That's a fair quality-of-life reason, but make sure the finances hold up on their own. Owning also brings repairs, upkeep and less flexibility to move. Plenty of rentals do accept pets, especially single-family homes rented by individual owners, and a pet deposit is far cheaper than closing costs. If you were already planning to stay put for years, though, the dog is a perfectly good tiebreaker.
We found a house we love but the inspection found foundation cracks. Seller says it's cosmetic. We waive and close?

Don't take the seller's word for it, since they have every reason to downplay it, and foundation problems can cost tens of thousands to fix. Get a structural engineer to evaluate the cracks before you close, which usually costs a few hundred dollars and is cheap insurance on a purchase this size. If the engineer finds real issues, use the report to negotiate repairs or a lower price, or walk away if your contract's inspection contingency still lets you.
Heard about something called superfunding a 529. explain quickly

Superfunding lets you contribute up to five years' worth of the annual gift tax exclusion to a 529 in a single year, per child, without using up your lifetime exemption. Married couples can double it. You have to elect it on a gift tax return, and you can't make further tax-free gifts to that child during those five years beyond the excess. It's useful for grandparents or high earners moving money out of their estate, and a tax professional should handle the filing.
Should I take out a loan to buy index funds since the market always goes up long term?

I wouldn't. The market goes up over long periods, but it can drop 30 to 50 percent and stay down for years, and you'd still owe loan payments the whole time. Borrowing turns a temporary paper loss into real financial stress or a forced sale at the worst moment. Invest from your income instead and let consistency do the work.
There's a new coin launching tomorrow, my coworker says it'll 100x. Should I get in early?

Almost every pitch along the lines of 'new coin, get in early, it'll 100x' turns out to be a pump-and-dump or a rug pull, where the insiders sell to latecomers and the price collapses. You'd have no track record to look at, no real liquidity, and nobody to turn to if it disappears. If you're determined to gamble, treat whatever you put in as already gone, but the smart move is to pass.
Hardship program from my card company — what's the catch?

The usual catch is that your card gets frozen or closed while you're in the program, which can lower your credit score a bit because your available credit drops. In exchange you often get a much lower interest rate, sometimes in the single digits, plus reduced payments for six to twelve months, which is usually worth it if you're struggling. Get the terms in writing and confirm whether it gets reported as anything other than paid as agreed.
I'm 67, living on $1,300 social security. Is there anything I'm missing that could help?

Quite possibly, because a lot of seniors on fixed incomes qualify for help they never apply for. Check whether you're eligible for Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help with prescription drug costs, both of which can save hundreds a year, along with SNAP and property tax or utility relief programs in your state. Your local Area Agency on Aging can walk you through all of it for free, and a SHIP counselor can review your Medicare costs specifically. It's worth an hour on the phone, since the savings can be meaningful.
S&P 500 or total market fund, which is better?

They're very similar since the S&P 500 makes up roughly 80 percent of the total US market, and their returns have tracked closely over time. A total market fund adds small and mid-sized companies for slightly broader diversification. Either is a great choice, so pick the one with the lowest fee available in your account.
My aunt left me her IRA. Can I just cash it out?

You can, but the whole amount would be taxed as ordinary income that year, which could push you into a much higher bracket. Most non-spouse heirs can instead spread withdrawals over up to 10 years, and some may have to take yearly minimums depending on her situation. Talk to a CPA before you withdraw anything, because the timing could save you thousands.
My dad wants $15k to put into crypto he says is 'guaranteed' to 10x. He'll pay me back double. Tempting honestly.

Guaranteed 10x is the classic sign of a scam or at best a wild speculation, so I'd say no. There's a real chance the $15k disappears and your dad ends up feeling awful too. It's worth gently asking where he heard about it, because older adults are frequent targets of crypto investment fraud. If someone is pressuring him, you can report it at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
I'm 23, first real job, they offered 52k. Is it rude to negotiate? I don't want them to pull the offer.

It's not rude, and employers rarely pull an offer over a polite, reasonable counter. Many build in some room expecting you to ask. Thank them, say you're excited, and ask whether there's flexibility to get closer to a specific number like $56-57k based on what similar entry-level roles pay locally. If salary truly won't move, ask about a signing bonus, extra PTO or an earlier review date instead.
my credit score dropped 40 points overnight and i didn't do anything?? what happened

A sudden 40-point drop usually means something new hit your report: a late payment, a card reporting a higher balance than usual, a closed account, or occasionally an account you don't recognize. Pull your free reports at annualcreditreport.com and compare them line by line against what you expect. If the cause is a high balance, the score will bounce back once a lower balance reports. If you find an account or inquiry you didn't open, freeze your credit with all three bureaus right away and file a dispute.
My financial advisor wants me to roll my 401k into a variable annuity inside an IRA. Thoughts?

Be skeptical, because variable annuities often carry total fees of 2 to 3 percent a year plus long surrender charges, and an IRA is already tax-deferred, so the annuity's main tax benefit is wasted. These products also tend to pay advisors large commissions. Ask in writing for all fees and whether the advisor is a fiduciary, and get a second opinion from a fee-only planner before signing anything.
avalanche or snowball, which one actually works

Avalanche, which means paying off the highest interest rate first, saves the most money, and it's the better choice if you can stay disciplined. Snowball, which means paying off the smallest balance first, costs a bit more but gives you quick wins that keep a lot of people motivated. The best method is the one you'll actually stick with for the next year or two. If your balances are close in size, go avalanche, and if you have one tiny debt you can kill this month, knocking it out first is a perfectly reasonable compromise.
HELOC for a kitchen remodel or just save up?

Saving is safer, but a HELOC can be reasonable for a remodel that adds real value, as long as you have a firm budget and a plan to repay it quickly. Most HELOCs have variable rates, and your home secures the debt, so you'd be in a bad spot if rates jump or your income drops. Get fixed contractor quotes, borrow only what you need and avoid letting the line become a general spending account.
A guy online says he can get my credit score up 150 points in a week so I qualify for a bigger business loan. Worth $800?

No, that's almost certainly a scam or credit-repair fraud, sometimes involving fake tradelines or disputing accurate information, and lenders can call your loan for misrepresentation if they find out. Real credit improvement comes from paying down balances, fixing genuine errors yourself for free at annualcreditreport.com, and time. In the meantime, apply for a smaller loan you qualify for now, or look at CDFIs, which weigh more than just your score.
What's the PDT rule exactly

The pattern day trader rule is a FINRA rule. It applies when you make four or more day trades within five business days in a margin account and those trades make up more than 6% of your total trades in that period. Once you're flagged, you have to keep at least $25,000 in equity to keep day trading, or your account gets restricted, typically for 90 days. Cash accounts aren't subject to it, but you can only trade with settled funds there.
My wife and I got 100k from her parents. We want a bigger house. Use it as down payment or invest?

It can make sense as a down payment if the bigger house is a real need and your budget can comfortably handle the higher payment, taxes, and upkeep. Make sure you keep a solid emergency fund afterward and that retirement savings are on track, so the house doesn't eat the whole windfall. Since it came from her family, you should also decide together how the money is titled, and an attorney can explain how your state treats inherited money.
Thinking of renting out my spare room on Airbnb. I rent my apartment though.

Check your lease first, because most leases ban subletting or short-term rentals without written landlord permission, and getting caught can mean eviction. Many cities also require short-term rental registration or ban it outright for renters. If your landlord says yes, get it in writing and make sure your renters insurance covers guests, since standard policies often don't. A longer-term roommate, also with permission, is usually lower risk and more stable income.
I'm 19, working retail. Should I take out a personal loan to buy forex trading bots? The seller shows 40% monthly returns.

Don't borrow money for this. A real 40% monthly return would make someone the richest person on earth within a few years, so the seller is either faking results or showing a short lucky streak before the bot blows up. With a loan, you'd lose the money and still owe it with interest. At 19, opening a Roth IRA and putting even small amounts into an index fund will do far more for you.
Saw a TikTok guy saying you can make $10k/month with dropshipping and his course is only $997. Worth it?

The people reliably making money in that setup are usually the ones selling the $997 course, not their students. Dropshipping can work, but margins are thin, ad costs are brutal, and most new stores lose money before they find a product that sells. If you're curious, test it cheaply with free tutorials and a small ad budget you can afford to lose before paying anyone for a course.
Grants vs loans for a minority-owned startup?

Grants are free money but they're competitive, often small and time-consuming to apply for, so they rarely fully fund a launch. Check sources like the Minority Business Development Agency, Amber Grant, Hello Alice and local economic development programs, and pair them with an SBA or CDFI loan for the bulk of your needs. Be wary of any grant that asks you to pay an application fee, since real ones generally don't.
My dad passed and left me his IRA. I'm 45. Do I just withdraw it all? It's $300k.

I'm sorry about your dad. Please don't withdraw it all at once, because a lump sum of a traditional IRA gets taxed as income in one year and could push a big chunk into a high bracket. Most non-spouse heirs now have to empty an inherited IRA within 10 years, and depending on whether he had started his required distributions, you may also need annual withdrawals in the meantime, so spreading it out is usually smarter. Have it retitled as an inherited IRA, not rolled into your own, and sit down with a CPA before taking anything out.
ok whats the minimum number to retire at 40 spending 40k

Plan on about $1.15M to $1.25M, which works out to roughly a 3.25% to 3.5% withdrawal rate, given that your money needs to last 50 years. A lean $1M at 4% could work, but it leaves little cushion for a bad market at the start or rising health care costs. Make sure your $40k includes health insurance and taxes.
Should I use my home equity to lend my brother $30k for his business?

That puts your house on the line for someone else's business, and most new businesses struggle in the first few years. If he can't repay, you still owe the bank, and missed payments can ultimately threaten your home. I'd pass on this. If you want to help, a smaller amount from savings you can afford to lose is far safer, and he should look into SBA loans or other business financing first.
Married, filing jointly vs separately — does it matter for my student loans? I'm on an income driven plan and my wife makes way more than me.

It can matter a lot. On most income-driven plans, filing separately means only your own income is used to calculate your payment, which could cut your payment significantly given your wife's higher income. The trade-off is that filing separately often raises your combined tax bill and costs you some credits and deductions, including the student loan interest deduction. Have a tax professional compare both scenarios, because whether the loan savings beat the extra tax depends on your specific numbers.
