I'm a bartender and I get a lot of cash tips. Honestly, nobody tracks them, so do I really have to report them?

Yes, cash tips are taxable income and you're legally required to report them, even if nobody seems to be tracking. The IRS audits service workers by comparing reported tips to typical tip rates for the business and to the employer's credit card data, and unreported income can bring back taxes, penalties and interest. Keep a simple daily tip log, report the total to your employer as required, and you'll also be building Social Security credits and documented income that helps when you apply for a mortgage or loan.
can i just not report my crypto gains, the irs can't see it right

They can see more than you'd think. US exchanges report to the IRS, the tax return asks directly about digital assets, and blockchain records are permanent and get analyzed. Getting caught means back taxes, penalties, and possibly fraud charges, which is far worse than the tax itself. Report it properly, and if you have unreported past years, a tax professional can help you amend them.
I'm a college student living on loans and a $600/month job. Is it bad to use my loan refund for spring break?

It's a bad trade, because that refund is borrowed money that will accrue interest and could easily cost you far more by the time you repay it. Use it for rent, books and food, and if there's extra, consider returning it to the lender, which reduces your loan balance. A cheap trip paid from your job earnings is fine, but don't finance vacations with debt.
I already lent my brother-in-law $5k six months ago and he hasn't paid anything. My wife doesn't want me to bring it up. What now?

Talk with your wife first and agree on a plan, since this involves her family and your shared money. Then a calm, private conversation with him works better than hints, for example "Can we set up a payment plan for the $5k, even a small amount each month?" If the money is truly needed for your own goals, put whatever you agree on in writing. If it isn't, some couples quietly decide to treat it as a gift and simply not lend again, which can protect the relationship.
I have 6 months saved. Is there such a thing as too much in an emergency fund?

Yes, once you're well past your target, extra cash loses value to inflation compared to investing it. Six months is a healthy amount for most people, so new savings beyond that should usually go to retirement accounts, a brokerage account or other goals. The exceptions are if you're self-employed, a single-income household, in an unstable industry, or saving for a big near-term purchase, and in those cases more cash can make sense.
Can I put my student loan payments on a credit card for the points?

Most federal servicers don't accept credit cards, and lenders that do often charge a fee that wipes out the rewards. Third-party payment services also charge fees that usually cost more than the points are worth. And if you carry that balance even one month, you're swapping a single-digit loan rate for 20%-plus card interest. It's generally not worth it.
Is it dumb to save an emergency fund while I still have credit card debt at 24% APR?

Not dumb at all, but keep it small at first. A starter cushion of around $1,000 keeps a surprise expense from going straight back onto the card and undoing your progress. Once that's in place, throw everything extra at the 24% debt, because paying it off is effectively a guaranteed 24% return. After the card is gone, go back to building the full three-to-six-month fund.
I'm 74 and inherited $90k from my sister. Bank guy wants me in a 10 year annuity. Fine?

Be careful. Locking money up for 10 years at 74 can mean heavy surrender charges if you need it for health care, and bank-sold annuities often pay the seller hefty commissions. Simpler options like CDs, Treasury bills, or a conservative bond fund keep your money safe and available. Ask the banker for the annuity's fees and surrender schedule in writing, and have a fee-only fiduciary review it before you sign.
Online friend I've been talking to for 2 months showed me a crypto platform where she made a lot. She's helping me invest. I've put in $8,000 and it's up 40%. Should I add more?

Stop and don't send anything more. This matches a 'pig butchering' scam: a friendly relationship built over weeks, a private platform, and quick fake gains to get larger deposits. Try withdrawing your money now, and if they ask for fees or taxes first, that confirms it. Report it to the FBI's IC3.gov and your bank right away, and be wary of anyone who later offers to 'recover' your funds for a fee, since that's a second scam.
Honestly how much life insurance do I need? Wife, two kids, I make 85k, mortgage 280k.

A common starting point is 10 to 12 times income, which puts you around $850,000 to $1 million, and when you add up the mortgage payoff, years of income replacement and college goals, that range holds up for your situation. A 20- or 30-year term policy at that size is often surprisingly affordable for a healthy person. Your wife should be covered too, even if she earns less or stays home, because replacing childcare and household work costs real money.
What's the 5% rule people talk about for rent vs buy?

It's a quick rule of thumb from Ben Felix. You multiply the home's price by 5 percent and divide by 12 to estimate the unrecoverable monthly cost of owning. That 5 percent roughly covers property taxes, maintenance and the cost of tying up your capital. If comparable rent is lower than that figure, renting and investing the difference may come out ahead financially. It's a starting point rather than a verdict, so check it against your actual local taxes, rates and plans.
Can I count my Roth IRA as my emergency fund since I can withdraw contributions?

You can treat it as a deep backup, but don't make it your primary fund. You can withdraw contributions without tax or penalty, but you can't put them back beyond the annual limit, so you permanently lose years of tax-free growth. It's also invested, so the value might be down when you need it, so keep real cash in savings first.
ugh my homeowners premium went up 30%. switch?

Shop it, absolutely, because loyalty rarely gets rewarded in insurance and an independent agent can quote several carriers at once. Before you switch, compare coverage line by line, not just price, especially dwelling coverage, replacement cost versus actual cash value, and wind or hail deductibles. Also make sure the new policy starts before the old one ends, since your mortgage lender requires continuous coverage. If rates are up everywhere in your area, raising your deductible may be the best lever left.
Dealer says I'm approved for $520 a month on a 84-month loan for a truck. That's affordable for me, so I should just sign, right?

Don't sign based on the monthly payment alone, because an 84-month term can hide a high price and a lot of interest. Ask for the out-the-door price, the APR and the total amount you'll pay over the life of the loan, then compare that against a 60-month term. Long loans also leave you owing more than the truck is worth for years, which hurts if it's totaled or you need to sell. Get a preapproval from a credit union first so you have a real rate to beat.
I'm 67, retired, and terrified because I got a letter from the IRS saying I owe $3,400. What do I do?

Take a breath. Most IRS letters are routine mismatch notices, and they are often wrong or fixable. Read it carefully, compare it against your return, and check whether it's about something like an unreported 1099-R or Social Security form. Be wary of anyone who calls or emails demanding immediate payment, because the real IRS communicates by mail. If the notice is confusing, a local VITA or Tax Counseling for the Elderly volunteer can help you respond for free before the deadline listed on the letter.
How much should I spend on rent if I make $25k a year?

The usual guideline is no more than 30 percent of gross income, which works out to about $625 a month on $25,000. In many cities that's hard to find, so a lot of people end up going higher, but past 40 percent the rest of the budget gets very fragile. Roommates, a room rental or living a bit farther out with cheap transit are the most common ways to get the number down. Also check whether you qualify for local housing assistance or income-restricted apartments, which can have long waitlists, so it's worth applying early.
Thinking of a HELOC for a kitchen remodel. Any gotchas?

The big one is that most HELOCs have variable rates, so your payment can climb. Payments can also jump when the draw period ends and you have to start repaying principal. Get firm contractor bids before you borrow, and add a 15 to 20 percent cushion for overruns. Compare a fixed-rate home equity loan too, which can be safer for a one-time project like a remodel.
Inflation is eating my savings alive. Should I just move everything into gold before it gets worse?

Gold can be a reasonable slice of a portfolio, but going all-in is a bet, not a hedge, because it can go years with flat or falling prices and pays no income. Keep your emergency fund in cash or a high-yield savings account, and put long-term money into a diversified mix like broad stock index funds plus inflation-protected bonds. If you want gold exposure, 5 to 10 percent through a low-cost ETF is plenty.
Is it smart to keep my emergency fund in a CD for the higher rate?

Partly, but not all of it. CDs charge early withdrawal penalties, so keep at least one to two months of expenses in a liquid high-yield savings account for immediate needs. If you want a better rate on the rest, a CD ladder with staggered maturities, or no-penalty CDs, gives you some extra yield while keeping money accessible.
recruiter wants my current salary. do i have to tell them

No, and in a growing number of states and cities it's illegal for employers to even ask, so check your local rules. A clean deflection works well: say you'd rather focus on the market value of this role and ask what budget they have in mind. If they push, give the range you're targeting for the new job instead of your current pay.
My emergency fund is at $40k, way more than 6 months. Is that too much?

Probably, if your job is stable, because cash beyond your real needs loses ground to inflation over the years. Work out six months of essential expenses, keep that plus a buffer for known big costs like a car replacement, and invest the rest in retirement accounts or a diversified index fund. If you're near retirement, self-employed or feel much calmer with extra cash, holding more is a reasonable choice, not a mistake.
Signed the offer last week, now I realize I undersold myself. Can I renegotiate before I start?

Reopening a signed offer is risky and usually goes badly, so I'd generally let it stand unless something material changed, like the job duties expanding. The better play is to excel early, document your wins, and ask your manager about an early compensation review around six months in. You'll have real leverage then instead of pure regret.
29 y/o, I make 140k, how much should I be saving to retire by 45?

Retiring in 16 years usually takes a savings rate of 45 to 55% of take-home pay, depending on your spending and market returns. The core math is simple: aim for about 25 to 30 times your expected annual spending, then work backward from there. Max your 401k and IRA first for the tax benefits, then use a taxable brokerage account for the money you'll need before 59½. Your spending matters as much as your income, because it sets both how fast you save and how much you need.
I keep borrowing from my 401k to cover gambling losses. I'm in too deep. please help

Reaching out is a real first step, and you can stop this before it gets worse. Call 1-800-GAMBLER today. It's free, confidential and open 24/7, and they can connect you with counseling and with Gamblers Anonymous meetings near you. Ask your plan administrator to block further loans if they can, or lower your access, and look into self-exclusion from the casinos and apps you use. A nonprofit credit counselor can help with the money side once the gambling itself is getting addressed.
just tell me which single stock will make me the most money this year

Nobody can reliably tell you that, and anyone who claims they can is guessing or selling something. Even the best-known winners have dropped 30 to 50 percent in a single year without warning. If you want growth with much less chance of a nasty surprise, a low-cost total market index fund is the boring answer that actually works.
Friend wants me to join a 'gifting circle' where you put in $5k and get $40k back once you move up to the center. Everyone says it works.

Gifting circles are pyramid schemes, plain and simple; the $40k only exists if eight new people each put in $5k below you, and the math runs out fast, so most participants lose their money. They're illegal in most states, and people who received payouts have been forced to return them or faced charges. Pass on it, and if you care about your friend, gently let them know you've read these always collapse.
Got laid off yesterday. I have about 4 months saved. What do I do with it now?

Sorry, that's a rough hit, but four months is a real cushion and this is exactly what it's for. File for unemployment benefits right away, then cut your spending to essentials so the money lasts six months or more instead of four. Look into health coverage options such as COBRA or a marketplace plan, since a special enrollment period opens after job loss, and avoid tapping retirement accounts unless you truly run out of other options.
Is revenue-based financing a good idea for an ecommerce brand?

It can be a good fit, since you repay a fixed percentage of revenue, so payments drop in slow months and you don't give up equity. The total cost is often high, typically a 1.1x to 1.5x repayment cap, which works out to a steep effective rate if you pay it back quickly, so it makes the most sense for spending with a clear, fast return, like inventory you know will sell. Model the cost against a bank line of credit before you decide.
I'm 24, just started working, and my parents asked for a $2,000 loan. I only have $3,500 saved. Ugh.

That would leave you with very little cushion, and at 24 your emergency fund is what keeps a car repair or job loss from turning into credit card debt. It's okay to offer less, maybe $500 to $1,000, and be honest that you're still building a safety net. If you do lend, agree on a repayment timeline up front. Helping family matters, but not at the cost of putting yourself one bad month away from trouble.
Is it cool to deduct my whole apartment rent since I work from home sometimes?

No. The home office deduction only covers a space used regularly and exclusively for business, so a laptop at the kitchen table doesn't qualify. W-2 employees can't take it at all under current federal rules, and only self-employed people can claim it. If you're self-employed with a dedicated room, you can deduct that room's share of rent, or use the simplified method of $5 per square foot up to 300 square feet.
Won $10k on a sports parlay! Should I reinvest it all into more bets since I'm clearly good at this?

Congrats, but a single parlay win is mostly luck, since parlays have some of the worst odds in sports betting, and rolling it all back in is how most people give it back. Set aside money for taxes first, since gambling winnings are taxable, and then put most of the rest toward something lasting, like debt payoff, an emergency fund or an index fund. If you want to keep betting, carve off a small, fixed amount and treat the rest as off-limits.
I drive for DoorDash on weekends and made about $6,000 last year. Do I actually have to report that if they didn't send me a 1099?

Yes, you have to report it. All self-employment income is taxable whether or not you get a form, and once your net earnings hit $400 you owe self-employment tax too. The upside is that you can deduct business mileage, which for delivery driving often cuts your taxable income a lot, so pull your mileage from the app or your own log. Report it on Schedule C, and set aside about 25 to 30 percent of future earnings so April doesn't sting.
Ugh. Missed my car payment by 10 days. What happens now??

Pay it as soon as you can. Most lenders don't report a payment to the credit bureaus until it's 30 days late, so you probably haven't damaged your credit yet, though you may owe a late fee. Call the lender, explain what happened and ask whether they'll waive the fee, especially if you have a good payment history. Then set up autopay so it doesn't happen again.
I'm 19 and want to get rich quick. Options trading looks like the move. Good idea?

As a way to get rich quick, no, because most beginner options traders lose money, and leverage makes losses fast. Your huge advantage at 19 is time: steady investing in a low-cost index fund can grow massively over the decades ahead. If you're curious about options, paper trade first and only use a small amount you'd be fine losing entirely.
I'm 45, self-employed graphic designer. What retirement account should I use?

A Solo 401k or a SEP IRA are your main options. A SEP is simpler to set up, while a Solo 401k usually lets you put away more at moderate income levels because you can contribute both as employee and employer, and many offer a Roth option. At 45 with no employer plan, getting one of these open soon matters more than picking perfectly, and a CPA can help you calculate your exact maximum.
Are private credit funds a good idea for regular investors now? Brokers keep pitching 10% yields.

They can be legitimate, but that 10% is paying you for real risks: loans to smaller, more leveraged companies, limited ability to get your money out, and fees that are often well above an index fund's. Many of these funds cap withdrawals each quarter, so you might not be able to get out when you want to. For most regular investors, keeping it to a modest slice, if any, makes sense. Read the redemption terms carefully before buying.
Someone I met on a dating app is teaching me to trade crypto on a platform they recommended. I've made 40% in two weeks but they want me to deposit more before I can withdraw. Is this normal?

It isn't normal, and it's exactly how the scam called pig butchering works. The platform is fake, the gains on your screen are invented, and the withdrawal fee or extra deposit is how they take more money from you. Stop depositing right away, stop talking to this person, and report it to the FBI's IC3 site and your bank, and watch out for anyone who later offers to recover your money for a fee, because that's a second scam.
My 16 year old got her first job at a grocery store this summer. Does she need to file taxes?

She may not be required to if her earnings stay under the standard deduction for dependents, but she should probably file anyway. Grocery jobs usually withhold federal and sometimes state income tax, and filing is the only way to get that money back as a refund. The return will be very simple and can often be done for free through IRS Free File. It's also a great first lesson in how taxes work.
I live in NY but my company is remote. If I say I moved to Florida can I skip state tax?

Only if you actually move. New York is aggressive about residency audits, and it checks things like where you spend days, your driver's license, voter registration, and even phone and credit card records. If you genuinely relocate and cut ties, you can absolutely stop paying NY income tax. Claiming Florida while living in Brooklyn is a fast route to back taxes, penalties, and interest. If you're seriously considering it, a tax pro can walk you through properly breaking domicile.
Payday loan place says I can get $500 today. Rent is due Friday and I'm short. Just tell me if it's fine for one time.

I'd avoid it if there's any other option, because payday loans often carry effective annual rates of 300 percent or more, and the 'one time' frequently turns into rolling it over again and again. Call your landlord today, explain the situation and ask for a partial payment now with the rest in a week or two, since many landlords would rather do that than start an eviction. Also call 211 for emergency rental assistance, and ask your employer about a paycheck advance. If you're a credit union member, ask about small-dollar emergency loans, which cost far less.
my mom offered to loan me 25k for my salon. we're close so do we even need paperwork?

Yes, put it in writing, because paperwork is what protects a close relationship when money gets tight. A simple promissory note covering the amount, interest rate, repayment schedule and what happens if the salon struggles keeps expectations clear for both of you. For a loan this size she should charge at least the IRS applicable federal rate to avoid gift tax complications, and a quick consult with an accountant can confirm the details. Also be honest with yourself about whether she can afford to lose it, because new salons sometimes don't make it.
I'm 67 and living on $1,500 Social Security. Food prices are killing me. Any ideas?

Check whether you qualify for SNAP, since many seniors don't apply and the benefit can be meaningful, and your local Area Agency on Aging can help you apply and point you to senior meal programs and food pantries. Many areas also run a Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program and offer congregate or home-delivered meals for older adults. On the shopping side, store brands, buying staples like rice, beans and oats in bulk, and planning meals around weekly sales can cut your bill noticeably.
What's the difference between a Bitcoin ETF and buying actual Bitcoin?

A spot Bitcoin ETF lets you hold Bitcoin price exposure in a normal brokerage or retirement account. The fund handles custody, so you don't manage keys or deal with exchanges, though you pay a small annual fee. Buying actual Bitcoin means you can self-custody and move it freely, but securing it is your responsibility. For most people who just want a little exposure, the ETF is simpler and safer.
Market's crashing. Should I move everything in my 401k to cash until it recovers?

Selling in a crash usually locks in the loss, and most people who do it miss the recovery because the best days tend to come right after the worst ones. If you're years from retirement, keep contributing, since you're now buying shares on sale. If you're within a few years of retiring and the drop truly threatens your plans, the fix is a deliberate shift to a more conservative allocation, ideally after talking with a fiduciary advisor, not a panic move to cash.
do i need disability insurance if i have a desk job

Probably yes, because desk workers get disabled too. Most long-term disability comes from illness like cancer, back problems or mental health conditions, not accidents. Your income is likely your biggest asset, and if you couldn't work for a year or more, savings run out fast. Check whether your employer offers long-term disability, since group coverage is often cheap or free. If it doesn't, or if it only replaces around 60% of your base pay, look at an individual own-occupation policy.
is it smart to have the cheapest possible deductible on everything

Usually not. Low deductibles mean higher premiums, and over time you often pay more in premiums than you'd ever save on small claims. A better approach for most people is to pick deductibles you could comfortably cover from your emergency fund, like $1,000, and pocket the premium savings. Insurance works best for big losses you can't absorb, not small ones you can. The exception is if you truly don't have savings yet, in which case a lower deductible makes sense until you build a cushion.
Wife and I want to start a weekend food truck. We'd need about $60k. We have $70k in our emergency fund + savings. Thoughts?

Don't drain your safety net for this. Food trucks have high failure rates, surprise repair costs and permitting headaches, and you'd be left with almost no cushion if a job loss or medical bill hit at the same time. A safer path is to test demand by catering events or renting a commissary kitchen for a few pop-ups first. If it works, look at buying a used truck or an SBA microloan so you keep at least six months of expenses untouched. Talking to a small business advisor through SCORE, which is free, would be a smart move too.
My step-dad wants me to lend him money for a 'sure thing' investment a guy at church told him about. Red flag?

Yes, 'sure thing' plus a personal connection is the classic setup for affinity fraud, where scammers target close-knit communities. Before anyone puts in money, he should check whether the person and investment are registered using FINRA BrokerCheck or the SEC's search tools. I'd politely decline to lend and encourage him to have a fee-only advisor look at it.
quick q: index fund expense ratio of 0.5%, is that high?

Yes, that's high for an index fund. Broad market index funds from Vanguard, Fidelity, Schwab and iShares usually charge between 0.00% and 0.10%. Over 30 years, an extra 0.4% a year can cost you tens of thousands of dollars. Check whether your account offers a cheaper fund that tracks the same index.
can i just pull all my equity out to buy crypto? house is worth way more than i owe

I'd strongly steer you away from that, because you'd be putting your home on the line for one of the most volatile assets around. If crypto drops 60 percent, which it has done more than once, you still owe the full loan, and your house is the collateral. If you want crypto exposure, use a small slice of money you could afford to lose completely, not borrowed equity.
21, senior year. Is it worth getting a part-time job to pay interest on my unsubsidized loans while in school?

Yes, if you can do it without hurting your grades, because unsubsidized interest builds up while you're in school and typically gets tacked onto your balance when repayment starts. Even paying $50 to $100 a month toward that interest keeps your balance from growing and can save you real money over a 10-year repayment. Just keep your coursework the priority, since finishing on time is worth far more than the interest.
Coverdell ESA still a thing? worth it over a 529?

It still exists, but it's rarely the better choice today. Contributions are capped at $2,000 per child per year, there are income limits for contributors, and the money generally has to be used by age 30. Its main appeal used to be K-12 expenses and wider investment choices, but 529s now cover some K-12 tuition and offer far higher limits. Most families are better served sticking with a 529.
Should I refinance to a 30 year again? I'm 8 years into my current one.

Resetting to a fresh 30-year can lower your payment, but it can also add years of interest and cost you more overall, even at a lower rate. Look at shorter terms, such as 20 or 15 years, or a lender that offers a custom term that matches the time left on your current loan. Compare the total interest paid under each option, not just the monthly payment.
Our 529 dropped 15% this year and my daughter starts college in 18 months. Should I pull everything out to cash right now?

Don't make a panicked move, but with 18 months to go it is reasonable to make the account more conservative. Shift the money you'll need for freshman and sophomore year into the plan's cash or stable value option, and consider leaving the later years in a balanced allocation so they have time to recover. Selling everything after a drop locks in the loss, so look at what you'll actually need and when before you move anything. If the account is large or you're unsure, a fee-only planner can help you map the withdrawals.
Do lottery pools at work make sense?

They're a fun, low-cost way to play and they do increase your group's odds, though only proportionally to the extra tickets you buy, and you'll split any prize. The real risk is disputes, so put the arrangement in writing: who's in, how much each person paid, who holds the tickets, and how winnings get split. Have the organizer photocopy or photograph every ticket and share it with the group before the drawing. Those few minutes of paperwork prevent the lawsuits that sometimes follow big office wins.
Should I put my whole FIRE portfolio in TQQQ to get there faster? 28yo, 15 year horizon is too long.

No. Leveraged ETFs like TQQQ reset daily, so in choppy or falling markets they can lose far more than three times the index, and in 2022 TQQQ fell roughly 79%. A wipeout like that could set you back a decade rather than saving you five years. Raising your savings rate and holding broad, low-cost index funds is the reliable way to shorten the timeline.
Divorce finalizing. My ex and I are both on the mortgage. Can I just let them keep the house?

You can, but the divorce decree doesn't remove you from the loan. If they stop paying, the lender can still come after you and your credit takes the hit. Make sure the agreement requires them to refinance into their own name, or sell the house, by a specific deadline. Have your divorce attorney write that language in carefully before you sign.
My employer stock is 70% of my 401k. They're doing great so it's fine right?

That's a risky setup, because your paycheck and your savings both depend on one company, and if it stumbles you could lose both at once. Employees at Enron and Lehman learned this painfully. A common guideline is to keep employer stock under 10 percent and move the rest into the plan's broad index or target-date funds, and an advisor can help you handle any vesting or tax wrinkles.
I'm a single mom making 38k. College saving feels impossible. Is there any point?

Yes, and smaller amounts matter more than you might think. At your income your child will likely qualify for significant need-based aid, including Pell Grants, so you don't need a huge fund. Even $10 or $20 a month in a 529 builds a cushion for books, fees, and a laptop, and research suggests kids with any college savings are more likely to attend. Check whether your state offers matching grants or seed deposits for 529s, since many do for lower-income families.
My savings account pays 0.5%. Is that... normal?

No, that's low. Many FDIC-insured high-yield savings accounts at online banks currently pay several times that with no fees and the same insurance protection. Moving your money takes about 15 minutes online, and on a few thousand dollars it's an easy win.
What happens to the 529 if my kid doesn't go to college?

You have several good options. You can change the beneficiary to a sibling, cousin, or even yourself, or hold the money in case they go later, since there's no deadline. Under current rules up to $35,000 can also be rolled into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary if the account has been open at least 15 years and annual contribution limits are respected. If you just withdraw it, you pay income tax plus a 10% penalty only on the earnings, not on your contributions.
My grandma left me $40k and I'm 23. My buddy says just throw it all into Nvidia since AI is the future. Good idea?

Putting an entire inheritance into one stock is how people turn $40k into $15k, no matter how good the story sounds. If you want AI exposure, a broad index fund like a total market or S&P 500 fund already holds Nvidia and hundreds of other companies, so one bad year for a single stock won't wreck you. Set aside an emergency fund first, then invest the rest broadly, and cap any single-stock bets at a small slice you could afford to lose.
is inflation bad for people with debt?

It depends on the type of debt. Fixed-rate debt like a 30-year mortgage at a low rate gets easier to carry, because you repay it with dollars worth less while wages usually rise. Variable-rate debt like credit cards and adjustable loans tends to get more expensive as rates climb with inflation, so pay those off first.
is ethereum a better long term hold than bitcoin

They're different bets. Bitcoin is mostly a store-of-value play, while Ethereum is a platform whose value depends on smart contracts and app usage, so ETH carries more technology and competition risk. Neither is guaranteed to win long term. Many people who hold both keep Bitcoin as the larger position.
Ugh. Just tell me the fastest way to get rid of $7k in card debt.

Stop adding to it, move it to a 0% balance transfer card if you qualify, then cut your budget hard and throw everything extra at it. Selling unused stuff or picking up side shifts for a few months can easily add $300 to $500 a month to your payments. At $800 a month with no interest, you're done in about nine months.
When does refinancing a car loan make sense?

It makes sense when you can get a meaningfully lower rate, usually because your credit improved, rates dropped, or you took dealer financing in a hurry. Check for prepayment penalties and refinance fees first, and keep the remaining term the same or shorter. Stretching the term just to lower the payment can cost you more overall. Credit unions and online lenders are good places to compare quotes, and rate shopping within a couple weeks counts as a single inquiry.
my dad wants to take out a HELOC to buy into a silver mining stock a newsletter is pushing. how do i talk him out of it

Start with the risk to the house, since that's the part that should worry him most. A HELOC puts his home on the line, and small mining stocks promoted by newsletters are classic pump-and-dump candidates; promoters often get paid to hype them. Ask him to look up who paid for the newsletter and what the company actually produces. Suggest you both meet with a fee-only advisor before he borrows a cent, which lets him save face while getting a neutral opinion.
I'm 34 and found out a newer hire with less experience makes $12k more than me. Furious. What now?

Channel that into a calm, data-driven ask, because walking in angry will make it harder to get what you want. You don't need to mention the coworker's salary directly. Request a compensation review and bring market benchmarks plus your accomplishments and tenure. If you suspect the gap is tied to gender, race or another protected trait, document everything and consider talking to an employment attorney, many of whom offer free consultations. Interviewing elsewhere is also a strong way to find out what you're actually worth.
Detailed one: we have $90k saved, $160k income, no debt, want to stay in our city ~10 years. Homes we like are ~$450k. Go or no go?

That's a strong position: $450k is under three times your income, a ten-year horizon gives time to absorb transaction costs, and no debt helps a lot. You could put around $60k to $70k down plus closing costs and still keep roughly $20k as an emergency fund, though you'd want to rebuild that toward six months of expenses fairly quickly. Make sure the full monthly cost, including taxes, insurance and maintenance, stays comfortable alongside your retirement saving, and if it does, this looks like a reasonable go.
Got a letter saying my loan was sold to a new servicer and to send payments to a new address. Scam?

Servicing transfers are normal, but verify before paying. Legitimately, you should get a notice from both your old and new servicer, and there's a 60-day grace period during which a payment sent to the old one can't be treated as late. Call your current servicer at the number on your existing statement, not the number on the letter, to confirm, since fake transfer letters are a real scam.
I keep revenge trading after losses. I know it's dumb. How do I stop?

Set hard rules before you start each day, like a maximum daily loss of 1-2% of your account, after which you close the platform, no exceptions. Some brokers let you set loss limits or lock yourself out, so use them, and keep a journal noting how you felt before every trade, which makes the pattern hard to ignore. If you keep breaking your own rules, take a few weeks fully off, because that's often a sign the trading has become more compulsion than strategy.
should i put 20% down or just 5% and keep cash?

Putting 20% down avoids PMI and lowers your payment, but don't drain your safety net to get there. If 20% would leave you with almost no emergency fund, putting down less and paying PMI is the safer choice. Conventional PMI can be removed once you reach 20% equity. Aim for a down payment that still leaves several months of expenses plus a cushion for repairs.
I refinanced two years ago. Is it too soon to refi again if rates dropped?

There's generally no rule against it once any seasoning period passes, which is often six months to a year. The question is whether the savings beat the new closing costs before you'd move. Watch out for one thing: refinancing into a fresh 30-year loan restarts the clock and can raise your total interest even with a lower rate. Consider a shorter term, or keep paying your old payment amount after you refinance.
how do i get a business loan with no revenue yet

Pre-revenue loans are hard to get, so most lenders will look at your personal credit, savings and a solid business plan. SBA microloans up to $50,000 and CDFIs are your best bets, and many of them include free mentoring. Expect to make a personal guarantee and possibly put in 10% to 20% of your own money. A free SCORE or Small Business Development Center advisor can help you build a plan that lenders take seriously.
how much of my portfolio can I 'play' with in individual stocks without being reckless

A common guideline is 5 to 10 percent, and only after you have an emergency fund, no high-interest debt, and your retirement contributions on track. The test is whether you could lose that entire slice without changing your plans or your sleep. Keep the other 90 percent or more in diversified index funds so your future doesn't depend on your stock picks.
I'm 19 and have no credit at all. Fastest way to build it?

The cleanest start is a secured credit card from a mainstream bank or credit union, where your deposit becomes your limit. Put one small recurring bill on it, like a streaming subscription, and set up autopay for the full statement balance every month so you never pay interest or miss a payment. Being added as an authorized user on a parent's well-managed card can also help quickly. Give it six months to a year of on-time history and you'll typically have a solid score and qualify for a regular card.
honestly just tell me the fastest way to get $50k for my business, I don't care about rates

You should care, because fast money is the most likely to trap you, and a high-rate advance can eat your margins and cash flow for months. Online term loans and SBA Express loans can fund in days to a couple of weeks at far better terms than MCAs. If you have an existing bank relationship, call them today about a line of credit. Speed and sanity aren't mutually exclusive.
is an escrow account mandatory? id rather pay taxes and insurance myself

It depends on the loan. FHA and VA loans generally require escrow, while conventional loans with 20% or more down often let you waive it, sometimes for a small fee or rate bump. Waiving gives you control, but you have to set the money aside reliably, because a missed tax or insurance payment can create serious problems. If you're disciplined and use a dedicated savings account, it's a fine choice.
I'm 24 and my cousin asked me to cosign his apartment lease. It's just a signature right?

It's much more than a signature: as a cosigner you're legally on the hook for the full rent and any damages if he doesn't pay, and missed payments can hit your credit. Landlords can come after you directly without chasing him first. Unless you could comfortably cover his rent for months yourself, it's safer to say no and help him find options like a guarantor service or a cheaper place.
Can I use a martingale system on roulette? Double after every loss, eventually you win.

It feels unbeatable but it isn't. A losing streak of seven or eight spins, which happens more often than people expect, pushes your bet into the thousands or hits the table maximum, and then one wipeout erases all the small wins. The house edge stays the same no matter how you size bets. If you play roulette, use flat small bets and a hard stop amount.
my cousin says if i put $500 into his trading group's signal app i'll make $3k a month guaranteed. is this legit?

No legitimate trading service can guarantee $3,000 a month on $500, and the word "guaranteed" alone is the biggest red flag in finance. Signal groups like this usually make their money from subscription fees or recruiting, not from trading well, and the few that show huge wins are cherry-picking or faking screenshots. Keep your $500, and if your cousin pushes back, ask him for audited results over several years, which he won't have.
What's a realistic high yield I can get right now without much risk?

For genuinely low risk, look at high-yield savings accounts at FDIC-insured banks, money market funds, Treasury bills, and CDs, which have recently paid roughly 4 to 5% depending on rates. I-bonds and short-term Treasury funds are also solid. Anything promising much more than prevailing Treasury yields is taking real risk, whether or not the pitch admits it.
Is now a bad time to invest my inheritance? Market seems high

The market is at a record high a lot of the time, and waiting for a dip usually costs more than it saves. If investing it all at once feels too scary, spread it out in monthly chunks over 6 to 12 months. That way you're investing either way and won't be frozen by regret.
My brother says bitcoin is the only real hedge against inflation and I should put my whole emergency fund in it. Thoughts?

Please don't put your emergency fund in bitcoin. It has fallen 50 percent or more several times, including during periods of high inflation, so it hasn't behaved like a reliable hedge. An emergency fund has one job, which is to be there in full when your car dies or you lose your job, so keep it in a high-yield savings account. If you're curious about crypto, use a small amount of money you could afford to lose entirely.
The finance guy is pushing gap insurance, extended warranty, and paint protection. Need any of it?

Gap insurance is worth having if you're putting little down or taking a long loan, but your own auto insurer or credit union usually sells it for a fraction of the dealer's price. Extended warranties are heavily marked up and often negotiable or skippable, especially on a reliable car. Paint protection is almost pure profit for the dealer, so decline it. Remember that anything rolled into the loan also accrues interest.
I need $5k by Friday for inventory or I lose a big wholesale order. Any fast options that aren't scams?

Ask the wholesale buyer for a deposit or partial upfront payment, which is common for large orders and costs you nothing. Next, try a business credit card or an existing bank line of credit, and consider purchase order financing, which advances funds against confirmed orders. Avoid anyone promising guaranteed approval for an upfront fee, because that's a classic scam.
can a credit card just be my emergency fund? i have a $10k limit

It's a backup, not an emergency fund, because at typical rates of 20 percent or more a $5,000 emergency can cost you over $1,000 a year in interest if you can't pay it off quickly. Card issuers can also lower your limit or close your account, often during recessions when you're most likely to need it. Keep the card for true worst-case gaps and build up real cash savings alongside it.
do i need a written agreement to lend my uncle 2k

Yes, even a short one is worth it, because it prevents the 'I thought you said whenever' problem that ruins a lot of family loans. Write down the amount, the repayment schedule, any interest, and what happens if a payment is missed, then both sign and keep copies. It doesn't need a lawyer at that size, just clarity.
A tax guy in my neighborhood says he can get me a $6,000 refund and he just takes a percentage of it. Sounds good?

That's a major red flag. Preparers who promise a big refund up front and charge a percentage of it are often inflating credits or inventing deductions, and you're the one legally responsible when the IRS claws it back with penalties. A legitimate preparer charges a flat or hourly fee, signs the return with a PTIN, and never has your refund deposited into their own account. If your income is moderate, try IRS Free File or a VITA site for free, trustworthy help.
Got 25k from a settlement. Want to put it all in crypto and 10x it. Which coin?

I'd steer you away from betting the whole thing, because a 10x shot also comes with a real chance of losing most of it, and settlement money is often meant to cover something important. A saner approach is to secure your emergency fund and debts first, invest the bulk in diversified index funds, and cap speculation at maybe 5% of the total, money you could watch go to zero without it hurting. If you still want crypto exposure within that slice, stick to the largest, most established coins rather than chasing small ones promising huge returns.
I received a $200k structured settlement and a company keeps calling offering a lump sum for my payments. Should I take it?

Usually no. These companies typically buy payments at steep discounts, so you could give up a large chunk of what you're owed. Structured settlements are designed to protect you with steady, often tax-free income. If you truly need cash, get quotes from several buyers, have your own attorney review the deal, and remember that a court has to approve the transfer, which is there for your protection.
My dad's asking me to take out a personal loan in my name for him because his credit's bad. I'd do it for him.

It's generous, but you'd be fully responsible for that loan and any missed payments would land on your credit report, not his. His bad credit is a sign the lender sees real risk, and you'd be taking that risk on yourself. If you want to help, consider giving or lending a smaller amount you already have, or helping him talk to a nonprofit credit counselor about his options.
Inflation's high so should I quit contributing to my 401k and just spend the money while it's worth more?

That would likely cost you far more than inflation ever will, especially if you'd be giving up an employer match, which is free money. Retirement investments are exactly the kind of long-term assets that tend to outgrow inflation. If your budget is truly squeezed, at minimum keep contributing enough to get the full match while you trim elsewhere.
In the offer stage they asked for my current salary. I'm way underpaid right now. Do I have to tell them?

In many U.S. states and cities, employers are legally barred from asking about salary history, so check your local rules first. Either way, you can decline politely by saying you'd rather focus on the market value of this role, and then give your target range. Don't inflate your current salary, because it can be verified and a misrepresentation could get the offer withdrawn.
quick q - which state's 529 should i use

Start with your own state's plan if it gives you a tax deduction or credit for contributions, since that's free money. If your state offers no benefit, you can use any state's plan, so shop for low fees and solid index-based portfolios. Utah, Nevada, and New York plans are frequently cited examples. You're not restricted to colleges in that state either.
my credit score is 590, can i still buy a house

You might qualify for an FHA loan, which can go as low as 580 with 3.5 percent down. Expect a higher rate and mortgage insurance, so the loan will cost noticeably more. Spending six to twelve months raising your score first can save you tens of thousands over the life of the loan. Paying down credit card balances and making every payment on time are the fastest levers. A HUD-approved housing counselor can help you build a plan for free or at low cost.
Is it ok to put my lottery winnings in a trust to stay anonymous?

In some states you can claim through a trust or LLC to keep your name out of public records, and it's a smart move if your state allows it. Rules vary a lot, since some states require the winner's name be released no matter what, so talk to an estate attorney in that state before you claim. Do this before you go to the lottery office, because once your name is attached to the claim, it's usually too late.
honestly can i just put my emergency fund in crypto so it grows faster

I'd keep it out of crypto, because an emergency fund's whole job is to be there at full value when something goes wrong, and crypto can drop 30% or more in a week, often right when the broader economy is struggling and layoffs hit. Park it in a high-yield savings account or money market fund instead, where you can earn a decent rate with no risk to the principal. If you want crypto exposure, use money beyond your emergency fund that you could afford to lose.
Is crypto a good way to speed up FIRE? Thinking 50% allocation.

Half your portfolio in an asset that has fallen 70-80% multiple times would mean your retirement date depends on luck. If you want some exposure, keep it to a small slice you could see cut in half without changing your plans, typically around 5% or less. The parts that reliably get people to FIRE are a high savings rate and low-cost diversified index funds.
My buddy says sequence of returns risk is overblown. Is it?

It isn't overblown, and it's one of the biggest risks early retirees face. A crash in the first few years of withdrawals forces you to sell assets at low prices, and the portfolio may never recover even if average returns later look fine. Common defenses are holding two or three years of expenses in cash or bonds, using a bond tent that is more conservative around your retirement date, and being willing to cut spending or earn some income if the market tanks early. Plan for it rather than hoping it doesn't happen.
I'm 22 and just got my first credit card. How do I build a good score fast?

Use the card for one or two small recurring charges, like a streaming subscription, and set up autopay to pay the full statement balance every month. Payment history is the biggest factor in your score, so never missing a payment matters more than anything else you do. Keep the balance reported on your statement low, ideally under 10 percent of your limit, and resist opening a bunch of new cards at once. Time is the one ingredient you can't rush, but with a clean record you can be in the 700s within a year or so.
What counts as an actual emergency? I keep dipping into mine for concerts.

A real emergency is unexpected, necessary and urgent: job loss, medical bills, essential car or home repairs, or emergency travel for family. Concerts, sales and vacations don't qualify, even when they feel urgent. Try opening a separate 'fun money' savings account so those wants have their own home, and your emergency fund stays untouched for actual crises.
I'm so stressed. Rent's due, I've got $200 in the bank, and every month I'm short. How do I possibly save anything?

When you're this tight, the first goal is stability, not a big fund, so start by listing every expense and looking for one or two things to cut or renegotiate, like phone, insurance or subscriptions. Call 211 or check local assistance programs for help with rent or utilities, and ask creditors about hardship plans before you miss payments. Then save even $10 or $20 a week into a separate account, because a small buffer really does cut down the panic over time.
Is it smarter to bring in an investor or take a loan for my landscaping company? Need about $60k for trucks.

For trucks, a loan is almost always the better fit, because equipment and vehicle financing is easy to get when the trucks serve as collateral, and you keep 100% of your company. Investors make more sense for high-growth businesses that can't support debt payments, and giving up equity in a steady landscaping business is an expensive way to buy vehicles. Run the numbers to confirm your monthly revenue comfortably covers the payment even in a slow winter.
Married, my wife stays home with our kids and has no income. Can she even have an IRA?

Yes, through a spousal IRA. If you file jointly and you have enough earned income to cover both contributions, she can contribute up to the normal annual limit in an IRA in her own name. It's a great way to keep her retirement savings on track while she's out of the workforce, and it can be either Roth or traditional.
I'm 67 and retired. Does my credit score even matter anymore?

It still matters more than people expect. Insurers in most states use credit-based scores to price auto and home insurance, and you may need decent credit to rent, downsize, refinance, or co-sign for family. Keeping one or two cards active with small charges you pay in full each month is enough to maintain it. A credit freeze at all three bureaus is also smart protection, since retirees are frequent targets of identity theft.
Estate is still being settled but I'm expecting around $600k. Can I start spending against it now?

Hold off. Estates often take longer and pay out less than expected once debts, taxes, legal fees, or disputes are settled. Borrowing against it with inheritance advance companies is usually very expensive. Wait until the money is actually in your account, and in the meantime, line up a CPA and a fee-only planner so you're ready when it arrives.
is a 9% yield dividend stock a good buy or a trap

It can be either, but a yield that high often means the stock price has fallen because the market expects a dividend cut. Look at the payout ratio and free cash flow: if the company is paying out more than it earns, the dividend is at risk. Don't buy on the yield alone, and keep any single stock to a small slice of your portfolio.
Is it smarter to take the lump sum or annuity if I win the jackpot

It depends on your discipline and on the numbers, so run it by a fee-only financial planner and a tax pro before you claim. The lump sum is smaller but gives you control and the chance to invest. The annuity pays more in total, spreads the taxes out over about 30 years and protects you from blowing it all at once. For many people who've never managed a large sum, the annuity's built-in guardrails are worth more than the higher theoretical return.
Is it smart to refinance every time rates drop a little?

No, because each refinance carries closing costs, often 2 to 5% of the loan, and resets part of your amortization. A drop only pays off if your monthly savings recover those costs well before you plan to sell or refinance again. Run the breakeven math every time, and watch out for no-cost refinances, which usually bury the fees in a higher rate.
Worried. I got a 1099-K from PayPal for $11k but that was mostly friends paying me back for a group trip. Do I owe tax on that??

No, reimbursements from friends aren't income, so you don't owe tax on them, but you shouldn't just ignore the form. Report the 1099-K amount on your return and back out the personal reimbursements so it nets to zero; IRS instructions for Form 1099-K explain how. Gather records like the trip booking, receipts, and payment memos in case the IRS asks. In the future, use the 'friends and family' option for personal transfers so they aren't flagged as sales.
my emergency fund is sitting at 0.01% interest at my big bank. worth moving?

Definitely, because online high-yield savings accounts often pay dramatically more, which can mean hundreds of dollars a year on a decent balance. Just confirm the new bank is FDIC-insured and transfers to your checking within a day or two. The switch takes about 15 minutes.
fastest way to build an emergency fund? i need like $3k in 3 months

That's $1,000 a month, so look at both sides: cut hard on a few big items, like eating out, subscriptions and a lower phone plan, and add income through extra shifts, overtime, selling unused stuff or a short-term gig. Automate a transfer on payday so the money leaves before you can spend it, and put any windfalls such as a tax refund straight in. Skip anything sold as a fast-money scheme, because the legitimate fast route is just aggressive budgeting plus extra work.
My grandson asked for money for crypto, says he'll triple it and pay me back double. I'm 71 and retired.

Please don't lend retirement money for crypto. It can drop sharply in days, and a promise to pay back double is a red flag no matter who makes it. At 71, your savings need to last and you have little time to recover from a loss. If you'd like to help him, a modest gift he can learn on is far safer, and if anyone pressures you, talking it over with a trusted advisor is a good step.
Moved from California to Texas in July. How does that work for taxes?

You'll file a part-year resident California return covering income earned while you lived there, and Texas has no state income tax, so there's nothing to file there. Keep proof of the move date, like your lease, new driver's license and voter registration. California is known for scrutinizing people who leave. Watch for income like bonuses, stock vesting or deferred compensation tied to your California work period, because that can still be taxable there even after you've left.
thinking about using my 401k to fund a sports betting bankroll since I've been on a hot streak

Don't do it, because an early withdrawal hits you with income tax plus a 10% penalty before you place a single bet, and a hot streak in sports betting is almost always short-term variance, not skill. Your retirement money compounds for decades, and losing it to the vig would set you back for years. If betting is fun, cap it at a small monthly amount from your regular budget and leave the 401k alone.
just tell me the fastest way to turn $1000 into $10000 with betting

Realistically, there isn't a reliable one. Any bet with 10x upside, like a long-shot parlay or a single roulette number, will lose your $1,000 most of the time. If you're under financial pressure that makes a shortcut feel necessary, a nonprofit credit counselor can help you find options that don't put the money at risk. Invested steadily, that $1,000 grows slowly but doesn't vanish overnight.
I'm 52 and cosigned my daughter's private loans. She's stopped paying and they're calling me. What do I do?

As cosigner you're legally on the hook, so the late payments are already hurting your credit too. Call the lender now and ask about hardship forbearance, a modified payment plan, or a cosigner release if your daughter can eventually qualify on her own. Have a direct conversation with her about what's going on, and if it starts heading toward collections or a lawsuit, talk to a consumer protection attorney before you agree to any settlement.
34, single, $60k student loans at 6.8%, just inherited $70k. Pay off the loans or invest?

Paying off a 6.8% loan is a guaranteed 6.8% return with zero risk, and that's hard to beat reliably in the market. I'd wipe out the loans, keep the remaining $10k as an emergency fund, and then redirect your old loan payment into investments every month. If your loans have any forgiveness eligibility or special federal protections you'd be giving up, double-check that first.
scam?? 'guaranteed 7% monthly from Amazon store automation, passive income'

Almost certainly a scam. No business can guarantee 7% a month, and the FTC has sued several 'Amazon automation' operations that took large upfront fees while the stores lost money or never launched. Real e-commerce businesses can fail, need active work, and don't come with guarantees. Keep your money, and report any pushy sellers to the FTC.
Debt consolidation loan vs balance transfer, which is better for $15k?

For $15k, a consolidation loan is often more realistic, because balance transfer limits are frequently lower than that and you'd need to pay $1,000+ a month to beat a typical 15 to 18 month promo. A personal loan at, say, 10 to 14% with a fixed three-year term gives you a clear end date. Compare offers with prequalification, which uses a soft pull, and avoid any loan with an origination fee that eats up the savings.
Freelance graphic designer here, income swings wildly month to month. How big should my emergency fund be?

With irregular income, aim for six to twelve months of essential expenses, since a slow quarter is normal for freelancers rather than a true emergency. It also helps to keep a separate buffer account: pay yourself a steady "salary" from it and top it up in good months. Remember to set aside your estimated quarterly taxes in their own account so the emergency fund never ends up covering a tax bill.
My dad passed and left me $200k. I've had gambling problems in the past. I'm scared I'll blow it.

Recognizing that fear is a strong first step, and you can put up guardrails before temptation hits. Ask a fee-only fiduciary advisor to help set up an account with withdrawal restrictions, or a trust with a trusted person as co-signer. Reconnect with Gamblers Anonymous or a counselor now, while things feel stable, and self-exclude from casinos and betting apps. Locking the money down before you feel the urge is what protects it.
How much should I have in an emergency fund if I barely make enough?

Start with a small target of $500, because that covers most minor emergencies like a car repair or a medical copay and keeps you away from high-interest borrowing. Even $10 or $20 a paycheck adds up if you set it to transfer automatically. Once you hit $500, aim for one month of expenses, and work toward three months over time.
I got laid off yesterday. I have about 4 months of savings. What do I do with it right now?

I'm sorry, that's a rough hit, but four months of cushion puts you in a better spot than most people. Apply for unemployment benefits today, since delays cost you money, and switch to a bare-bones budget right away so your savings stretch further. Keep the money in savings rather than paying down debt early, and call your lenders and insurers to ask about hardship options and continuing your health coverage before the deadlines pass.
Someone on Instagram DM'd me offering to flip my $200 into $2000 with 'binary options.' They have tons of testimonials. Real?

It's a scam, and the testimonials are fake or bought; "flip your money" DMs are one of the most common cons on Instagram. Once you send the $200, they'll show fake gains and then ask for more "fees" to release it, and you'll never see any of it. Block and report the account, and never send money to strangers who message you first about investments.
Thinking about doing a cash-out refinance on my house to pay off $30k in credit cards. Rate on the new mortgage would be about 6.5%.

The rate math looks good, but you'd be turning unsecured debt into debt secured by your home, so if things go wrong you could lose the house instead of just your credit score. You'd also pay closing costs, and stretching $30k over 30 years can cost more in total interest than paying it down hard over a few years. It's worth getting a second opinion from a fee-only planner, and only doing it if you've fixed whatever caused the balance to build up in the first place.
What's the best casino game for actually winning money?

None of them favor you over time, but the house edge varies a lot. Blackjack with basic strategy and good rules, craps pass line bets, and baccarat banker bets have some of the lowest edges, often around 1 percent. Slots and keno are usually far worse. Even the best games lose slowly on average, so the smart way to play is with cash you've already set aside as spending money for the night.
inherited 200k, 34, no debt, decent job. lump sum or dollar cost average?

Historically, investing a lump sum all at once beats dollar-cost averaging about two-thirds of the time, simply because markets rise more often than they fall. That said, if a big drop right after investing would make you panic-sell, spreading it over 6 to 12 months is a perfectly reasonable behavioral hedge that costs little. At 34 with no debt, max out your tax-advantaged accounts first, then put the rest in a simple, broadly diversified index portfolio. With a sum this size, a fee-only fiduciary is worth a consult to check taxes and allocation.
Is a prepaid tuition plan a good idea? Locks in today's prices

It can be, but read the fine print. Prepaid plans lock in in-state public tuition, which is great if your child ends up attending one of those schools. The value can shrink if they go private, out of state, or skip college, and some plans have had funding problems or closed to new enrollees. For most families a regular 529 savings plan offers more flexibility. A prepaid plan makes most sense if you're confident about an in-state public school and your state's plan is financially solid.
Can I use a credit card to buy stuff now before prices go up more?

Only if you pay the full balance before interest kicks in. Card interest often runs over 20 percent a year, which dwarfs any savings from beating a price increase. Buying necessities you'd purchase anyway a bit early is fine, but stockpiling on credit you can't clear quickly is a losing trade.
What's the deal with mileage deductions for rideshare

For 2024 the IRS standard mileage rate is 67 cents per mile, and it covers business miles, including the miles you drive while waiting for or heading to a pickup with the app on. That deduction often wipes out a big share of a rideshare driver's taxable income, so tracking matters a lot. Use an automatic tracker or a contemporaneous log, because in an audit the IRS wants records made at the time. The standard rate usually beats deducting actual gas and repairs unless you drive an expensive car or have huge repair bills.
My husband has terrible credit. Will marrying him wreck mine?

No, marriage doesn't merge your credit reports, and his history stays on his file while yours stays on yours. Your credit only gets tied together through joint accounts or if you co-sign for him, so be deliberate about anything you open together. When you apply jointly for a mortgage, lenders look at both scores and his could raise your rate, so it can sometimes make sense to apply in only one name. A good loan officer can run those numbers for you.
student loans in deferment - do they hurt my score?

Deferred loans reported correctly as deferred don't count against you, and they still contribute to your credit history. Log into your servicer and check your credit report to confirm they show as deferred and not delinquent, since servicer errors happen. Also note the deferment end date, because a missed first payment afterward is a common, painful surprise.
My dad died and he had Parent PLUS loans for my college. Do I have to pay them now?

No, and I'm sorry about your dad. Parent PLUS loans are discharged when the parent borrower dies, and you aren't responsible for them. A family member or the estate should send a copy of the death certificate to the loan servicer to start the discharge. Under current federal tax law, the discharged amount generally isn't treated as taxable income either.
My husband wants to cash out his 401k to join a real estate flipping 'mentorship' that costs $25,000. They say we'll make it back on the first deal. I'm scared.

Your instinct is right to slow this down. Cashing out a 401k early usually means income tax plus a 10% penalty, so he could lose a big chunk before spending a dollar, and high-priced flipping mentorships are well known for upselling and overpromising. Before signing anything, sit down together with a fee-only financial planner, and look up the company's complaints and any lawsuits. Legitimate opportunities can survive a couple of weeks of careful checking.
is lean fire a bad idea

It isn't inherently bad, but it has very little margin, so a medical bill, a car repair or a bad market year early on can force you back to work. If you go lean, keep a sizable cash buffer, line up solid health coverage and stay open to earning some income. Many people find a slightly bigger target lets them sleep a lot better.
What withdrawal order should I use: taxable, traditional, or Roth first?

The usual default is taxable first, then traditional, then Roth, but early retirees often do better blending them, converting or withdrawing traditional money up to the top of a low bracket each year. That keeps future required minimum distributions smaller. Because ACA subsidies and capital gains brackets interact, a CPA run-through in your first year usually pays for itself.
Someone on Instagram offered to 'flip' my $1000 into $10,000 with cash app in an hour. They have testimonials.

That's a scam every time. The money-flipping pitch is simple theft: you send the $1,000 and they disappear, or they ask for more 'fees' first. Testimonials like those are fake accounts or stolen screenshots. Block them, and remember that Cash App payments are very hard to reverse.
is it dumb to put my whole tax refund into lottery tickets? jackpot is huge this week

Yes, financially it is. The odds of winning a big jackpot are around one in 300 million, no matter how large the prize is, so the expected return on each ticket is well below what you pay for it. Buying a ticket or two for fun is fine. Putting the whole refund toward debt, savings, or an index fund will actually change your finances.

Detailed question: I'm 45, have $80k in savings, a stable job, no debt besides mortgage. A friend's startup is raising money with a promised 20% annual return paid quarterly for 5 years. They say it's a 'note,' not equity. Is this a reasonable bet with maybe $30k?

A startup promising a fixed 20% a year is a warning sign, because young companies rarely have the cash flow to pay that, and fixed payouts are sometimes funded by the next investors' money. Even if your friend is honest, most startups fail, and as a noteholder you'd get repaid only if there's money left over. Putting $30k, more than a third of your savings, into one private note is far too concentrated. If you still want to support your friend, have an attorney review the note and limit it to something like $5k that you could lose without hurting your plans.
honestly i spend a lot on takeout and i know its bad. how do i stop

Don't try to quit cold turkey, just set a weekly takeout allowance, maybe one or two meals, and pay for it in cash or from a separate account so you can see it run out. Most takeout happens when you're tired with nothing easy at home, so keep a few ten-minute fallback meals around like frozen dumplings, eggs and toast, or pasta with jarred sauce. Delivery apps add fees and markups that can double the cost, so picking up yourself saves real money when you do order. Track it for two weeks and you'll likely be surprised how much the swap frees up.
Is now a good time to buy? Price just dropped 20%.

Nobody can reliably call the bottom. A 20% drop can easily become 50%, or it can bounce tomorrow. If you want exposure, dollar-cost averaging works better than trying to time it: buy a fixed amount every week or month so you average in over time. Keep it to money you won't need for at least several years.
What hidden costs of owning do people forget?

Maintenance is the big one, and a common rule is to budget 1 to 2 percent of the home's value per year, more for older houses. Add property taxes that can rise after reassessment, homeowners insurance, HOA dues, utilities that were included in your rent, and furnishing a bigger space. Big-ticket replacements like a roof or HVAC system can run five figures. Factor all of it into your comparison, not just the mortgage versus rent.
My advisor wants me to buy an annuity to protect against inflation. Is that legit or a rip-off?

It can be either, so the details matter. Many annuities carry high fees and commissions, long surrender periods, and payouts that don't truly adjust for inflation unless you buy an expensive rider. Ask whether your advisor is a fiduciary, what they earn from the sale, and what the total yearly fees are. Before signing anything, getting a second opinion from a fee-only planner who earns no commission is worth it.
Inherited 30k. Pay off my car loan at 6.5% or invest it?

Paying off a 6.5% loan is a guaranteed 6.5% return with zero risk, which is hard to beat once you account for market ups and downs. Before you do, make sure you'll still have three to six months of expenses in savings afterward, because cash protects you better than a paid-off car does in an emergency. If anything is left after that, put it into a broad index fund.
I'm 34, I have zero retirement savings and two kids, 3 and 6. Should I put everything into their college funds first? I feel so guilty.

Put your own retirement first, and let go of the guilt, because this is the order that actually protects your kids. They can borrow for college, get scholarships, or work, but nobody lends money for retirement, and an underfunded retirement can make you a financial burden on them later. Get at least your full employer 401(k) match, build some emergency savings, and then add modest automatic contributions to their 529s. Even $25 a month each is a meaningful start.
Divorcing. Ex keeps the house but my name is still on the mortgage. Is that fine?

It's riskier than it looks. The divorce decree doesn't bind the lender, so if your ex misses payments your credit takes the hit and you can still be pursued for the debt. Ask your attorney to require your ex to refinance into their own name or sell by a firm deadline, and settle this before the divorce is finalized.
I'm 52 and I just found out my ex opened a card in my name years ago and maxed it out. Its in collections now. What do I do

That's identity theft, and you have real protections. Start by filing a report at IdentityTheft.gov, which generates an official affidavit and recovery plan. Next, place a freeze with Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion. Then dispute the account with each bureau and with the collector, including that report, and tell the collector in writing that the debt isn't yours. Because it involves an ex, a consumer attorney consultation is worth it if the collector pushes back, and many offer free initial calls.
I'm retired and on Social Security at 64. Will a part-time consulting gig mess up my benefits?

It might, because if you're under full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above an annual limit, which is about $23,000 in 2025. Those withheld benefits aren't lost forever, since your payment is recalculated upward once you reach full retirement age. Run your numbers with SSA's earnings test calculator or call them directly before signing a contract, and remember that consulting income also comes with self-employment tax.
Can I lie a little about my income on a car loan app? Everyone does it.

Don't. Lying on a loan application is fraud, and lenders often verify income with pay stubs or tax returns. It can lead to denial, an immediate demand to repay the loan, or legal trouble. It also means taking on a payment you can't actually afford, which is how repossessions happen. A cheaper car, a bigger down payment, or a legitimate cosigner are the honest ways to qualify.
Lent my cousin $800 a year ago. Nothing back. How do I bring it up without it being weird?

Keep it short, private and specific. Something like: I wanted to check in on the $800 from last year, could we set up a plan, even $50 a month? Offering a small, concrete payment makes it easy for him to say yes and keeps him from getting defensive. If he dodges again, decide whether $800 is worth more than the relationship. Many people quietly write it off and simply don't lend to that person again.
My bank keeps hitting me with overdraft fees. $35 each, three this month. Help

Call the bank today and ask them to refund the fees, because they often reverse at least one or two, especially if you ask politely. Then opt out of overdraft coverage so a purchase is declined instead of costing you $35. Consider switching to a credit union or an account with no overdraft fees. Turn on low-balance alerts so you get a text before you hit zero.
is it dumb to have like 18 months of expenses in savings? feels safe

It's not dumb if you have very unstable income, a single-income household with kids, or a health condition, but for most people with steady jobs it's more than needed. Cash slowly loses value to inflation, so you might keep six to nine months in savings and invest the rest for long-term goals. If you're holding extra because investing makes you anxious, a fee-only planner can help you find a mix you're comfortable with.
Just tell me yes or no. Buying a house is always a good investment?

No, not always. Homes often appreciate over the long run, but prices can stagnate or fall for years, and once you add interest, taxes, insurance, maintenance and the costs of buying and selling, owning can underperform renting and investing the difference, especially if you move within a few years. It's best thought of as a place to live that can build wealth if you stay long enough and buy within your means, not a guaranteed investment.
college student, part time job, $400 a month left over. emergency fund even worth it?

Absolutely, because even $500 to $1,000 saved covers the most common student emergencies, like a laptop dying, a car repair or a last-minute flight home, without turning to a credit card. Try putting $50 to $100 of that $400 into a separate savings account automatically each month. You'll have a solid cushion within a year and a habit that pays off for decades.
Got a $3,000 tax refund. I'm broke the rest of the year. What should I do with it?

Put at least $1,000 into a separate savings account as an emergency fund, because that one step can keep the next surprise bill off a credit card. Use the next chunk to pay down any high-interest debt, especially payday loans or cards above 20 percent. Keep a small amount, maybe $100 to $200, for something you'll enjoy so you don't feel deprived. If you're current on everything, prepaying a month of rent or a utility can also buy breathing room.
I'm 62 and thinking about pulling $20k from my 401k to wipe out my credit cards. Good idea?

At 62 you avoid the early withdrawal penalty, but the withdrawal is still taxed as ordinary income, so you'd need to pull more than $20k to net $20k and it could bump your tax bracket. You'd also be shrinking retirement money you can't easily replace at this stage. Before doing it, compare it against a 0% balance transfer or a nonprofit debt management plan, and run the numbers with a fee-only financial planner or tax pro, because this decision is hard to undo.
My uncle left me Apple stock worth $150k. Should I sell it all and diversify? Worried about taxes.

Good news: inherited stock usually gets a stepped-up cost basis to its value on the date of death, so selling soon typically triggers little or no capital gains tax. That makes this a great chance to diversify out of a single stock into broad index funds without the usual tax pain. Ask the executor for the date-of-death value and confirm it with your brokerage. If you're sentimental, keeping a small slice of Apple is fine.
What percent of my portfolio is OK to put in individual stocks?

A common rule of thumb is to keep individual stocks under 5 to 10% of your total portfolio, with the rest in diversified index funds.
