No. Keep returns and supporting documents for at least three years, or six if there's any chance you underreported income by a large amount. Hold on to records for anything with a cost basis, like home purchases, improvements and investments, until a few years after you sell. Scan what you keep, shred the rest securely, and hang on to copies of the returns themselves indefinitely because they're small and occasionally handy.
Is coast FIRE a real thing or just a cope

It's real, and the math is simple: once your invested savings can grow to a full retirement number by traditional retirement age without new contributions, you only need to earn enough to cover current expenses. For example, $300k at 35 growing at a conservative 5% real return becomes about $1.2M by 63. The catch is that it depends on your return assumptions and on not dipping into the money, so build in a margin. For many people it's a healthier goal than grinding toward full FIRE.
Can I just tell them I have a competing offer at 95k even though I don't? Everyone bluffs.

Don't invent an offer, because recruiters sometimes ask for details or call the bluff by telling you to take it, and then you've lost leverage and credibility at once. You can get most of the same effect honestly by saying you're actively interviewing and that market data puts the role closer to 95k. If you want real leverage, spend a couple of weeks pursuing actual interviews so any competing offer you mention is one you could accept.
how do I know if a high-yield savings account at 5% is legit or a scam

Check that the bank is FDIC-insured using the FDIC's BankFind tool, or that a credit union is NCUA-insured, and look it up under its exact legal name, since scammers clone real banks' names and websites. Rates around 4-5% have been genuinely available at online banks, so the rate alone isn't a red flag. Be wary if the 'account' is really an app or a crypto product, or if you're asked to wire money instead of making a normal transfer from your bank.
Discord group charges $199/month for day trading signals and shows huge wins. Legit?

Treat it with heavy skepticism. Paid signal groups often show only their winners, can't prove their track record, and sometimes profit from members piling into the same thinly traded stocks they're exiting. Ask yourself why someone with a genuinely profitable edge would sell it for $199 a month. Save the money, or put it toward a reputable book or course with no ongoing upsell.
My plan is to just use my credit card as my emergency fund. Smart, right?

It's riskier than it looks, because card issuers can cut your limit without warning, often during recessions when you're most likely to need it, and carrying a balance at 20%+ interest turns one emergency into a long-term problem. A card works as a short-term bridge while you wait for a transfer to clear, but it shouldn't be the plan itself. Build real cash savings, even slowly, and keep the card as a backup.
I just got 90k and I'm thinking of quitting my job to day trade full time. Good idea?

Research consistently finds that the large majority of day traders lose money, and doing it with your whole cushion and no paycheck adds a lot of pressure. Keep your job and invest most of the 90k in index funds. If you're curious about trading, practice with a small amount, say $2–5k, and track your honest results over a year before even thinking about going full time.
I want to put my entire $40k emergency fund into Nvidia because AI is the future. Talk me out of it or tell me to go for it.

Don't do it. An emergency fund exists for job losses and medical bills, and those tend to show up when markets are falling, so you could be forced to sell a volatile single stock at a 40 or 50 percent loss exactly when you need the cash. Keep that $40k in a high-yield savings account, and if you believe in AI, invest money beyond your safety net in a broad index fund, which already holds Nvidia, plus a small Nvidia position you could stomach losing half of.
Got a $15k bonus-ish windfall from a lawsuit settlement. Is it smart to just pay down my 3% mortgage?

Probably not first. A 3% mortgage is cheap money, and you'd likely do better covering your bases first. Check whether the settlement is taxable, since some are and some aren't, and set aside money for that if needed. Then clear any credit card or car debt, top up your emergency fund, and consider maxing out an IRA. Extra mortgage payments mostly make sense once all of that is handled and you value the peace of mind.
someone online says they can remove all the negative stuff from my credit report for $500. legit?

Almost certainly not. No one can legally remove accurate, timely negative information from your report, and companies that promise to wipe everything clean for an upfront fee are a classic scam pattern. Under federal law, credit repair companies can't even charge you before they've performed the services. You can dispute genuine errors yourself for free directly with Equifax, Experian and TransUnion, which is all a legitimate service would do anyway.
Teacher here, 4 years in, title I school. Is PSLF real or a scam? Everyone says nobody gets it.

It's real. Since the program was overhauled, over a million borrowers have had loans forgiven through PSLF. Teaching full-time at a public school counts as qualifying employment, so you need Direct Loans, an eligible repayment plan such as an income-driven one, and 120 qualifying payments. Certify your employment through the PSLF Help Tool on studentaid.gov every year so your count is tracked as you go. Most of the horror stories came from people with the wrong loan type or plan, which you can check today.
Someone on Instagram is offering to trade forex for me and split profits. They showed screenshots of huge gains. Thoughts?

This is one of the most common scams on Instagram, and screenshots prove nothing because they're trivially faked. The usual pattern is to show fake gains in a dashboard, then demand 'taxes' or 'release fees' when you try to withdraw. Don't send money, don't share account logins, and block and report the account.
what's sequence of returns risk in plain english

It's the danger that the market crashes right after you retire, while you're selling investments to live on. Selling during a downturn locks in losses and leaves less money to recover, so two people with the same average returns can end up in very different places depending on when the bad years hit. Common defenses are keeping one to two years of expenses in cash or bonds and cutting spending during down markets.
My uncle wants me to invest 20k in his friend's real estate fund that pays 15% monthly dividends. Family says it's safe.

Fifteen percent a month is a huge red flag regardless of who vouched for it, and affinity fraud spreads through families and communities precisely because people trust each other. Ask for the fund's SEC registration or offering documents, audited financials, and the name of the custodian holding the money, then look up the people involved on FINRA BrokerCheck and the SEC's site. If they get vague or offended by basic questions, that tells you what you need to know, and it's fine to say no to family on this.
my mom is 72 and keeps getting mail about final expense insurance. should she buy it?

Often these policies cost more in premiums over time than the small benefit they pay, and many guaranteed-issue versions only pay back premiums if she dies in the first two or three years. If she has savings to cover funeral costs, setting aside a dedicated account is usually better. If she does want a policy, compare a few quotes with an independent agent instead of responding to mailers, and watch out for high-pressure pitches aimed at seniors.
I'm 19, working part time at like $900/month and living with my parents. What should I be doing with my money?

You're in a great spot because your expenses are low, so aim to save a big chunk, even 40 to 50% if your parents aren't asking for rent. Build an emergency fund of a few hundred dollars first in a high-yield savings account, then keep growing it toward a few months of expenses for when you move out. If you have earned income and some left over after that, a Roth IRA is a powerful long-term move at your age, but don't lock away money you might need soon.
How long does a late payment stay on your credit?

Up to seven years from the date of the late payment. Its impact shrinks a lot after the first year or two, especially if everything since then has been on time. If it was a one-off and you have an otherwise good history with that lender, send a goodwill letter asking them to remove it, because that sometimes works.
What happens to my 401k when I quit my job?

The money is yours, and your own contributions are always 100% vested, though some of the employer match may be forfeited depending on the vesting schedule. Your usual options are to leave it in the old plan, roll it into your new employer's plan, or roll it into an IRA. Ask for a direct rollover, where the money goes straight from one account to the other, so nothing is withheld for taxes and you don't risk penalties. Avoid cashing it out, because taxes and the 10% penalty take a big bite.
renting at 45 with no house. am i screwed for retirement??

Not at all. Plenty of renters retire comfortably as long as they invest consistently, because the money a homeowner puts into equity can go into retirement accounts instead. The thing to plan for is that rent continues in retirement, so you'll want a bigger nest egg than someone with a paid-off house. A financial planner can run your numbers and tell you how much to save each year to get there.
I'm 19 and want to learn investing by picking stocks. Is that dumb?

It's not dumb at all, and learning early is a great move. A smart way to do it is to put most of your money in an index fund and use a small slice, maybe 10 percent, to pick stocks and learn how companies and markets behave. Track how your picks do against the index over a few years, which is one of the best lessons in investing you can get.
My landlord has insurance so I don't need renters insurance, right?

Your landlord's policy covers the building, not your stuff and not your liability, so if there's a fire or a break-in you'd be replacing everything yourself. Renters insurance usually runs $10 to $25 a month and also covers you if someone gets hurt in your place or you accidentally flood the unit below. It's one of the best-value policies out there, so get it.
So I'm a nurse and work crazy hours, no time to research. A guy offered to manage my $60k with 'monthly income of 2%'. Easier than learning, right?

Easier, yes, but 2% a month is about 27% a year, which no honest manager promises, and handing $60k to someone making that pitch is a big risk. If you want hands-off investing, there are legitimate ways to do it: a target-date index fund, a reputable robo-advisor, or a fee-only fiduciary advisor whose license you've verified on BrokerCheck. Real managers keep your money at a third-party custodian like Schwab or Fidelity, never in their own account.
My son is 14 and I have $0 saved for college. I have $40k I could throw into crypto to try and catch up. Thoughts??

Please don't. With four years left, a crypto crash could wipe out half that money right before tuition is due, and you'd have no time to recover. Put the $40k in a 529 using a fairly conservative mix, and plan to cover the rest with in-state or community college options, scholarships, and federal aid. Running the net price calculator on each school's website will show you what you'd really pay, and it's often a lot less than the sticker price.
I'm 62 and want to retire next year. Should I take Social Security right away or wait?

Claiming at 62 permanently reduces your monthly check, while waiting until 70 increases it substantially, so delaying is often the better deal if you're healthy and can cover expenses from savings in the meantime. If you're married, delaying also boosts the survivor benefit your spouse could receive, which matters a lot. Pull your actual numbers from ssa.gov, and consider a fee-only planner to model it alongside your withdrawals and taxes, because this is one of the biggest financial decisions you'll make.
just inherited 10k. options trading seems like the fastest way to grow it?

Options are also the fastest way to shrink it, and most retail options traders lose money, often all of it. For $10k, a broad index fund in a Roth IRA, if you have earned income, is a far better growth engine over time. If you're curious about options, learn on a paper-trading account before risking real money.
Lease or loan? I drive like 20k miles a year for work.

With 20,000 miles a year, a loan is almost certainly the better choice. Most leases cap you around 10,000 to 15,000 miles, and overage fees of 15 to 25 cents a mile add up fast. Buying lets you drive as much as you need, and the car keeps value as an asset once it's paid off. Pick something reliable and fuel-efficient, and if you're self-employed, ask a tax professional about deducting business mileage.
can i just open like 5 new cards at once to get more available credit and boost my score fast

That tends to backfire in the short term. Five hard inquiries plus five brand-new accounts will lower your average account age and can drop your score noticeably for months. Issuers may also start denying you partway through, since rapid applications look risky. A better move is to ask your current issuers for a credit limit increase, which often uses only a soft pull, or to add one well-chosen card if you genuinely need it.
retiring at 50 how do i handle health insurance till medicare

For most people under 65, the ACA marketplace is the main route, and because subsidies are based on income rather than assets, early retirees who control their taxable income can qualify for large premium credits. That means planning withdrawals carefully, for example drawing from cash or Roth contributions to keep reported income lower. COBRA can cover you for up to 18 months but is usually expensive. Budget $10k-$25k a year for a couple depending on your state and subsidy level, and don't go uninsured to save money, because one hospitalization can undo years of saving.
Can I just buy a bunch of crypto for my son's college fund? He's 4 so lots of time to recover if it crashes.

I'd keep crypto out of the core college fund. Fourteen years sounds long, but a crash right before his freshman year could wipe out money you can't replace on a deadline. A 529 in a diversified, age-based stock and bond portfolio gives you strong long-term growth plus tax-free withdrawals that crypto can't match. If you really want some crypto exposure, cap it at a small slice of your own money that you could afford to lose entirely.
I'm 24, just got my first real job, and I have $3,000 to invest. Should I buy individual stocks or an index fund?

Start with a broad, low-cost index fund like a total US market or S&P 500 fund. At your age the biggest advantage you have is time, and an index fund lets that time work without you having to pick winners, which most professionals fail to do consistently. Before investing, make sure you have a small emergency fund and that you're getting any 401(k) match your employer offers, since that match is an instant return you can't beat anywhere else.
selling my car to put everything into a stock my reddit sub says will 10x after earnings. yolo?

Please don't sell a car you need for a single earnings bet. Hyped stocks often fall after earnings even when the results are good, and a Reddit crowd can't predict that any better than a coin flip. If it goes wrong, you'll have lost the money and your transportation, which could cost you your job. If you want in, use a small amount you can lose without changing your life.
How does a Roth conversion ladder work, quickly?

You convert a chunk of a traditional IRA or 401(k) to a Roth each year and pay ordinary income tax on it, ideally in low-income early retirement years. Each converted amount can be withdrawn penalty-free after five years, so you need about five years of living expenses from other sources, like taxable savings, to bridge the gap. The tax math and timing are easy to get wrong, so it's worth running your plan by a CPA.
How much should I borrow? Want to borrow extra just in case.

Borrow what your plan actually requires plus a reasonable cushion, usually 10% to 20%, not a big extra amount you'll pay interest on while it sits idle. Build a month-by-month cash flow projection so the number comes from real costs rather than guesswork. If you're worried about surprises, an unused line of credit gives you backup without the interest cost of a larger loan.
My employer offers $5,250/year toward student loans. Any catch?

Usually no catch, and it's a great perk. Under current law, employer student loan payments up to $5,250 a year can be tax-free to you, though that cap is shared with any tuition assistance you get from them. Check whether payments go straight to your servicer and whether there's a vesting period or clawback if you leave early. If there is, read the terms before you plan to switch jobs.
Detailed question: I'm 34, $40k salary, $8k credit card debt, and I spend about $150/month on DraftKings. I win sometimes. Am I doing something wrong financially?

Yes. With $8k on credit cards likely charging 20%+ interest, that $150 a month would do far more good going to the debt, which would cut it substantially within a few years. Sports betting loses money for nearly everyone over time, and occasional wins tend to hide the overall trend. Check your total net result in the DraftKings history. If you're down, use that number as your reason to set a deposit limit or pause the app until the cards are clear.
quick q: crypto debit card worth it?

Usually not. Every purchase you make with it can count as a taxable sale of crypto, which creates a record-keeping headache, and the fees and exchange spreads cut into the rewards. A good cashback credit card paid off every month is simpler and often earns more.
I'm 31 and my parents think FIRE is a cult lol. Are they wrong?

The core idea is just saving a high percentage of your income and investing it in low-cost index funds, which is plain sound personal finance. Where it can go wrong is extreme deprivation, quitting before you have real margin, or underestimating healthcare. Treat it as building options, not a vow of poverty.
35, divorced, two kids, renting a 2br. I want stability for them but money is tight. Buy or keep renting?

Stability for your kids is a real and worthy goal, but a house that stretches your budget can actually make life less stable if one repair or job hiccup puts you behind. If money is tight, a longer lease with a reliable landlord can give your family much of the same consistency while you build savings. Look into your state's first-time homebuyer and down payment assistance programs, and consider a free HUD-approved housing counselor who can show you what's realistic and when.
I make decent money ($38k) but always run out before payday. Where's it going??

Pull your last two months of bank and card statements and sort every transaction into categories, because the leak is almost always small recurring stuff like food delivery, subscriptions and convenience purchases. Many people find $300 to $500 a month they didn't realize they were spending. Once you see it, pay bills and savings automatically right after payday. Then give yourself a fixed weekly spending amount for the rest.
should i just lie and say i have another offer for 90k? everyone does it

Don't invent a competing offer, because recruiters sometimes ask for details or call your bluff, and getting caught can cost you the job or your reputation in a small industry. You can still create leverage honestly by saying you're in other conversations if that's true, or by citing market data for the role. A confident ask backed by real numbers works nearly as well without the risk.
My mom wants to give me her savings now as an early inheritance, around $100k. Any downsides?

The main risk is to her. If she needs that money later for long-term care, gifts made within five years can affect Medicaid eligibility, and she gives up her safety net. Taxes are rarely an issue, since gifts over the annual exclusion just mean she files a gift tax return, and real tax is unlikely. Have her talk to an elder law attorney before she transfers anything.
My credit score is 590. Should I try to buy anyway with some kind of special loan?

You may qualify for an FHA loan, but at 590 you'll likely face a higher rate and stricter terms that cost you thousands over the life of the loan. Avoid lenders that promise guaranteed approval or push unusual products. Spending six to twelve months paying everything on time and getting card balances under 30 percent of their limits can move your score meaningfully. A HUD-approved housing counselor can help you build a plan for free or at low cost.
we're in our late 30s, decent income, already maxing 401ks. should we prepay 4 years of tuition at a state school with a prepaid plan?

It can work well if you're confident your child will attend an in-state public school, because the plan locks in today's tuition prices. The risk is that if your child goes out of state, goes private, or skips college, the payout may be limited to your contributions or a value set by a formula, which can be less than a market-invested 529 would have earned. Prepaid plans also often cover only tuition, not housing. Since you're already maxing your retirement accounts, many families in your position use a regular 529 for its flexibility, or split the money between the two.
is staking ETH on coinbase a scam too or is that different

That's different. Staking ETH through a major regulated exchange earns real network rewards, usually a few percent a year, and isn't a scam. You still take on ETH's price swings and some platform and lockup risk, so it isn't a savings account. Treat it as part of your crypto allocation, and only put in money you can afford to see drop sharply.
My uncle wants to invest $40k in my landscaping company. We're family so we don't need a contract, right?

You absolutely need a contract, precisely because it's family, since unclear terms are how relatives end up not speaking at Thanksgiving. Decide whether it's a loan with a repayment schedule and interest rate or equity with a defined ownership percentage, and spell out what happens if the business struggles or sells. Have a small business attorney draft it, which typically costs a few hundred dollars and protects both of you.
just tell me yes or no. 'risk-free arbitrage' fund 15% a year
No. True risk-free arbitrage opportunities get wiped out by big firms in seconds and never deliver 15% a year to retail investors, so that label is a sales line. Walk away.
found a DeFi pool paying 400% APY, too good to be true?

Almost certainly. Yields that high usually come from freshly printed tokens that crash in value, unaudited smart contracts that can be hacked, or outright rug pulls where the developers drain the pool. Sustainable yields in crypto look more like single digits. If you experiment anyway, use only a small amount you can lose and check whether the contract has been audited.
quick q - is 10x leverage on futures dumb for a beginner

Yes, it's dumb for a beginner. At 10x, a 10% move against you wipes out your entire margin, and futures can gap past your stop overnight. Futures can also lose more than the money you put in. If you want to learn futures, start with micro contracts sized so a bad day costs you a small percentage of your account, and paper trade first.
I'm a nurse and I want to threaten to quit unless I get a raise. Good strategy?

Only make that threat if you're truly prepared to leave and ideally already have another offer in hand, because employers sometimes accept a resignation rather than reward an ultimatum. A stronger first move is to bring local pay data for your specialty and shift, plus any certifications or extra duties you've taken on. Nursing demand is high, so a real outside offer is your best leverage if the internal ask fails.
Honestly terrified. I sold naked calls on a meme stock and it's up 60% premarket. What do I do??

Call your broker's trade desk right now. They can tell you your exact margin position and what they'll do at the open, and their margin team may close your position on their terms if you don't act first. Your real choices are to buy back the calls to cap the loss or to cover by buying shares, and with a squeeze underway, waiting and hoping is how a bad loss becomes a catastrophic one. Once you're out, don't sell uncovered calls again. The risk is theoretically unlimited, as you're seeing.
Lump sum or annuity if I win the big jackpot?

Many advisors lean toward the lump sum if you can be disciplined, because you control the money and can invest it, but the annuity protects you from blowing it all and from bad advice, which is a real danger for sudden winners. Before you claim, hire a fee-only financial planner, a tax attorney and a CPA, and check whether your state lets you stay anonymous. Don't make the choice in the first week of excitement.
best way to pay off car loan faster

Make extra payments and tell the lender to apply them to the principal, since some lenders otherwise count them toward future interest or payments. Splitting your payment into biweekly halves adds about one extra payment a year without much pain. Putting windfalls like tax refunds toward the balance also makes a big dent. If your rate is high, refinance first so more of each dollar goes to principal.
I have a collection account from an old medical bill. Should I just pay it?

First check whether it's even accurate, and send the collector a debt validation letter within 30 days of their first contact asking them to prove you owe it. Paid medical collections are now removed from credit reports by the three bureaus, and medical collections under $500 aren't reported at all, so paying can genuinely help. Get any agreement in writing before you send money, and never give a collector direct access to your bank account. If the debt is very old, ask a consumer attorney or legal aid office about your state's statute of limitations before making a payment.
is it dumb to own both an S&P 500 fund and a few big tech stocks

It's not dumb, but be aware you're doubling up, since the biggest tech companies already make up a large chunk of the S&P 500. That means your portfolio is more concentrated in tech than it might look. Keeping those extra stocks to a small slice keeps the overlap from turning into an outsized bet on a single sector.
I'm a freelance graphic designer, first year, and nobody told me about quarterly taxes. It's November. How screwed am I?

Not very screwed, just a little behind. Make an estimated payment now through IRS Direct Pay to cover as much of this year's tax as you can before the January 15 deadline, which will shrink any underpayment penalty, and that penalty is basically just interest. A good rule of thumb is to set aside 25 to 30 percent of each payment going forward. A CPA for your first freelance return can also help you find deductions you'd otherwise miss.
housing market's gonna crash soon right? should I wait to buy

Nobody can reliably time housing crashes, and people have been predicting one for years while prices kept climbing in many markets. A better approach is to buy when your own situation is ready: stable income, a solid down payment, an emergency fund and a plan to stay put for at least five years. If those are in place and the monthly payment is comfortable, a short-term dip matters a lot less because you won't be forced to sell.
Should I just cash out my 401k to wipe out my $15,000 in credit card debt? I'm 34.

Almost certainly not, because at 34 you'd likely owe income tax plus a 10% early withdrawal penalty, so wiping out $15k could easily cost you $20k or more of your retirement money. You'd also lose decades of compound growth on that money, which is the real hidden cost. A balance transfer card, a lower-rate personal loan or a nonprofit debt management plan can cut your interest without raiding your future. Talk to a nonprofit credit counselor first, since an NFCC member agency can review your options for free or very cheaply.
offer is 120k base plus equity at a startup. they say the equity could be worth millions. should i take less base for more equity

Treat startup equity as a lottery ticket that might be worth something, not as guaranteed pay, since most startups never produce a big payout for employees. Make sure the base salary covers your living costs and savings comfortably before trading any of it for shares. Ask for the number of shares, the total shares outstanding, the strike price and the vesting schedule, and if the grant is large it's worth having a tax professional look at it before you sign.
Can I day trade in my Roth IRA to avoid taxes on gains?

Technically yes, since Roth trades don't create taxable events, but it's usually a bad idea. IRAs are cash accounts, so you can't use margin, and settlement rules will limit how quickly you can reuse your money. The bigger problem is that losses inside a Roth can't be deducted, and you can only contribute a limited amount each year. That makes every blown-up dollar of tax-free retirement space permanently gone. Keep the Roth for long-term investing and do any speculation in a small taxable account.
58 and inherited 300k. retirement is behind. should i go aggressive to catch up?

Catching up is the right idea, but going aggressive at 58 can backfire, because a big crash right before retirement leaves little time to recover. A balanced mix of stocks and bonds, perhaps 50 to 60% stocks, gives you meaningful growth with less risk. You should also max out catch-up contributions to your 401k and IRA. With retirement this close, a fee-only fiduciary planner can model when you can actually retire and how to draw the money down.
My uncle offered to lend ME money at 0% to pay off my credit cards. Any downside?

Swapping high-interest card debt for a 0% family loan can save you a lot, so it's worth considering. The main risks are relational. Put the terms in writing and treat the payments as seriously as a bank loan. Most important, don't run the cards back up, because then you'd owe both your uncle and the banks. Consider freezing or closing the cards you don't need once they're paid off.
My uncle wants me to join his business where I recruit others and earn from their investments. Returns are 15% monthly. He's family so I trust him.

Earning money from recruits' investments, plus 15% monthly returns, is the textbook shape of a pyramid or Ponzi scheme, and your uncle may genuinely not realize it. People who recruit friends and family can face lawsuits to claw back what they earned when it collapses, which happens to all of them eventually. I'd skip it and gently encourage him to try withdrawing his own money while he still can.
Zillow says my house went up $80k. Time to pull equity and buy a rental?

Zillow estimates can be off by a lot, so get a real appraisal or comparable sales before planning around that number. Borrowing against your home to buy a rental doubles your exposure to housing. If the rental sits vacant or needs a new roof, you'll be paying two mortgages. If the numbers still work with conservative rent, a vacancy allowance, and reserves, talk to a CPA and a lender before deciding.
where's the best place to keep emergency money

A high-yield savings account at an FDIC-insured bank or NCUA-insured credit union is the best fit for most people, since it pays solid interest, stays liquid and is protected up to $250,000. Keeping it at a different bank from your checking account adds a little friction that makes it less tempting to dip into. Money market accounts work well too.
I'm a single mom and terrified to negotiate. I really need this job. Any script that won't risk it?

Try this: "Thank you so much, I'm really excited to join. Based on my experience and the market for this role, I was hoping we could get closer to $X. Is there any flexibility?" That wording is appreciative and low-risk, and reasonable employers expect it. If they say no, you simply accept, so you lose nothing by asking. Also ask about dependent care FSA, flexible scheduling and health insurance costs for your kids, because those can matter as much as salary.
I'm 58. Refinancing into a new 30-year to lower my payment — bad idea?

Not necessarily, but go in with eyes open. Restarting a 30-year clock means payments into your late 80s and often more total interest, which can strain a retirement budget. One option is to take the 30-year for the lower required payment but pay it like a shorter loan, or compare a 15- or 20-year refinance. Aim to have it paid off by retirement if you can, and check the numbers with a planner.
How much should I risk per trade if I'm day trading a $30k account?

A common guideline is to risk no more than 1% of the account per trade, which is about $300. That means sizing each position so that hitting your stop-loss costs you around that amount. This keeps a string of losses survivable, which matters because even skilled traders hit long losing streaks. Also set a daily loss limit, something like 2 to 3%, and stop for the day once you hit it.
Can I use a cash advance from one card to pay off another?

That's usually a losing move. Cash advances typically come with a 3 to 5% fee, a higher APR than purchases, and interest that starts immediately with no grace period. You'd likely end up paying more, not less. A real balance transfer offer or a personal loan at a lower fixed rate does what you're trying to do without the extra costs.
I'm 58, got laid off, and I need cash. Can I touch my 401k without the penalty?

Possibly yes, through the rule of 55. If you left the employer in or after the calendar year you turned 55, you can take withdrawals from that employer's 401k without the 10% penalty, though income tax still applies. This only works if the money stays in that plan, so don't roll it into an IRA first or you'll lose the exception until age 59½. Withdraw only what you need and set some aside for taxes, and file for unemployment benefits too.
My landlord raised rent 15% citing inflation. Is that even legal?

It depends entirely on your location and lease. Some cities and states have rent control or caps on increases, and many require advance written notice, often 30 to 90 days. Check your lease and your local tenant laws, and a local tenant rights organization or legal aid office can tell you quickly whether the increase is allowed. It's also worth negotiating, since landlords often prefer keeping a reliable tenant over finding a new one.
Our homeowners premium jumped 40% this year. I'm tempted to just cancel since the house is paid off. Thoughts?

I wouldn't cancel. A paid-off house is often your biggest asset, and a fire, tree or liability lawsuit could wipe it out with no way to rebuild. Instead, shop multiple insurers through an independent agent, raise your deductible to something your emergency fund can cover, and ask about discounts for roof upgrades, security systems or bundling. Premiums are rising almost everywhere, so a smaller hike from another company may be the best realistic outcome, but staying insured is the safe call.
Is it better to put a big down payment or keep cash in savings?

Make sure your emergency fund is solid first, ideally three to six months of expenses. Then put down as much as you comfortably can, aiming for at least 10 to 20 percent. A bigger down payment lowers your interest cost and keeps you from owing more than the car is worth. Just don't empty your savings to do it, because a surprise repair or job loss with no cushion is what really hurts.
Someone on Telegram has a forex bot that doubles money monthly. I'd put in 10% of my 200k inheritance as a test. Fine since it's just a test?

Please don't send them anything; a bot that doubles money monthly is a scam, and testing it with $20k just means losing $20k. These schemes often show fake early gains to lure people into depositing more, then make withdrawals impossible. Legitimate investing doesn't happen through strangers on Telegram. Keep your inheritance in a regulated brokerage or bank and report the account to the FTC and the platform.
what about those YouTube 'infinite banking' whole life insurance strategies to get rich

Treat them with real skepticism. Infinite banking is mostly a sales pitch for high-commission whole life policies, and the cash value builds slowly in the early years because of fees. For most people, term life insurance plus investing the difference in retirement accounts comes out ahead. If you're seriously considering it, have a fee-only advisor who earns no commission review the illustration first.
is Uber worth it after gas and wear on the car

Often less than it looks. Once you count gas, extra maintenance, faster depreciation and higher insurance, many drivers net well under minimum wage. Track your real costs for a few weeks and divide your profit by every hour you're logged in, including the waiting. It works best with a fuel-efficient car and when you stick to peak surge times, and check that your personal auto policy covers rideshare or add a rideshare endorsement.
Can I skip the home inspection to make my offer more competitive?

I wouldn't. Skipping an inspection can leave you on the hook for a failing roof, foundation or sewer line that costs tens of thousands to fix. If you need a stronger offer, a common compromise is to get the inspection but agree in advance not to ask for minor repairs, so you can still walk away from a major problem. Your agent can help you structure that.
what credit score do i need to get a good mortgage rate

The best conventional rates usually go to scores around 760 and up, and pricing gets noticeably worse below about 700. FHA loans accept scores in the 500s, though with higher costs. If you're a few months from buying, pay down card balances, avoid new credit, and check your reports for errors at annualcreditreport.com. Even a 20–40 point bump can meaningfully lower your rate.
how do merchant cash advances work, my bakery needs cash quick

An MCA gives you a lump sum in exchange for a cut of your daily card sales until a fixed amount is repaid. The effective annual cost often runs 40 to 150 percent or more, and the daily withdrawals can choke your cash flow. Before taking one, ask your bank about a line of credit, look into an SBA Express loan, or contact a local CDFI, since all of them are usually far cheaper.
How do I stop impulse spending when I'm stressed? I know I do it.

Add some friction, such as deleting saved card info from shopping apps and unsubscribing from store emails. A 48-hour wait rule on anything that isn't essential also helps, because most urges fade. Keep your spending money in a separate account or as cash so you can see when it's gone. If stress spending feels out of control, talking with a counselor can help with the root cause, and some offer sliding-scale fees.
can you recommend a good stop loss % for day trading

There's no universal number. A stop belongs at the price that proves your trade idea wrong, not at an arbitrary percentage. A more useful rule is to size each position so that hitting the stop costs you no more than 1 to 2% of your account. That way a string of losers won't knock you out of the game.
Honestly I don't trust myself with my $130k inheritance. I've blown money before. What would protect me from me?

That self-awareness is a real advantage. Put a cooling-off period between you and the money: invest it in a separate brokerage account with no debit card, and give yourself a 72-hour rule before any withdrawal. Some people go further and use a fee-only advisor or a simple trust so a second person has to sign off on big moves. Leaving yourself a small fun-money allowance also helps, since total deprivation is usually what leads to blowouts.
Should I use my 401k to pay off my mortgage early? I hate debt.

I'd hold off. Withdrawing from a 401(k) usually triggers income tax plus a 10% penalty if you're under 59½, so you could lose a third or more of the money just to wipe out a low-interest, tax-deductible debt. You'd also lose years of tax-advantaged growth. If debt freedom matters to you, make extra payments from your regular income instead, and run big moves past a fee-only planner first.
my wife and I are drowning, 3 months behind on the mortgage. terrified we lose the house. what do we do

Call your loan servicer today and ask about loss mitigation options such as forbearance, a repayment plan, or a loan modification. Servicers generally have to consider these before foreclosing, but you have to ask. Also contact a HUD-approved housing counselor, which is free and can be found at hud.gov or by calling 800-569-4287. They can negotiate with you and help you avoid scams. Be very wary of anyone who charges upfront fees promising to save your home.
My manager said no raise this year due to budget. I'm thinking of just quitting with nothing lined up to make a point.

I'd hold off on quitting without another job, because the gap can drain your savings fast and makes your next negotiation weaker since you're no longer employed. Ask your manager what specific results would earn a raise and when it could be revisited, and get that in writing in an email afterward. Meanwhile start interviewing quietly, since an outside offer is usually the fastest route to a real pay jump.
is VOO better than VTI

They're close enough that either one is a great choice. VOO tracks the S&P 500, which is about 500 large US companies, and VTI tracks the total US market, so it adds small and mid-sized companies on top of those. Both cost about 0.03% a year and have performed nearly the same over long periods. Pick one and stick with it, because consistent contributions matter far more than which of the two you chose.
Picked 5 stocks last year, 3 are down 40%. Do I hold, sell, or double down?

Don't double down just to make the losses feel smaller, because that's how a bad position becomes a disaster. Ask yourself whether you'd buy each stock today at its current price based on the business, not on what you paid for it. If the honest answer is no, selling, possibly harvesting the tax loss, and moving that money into an index fund is a perfectly respectable reset.
how do people even lose crypto? like what are the main ways

The big ones are scams and phishing that trick people into revealing their seed phrase, exchanges that get hacked or go bankrupt, and simple mistakes like losing the recovery phrase or sending coins to the wrong address. Transactions can't be reversed, so a single error is usually permanent. Use reputable platforms, turn on app-based two-factor authentication, keep your seed phrase on paper offline, and send a small test transaction before any large transfer.
I'm 55, got a buyout offer, $1.3M saved. Take it and retire?

It could be a great bridge, especially because leaving at 55 may let you take penalty-free withdrawals from that employer's 401k under the rule of 55, so don't roll it into an IRA without thinking. Calculate the buyout after taxes, your health coverage until Medicare at 65, and when you'll claim Social Security, since delaying to 70 greatly boosts lifetime income. With $1.3M you're probably fine if spending is around $50k to $55k, but a planner review is worth it before signing.
My dad passed and left me his traditional IRA, about $200k. Can I just cash it all out?

You can, but cashing it all out in one year could push a big chunk of it into high tax brackets and cost you tens of thousands. Most non-spouse heirs now have up to 10 years to empty an inherited IRA, and if your dad had already started required distributions, you may also need to take annual withdrawals. Spreading withdrawals across lower-income years usually saves a lot. Don't roll it into your own IRA by mistake, because that can trigger tax on the full amount. Have the custodian set it up as an inherited IRA, and get a CPA's help on the plan.
I just left my job and the HR lady said I can roll my 401k into an IRA. Is there any catch? I'm nervous about messing up taxes.

The cleanest way is a direct rollover, where the money moves straight from your old plan to the IRA provider and nothing is withheld or taxed. Avoid having a check made out to you personally, because the plan will withhold 20% and you'd have only 60 days to deposit the full amount, including the withheld part, to avoid taxes and penalties. Open the IRA first, then ask the old plan for a trustee-to-trustee transfer, and you'll be fine.
Is there any lottery strategy that actually improves my odds?

Buying more tickets raises your odds by a tiny amount, but no pattern, 'hot number' or system changes the math, because every draw is random. The one useful trick is picking less popular numbers, like numbers above 31, which doesn't make you more likely to win but means you're less likely to split a jackpot. Treat tickets as entertainment money you're fine losing, not as a plan.
I got a 1099-K from PayPal but it's mostly just friends paying me back for dinners. Am I screwed?

No, you're fine, you just need to report it correctly. Personal reimbursements aren't income, and the IRS has guidance for reporting a 1099-K amount and then backing out the non-taxable portion so you aren't taxed on it. Gather the records showing those payments were splitting costs, like texts or receipts, in case anyone asks. Going forward, use the 'friends and family' option for personal payments, and if your situation is messy, a one-time visit with a tax preparer is worth it.
I owe $140k from law school and make $68k at a public defender's office. Honestly feels hopeless.

It's far from hopeless, because you're close to the textbook case PSLF was built for. Make sure your loans are federal Direct Loans, get on an income-driven plan, and certify your employment with the PSLF Help Tool now. Your monthly payment will be tied to your income instead of that $140k balance, and whatever is left after 120 qualifying payments is forgiven tax-free. Just don't refinance into a private loan, because that would end your PSLF eligibility for good.
I'm 72, inherited 150k. Kids say I should put it in stocks but I'm nervous.

Your nervousness makes sense, and at 72 the main questions are when you'll need the money and how much risk lets you sleep. A common approach is to keep a few years of planned spending in safe things like high-yield savings, CDs, or Treasuries, and put only the longer-term portion in a balanced, diversified fund. Retirees can still benefit from some stock exposure to keep up with inflation, but it doesn't need to be all of it. A fee-only fiduciary advisor can tailor the mix to your income and health needs, without pushing products.
What even is PMI and how do I get rid of it?

Private mortgage insurance protects the lender, not you, and it's usually required on conventional loans when you put down less than 20%. On conventional loans you can request cancellation once you reach 20% equity based on the original value, and it ends automatically at 22%. If your home has appreciated, ask your servicer whether a new appraisal can get you there sooner. FHA loans work differently and often require a refinance to drop the mortgage insurance.
I make $42k and my payment is $510/month. I'm drowning. Anything I can do TODAY?

Yes. Log into studentaid.gov or call your servicer today and apply for an income-driven repayment plan, which ties your payment to your income and family size. At $42k that should be meaningfully lower than $510, and possibly much lower. If you need breathing room while the application processes, ask the servicer for a short forbearance, but use it as a bridge, not a long-term fix, because interest can keep building.
My grandma just left me $80k and I'm 24. Honestly I want to put it all into crypto while I'm young enough to recover. Good idea?

Being young does give you time to recover, but that's an argument for owning stocks, not for betting everything on one volatile asset class that can drop 70% in a year. A smarter move is to park three to six months of expenses in a high-yield savings account, kill any high-interest debt, and put the bulk into a low-cost broad index fund. If crypto excites you, cap it at around 5% so a crash stings without wrecking the whole gift. That way your grandma's money is still working for you in 20 years no matter what Bitcoin does.
A recruiter offered me a remote job where I receive payments into my account and forward them via gift cards, keeping 10%. Easy money for a stay at home mom. Should I take it?

Please don't take it. This is a money mule scheme: the money is almost always stolen, and the person moving it can have accounts frozen and face criminal charges even without knowing what was going on. Stop contact, don't share your bank details, and report it to your bank and the FTC, and if you want real remote work, look for jobs that never ask you to move money for them.
ugh landlord raised rent 15%. buying has to be better now right

A big rent hike is a good prompt to run the numbers, but don't let frustration rush you into a purchase. Compare your new rent to the full cost of owning, including taxes, insurance, maintenance and closing costs, and check whether you have a down payment plus an emergency fund. Remember that homeowners face rising costs too, like property tax and insurance increases. If buying still pencils out and you plan to stay five-plus years, go for it carefully. Otherwise, negotiating or shopping around for rent may be the better short-term fix.
I'm 58 and down 40% on options this year. I want to go all in on one big trade to make it back before retirement. Help me pick one.

I'd strongly urge you not to do this, because one all-in trade is how a 40% loss becomes a 100% loss, and at 58 you have little time to rebuild. The urge to win it back fast is exactly the trap that turns bad years into ruined retirements. Stop trading options for now, take stock of what's left, and talk to a fee-only fiduciary financial planner about a realistic retirement plan. A steady, diversified approach from here will do far more for you than any single bet.
im drowning in loans can i just declare bankruptcy

Student loans are much harder to wipe out in bankruptcy than credit cards, but it's not impossible. You have to prove undue hardship, and the process for federal loans has become somewhat more workable in recent years. Talk to a bankruptcy attorney before deciding, since many offer a free consultation and can tell you if your situation has a real shot. In the meantime, get on an income-driven plan, because it may bring your payment down to something you can survive.
Is it smart to put crypto in my IRA?

It can work, and the tax advantages are real, since gains in a Roth IRA are tax-free. The simplest route is a spot bitcoin ETF inside a regular brokerage IRA, which avoids the high fees and custody risk of specialty 'crypto IRA' companies. Keep it a small slice of your retirement money, because retirement accounts are the wrong place for big bets.
Is it true that checking my own credit score hurts it?

No, checking your own score is a soft inquiry and has zero effect, no matter how often you do it. Only hard inquiries, which happen when a lender pulls your credit because you applied for something, can shave off a few points. Check as often as you like through your bank, card issuer, or a free monitoring service.
Detailed question. I'm 38, make $145k, married filing jointly, wife makes $60k. We both have 401(k)s. Should we do Roth or traditional contributions?

At about $205k combined, you're likely in the 22 or 24 percent federal bracket, which tends to favor traditional contributions, since you get the deduction now at a fairly high rate. Many couples at your income split it, keeping traditional as the default and putting some money into Roth to diversify against future tax rates. If you expect big pensions, large inheritances, or a higher income in retirement, lean more Roth. It's also worth checking whether you qualify for a Roth IRA or should do a backdoor Roth. A fee-only planner can model this precisely with your full picture.
I accepted the offer verbally yesterday but now realize it's low. Can I still negotiate?

It's awkward, but you can try once if you have a solid reason, such as new market data or details you didn't have before. Be upfront: say you've reviewed the full package and ask whether there's any flexibility on base or a signing bonus. Keep it gracious and accept their answer either way, because backtracking on a verbal yes uses up some goodwill. For future offers, get a day to review before saying yes.
I'm 58 and planning to retire in about five years. Do I still need an emergency fund if I have a big 401k?

Yes, and it matters even more as you approach retirement, because pulling from a 401(k) for an emergency can trigger taxes, possibly penalties before 59½, and force you to sell investments at a bad time. Keep six months to a year of expenses in cash, and many planners suggest growing that to one to two years of spending right before and after retirement to ride out market dips. A fee-only fiduciary financial planner can help you map out the right cash buffer alongside your withdrawal strategy.
honestly how likely am I to get audited if I round up some deductions

Audit rates for typical earners are low, but the IRS's automated matching catches mismatches far more often than a formal audit does. Padded deductions also tend to cluster in the categories it already screens. If you're caught, you'd owe the tax plus interest and penalties of 20 percent or more, and possibly more if it's seen as intentional. Claim what you can document and keep the receipts. You'll probably find legitimate deductions you've been missing anyway.
Should I get a bunch of store credit cards to raise my total credit limit? Target, Kohl's, Amazon, etc.

Opening several at once means multiple hard inquiries and a lower average account age, so your score will likely dip short-term. Store cards also tend to have high interest rates and low limits. If you want more available credit, request a limit increase on a card you already have, which is often a soft pull, or add one solid general-purpose card. One or two well-chosen cards beat a wallet full of retail ones.
Moving from NYC to remote, company wants to cut my pay 15% for 'location adjustment'. Push back?

Yes, push back by emphasizing that your output and value haven't changed. Ask whether the cut could be smaller or phased in, or whether you could keep your current salary in exchange for a hybrid arrangement or occasional office visits. Check whether they actually adjust pay downward for others, because inconsistent policies give you leverage. Run the numbers too, since a 15% cut might still leave you ahead once lower living costs and state taxes are counted.
My friend says I should just declare my house uninsured since it's paid off and put the premium into stocks. Self-insure basically. Thoughts?

Self-insuring makes sense for small things, but not for your house. A fire, tornado, or burst pipe could destroy an asset worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, and homeowners insurance also carries the liability coverage that protects you if someone gets hurt on your property. Unless you have enough liquid wealth to rebuild out of pocket without blinking, keep the policy. A higher deductible is a more reasonable way to trim the cost.
What's the deal with staking? Free money?

Not free, but it's real yield: you lock up coins like ETH or SOL to help secure the network and earn roughly 3 to 7% a year, paid in that same coin. The catches are that the coin's price can fall far more than the yield earns, your funds may be locked for a while, and staking through an exchange or third-party protocol adds the risk that the platform fails. In the US, staking rewards are generally taxed as income when you receive them. Treat it as a bonus on crypto you already planned to hold long term, not a reason to buy.
What's the max I can lose buying a call option?

Your maximum loss is the premium you paid plus any fees, so if you paid $2.50 for one contract, that's $250. That defined risk is one of the appeal of buying options. Just remember that losing 100% of the premium is common, especially with short-dated or far out-of-the-money contracts. Size each position as if it could go to zero.
rent vs buy calculator says buy. good enough?

It's a good start, but a calculator is only as good as what you put into it. Double-check your assumptions about how long you'll stay, home price growth, maintenance, HOA fees and what your down payment would earn if you invested it instead. Try a pessimistic version with flat prices and higher costs. If buying still wins, or comes close, you can feel fairly confident about it.
Insurance company lowballed me on my totaled car. They offered $8k, similar cars are selling for $11k. What can I do?

Push back, because the first offer is often negotiable. Ask for their valuation report and check it for errors in mileage, trim or options. Then send them three or four comparable local listings or recent sales, plus receipts for any recent upgrades like new tires. If they still won't budge, check whether your policy has an appraisal clause, which lets each side hire an appraiser. You can also file a complaint with your state insurance department, and a public adjuster or attorney is worth considering if the gap stays large.
Are credit repair companies worth paying for?

Mostly no. They can't legally do anything you can't do yourself for free, like disputing inaccurate items with the bureaus, and accurate negative information can't be removed by anyone. Watch out for companies that charge upfront fees or promise to erase legitimate debt, since that's illegal under federal law and a common scam. If you want guided help, a nonprofit credit counselor affiliated with the NFCC is the safer, cheaper route.
Can I open a 529 for myself? I want to go back to school at 41.

Yes, you can be both owner and beneficiary of your own 529, and it covers qualified costs at accredited colleges, grad schools and many vocational programs. If you'll start within a year or two, keep the money conservative, since you won't have time to recover from a market dip. Check whether your state offers a tax deduction on contributions, which can make even a short-term 529 worthwhile. Also look into the Lifetime Learning Credit for when you're paying tuition.
Is it smart to buy a fixer-upper to save money? I've watched a lot of HGTV.

Fixer-uppers can save money, but TV makes it look faster, cheaper and easier than it is. Renovations routinely run 20 to 50 percent over budget, and problems like foundation, roof, electrical or plumbing can swallow your savings. Get a thorough inspection and contractor quotes before you make an offer, and keep a cash buffer for surprises. If you don't have that buffer or real renovation experience, a move-in-ready home is usually the safer bet.
Inherited a bunch of my grandpa's Exxon stock, like $85k worth. Keep it for sentimental reasons?

Sentiment is understandable, but holding $85k in a single stock is real concentration risk. The good news is you likely got a stepped-up basis, so selling now probably triggers little or no tax. Consider keeping a few shares as a keepsake and diversifying the rest into broad funds.
I'm 19 and my friends are all on sports betting apps. Is a little betting fine or is it a bad idea?

Small amounts for fun can be fine, but betting apps are designed to keep you playing, with constant notifications, bonuses and parlays that look easy but have terrible odds. Young adults are at higher risk of developing gambling problems, so set a strict monthly cap you'd be fine losing, like the cost of a concert ticket, and never bet with borrowed money. If you notice yourself chasing losses or hiding it, that's the signal to stop.
honestly I'm 31 with zero retirement savings and feel like a failure. where do I even start

You're not behind enough to panic, because 30-plus years of compounding is still a huge runway. Start by enrolling in your workplace 401k to get any match, or open a Roth IRA at a low-cost brokerage if there's no plan. Set up automatic contributions into a target-date or broad index fund, even 50 or 100 dollars a paycheck, and raise it with every raise.
I have $15k saved. Should I put all of it into my Etsy business to scale it?

I wouldn't put in all of it, so keep at least three to six months of personal expenses as an emergency fund before investing a dollar in the shop. Then put money in stages, perhaps $3k to $5k toward whatever has a clear return, like inventory for your best sellers or tested ads, and track the results before adding more. Growing on proven results is slower but far safer than betting your whole cushion at once.
Quick one: international index fund or just US?

Holding some international exposure, often 20 to 40 percent of your stocks, adds diversification, because the US hasn't led the world in every decade. A total world fund like VT handles this in one ticket if you want simplicity. A US-only portfolio isn't crazy, but it is a bet that the US keeps outperforming.
Is it smarter to invest instead of paying extra on my 3% student loans? I'm 26.

At 3%, investing usually makes more sense, especially at 26 with decades of compounding ahead of you. Grab any employer 401(k) match first, since that's an instant return no loan payoff can beat, and then consider a Roth IRA. Just keep making your regular loan payments and have an emergency fund in place before you put money into the market.
Can I negotiate my interest rate down or is that a myth?

It's real, and it works more often than people expect. Call the number on the back of your card, say you've been a loyal customer, and mention that you're considering a balance transfer to a lower-rate card, then ask directly if they can reduce your APR. If the first rep says no, politely ask for a supervisor or retention department, or try again in a few weeks. Even a few percentage points off a large balance adds up to real savings.
what's IV crush

IV crush is when an option's implied volatility, and with it the option's price, drops sharply after an expected event like earnings passes. Traders often buy calls or puts before earnings, then get the direction right and still lose money because the volatility premium they paid evaporates overnight. If you trade around earnings, check how big a move the options are already pricing in before you buy.
Is matched betting a get rich quick scheme?

Not really. It's a legitimate way, where it's legal, to extract a modest profit from bookmaker sign-up offers by betting both sides. The money is real but limited, usually a few hundred to a couple thousand dollars before the offers run out or your accounts get restricted. Do it carefully with spreadsheets or a calculator, and treat it as a side hustle, not a career.
I make $95k and have $22k on cards. What's a realistic timeline?

On that income, you could realistically clear it in 18 to 24 months if you can commit around $1,000 to $1,300 a month, and faster with a lower rate. A 0% balance transfer for part of it, or a personal loan in the low teens, would save a lot of interest and speed things up. Pick a fixed monthly amount and automate it so it happens before you can spend the money elsewhere. Pausing extra spending like travel or dining out for a year or so can make a huge difference at your income level.
Honestly I'm tired of 4% in savings. What's the highest yield I can get that's not insane?

If you want more than savings without doing anything crazy, a low-cost broad stock index fund has historically averaged somewhere around 7 to 10% a year over long stretches, but it can drop 30% or more in a bad year, so it's only for money you won't need for at least five years. For money you need sooner, Treasury bills, CDs and money market funds are about as good as it gets, and they're paying close to what you already have. Nothing safely pays much more than that, so any yield well above those levels means you're taking on more risk, whether or not anyone tells you so.
is 12% fixed annual return on a real estate note legit or too good to be true

It can be legit, but 12% fixed means the borrower is risky or the deal is structured so you absorb losses if it goes bad. Before investing, confirm the note is secured by a recorded lien on a specific property, check the loan-to-value ratio, and look up the sponsor on the SEC's EDGAR and FINRA BrokerCheck. If they can't give you clean documents and a track record of defaults handled, walk away.
I've been paying on an income-driven plan for 6 years. Do I have to recertify every year? What if I forget?

Yes, you generally need to recertify your income and family size every year, though if you give consent for the government to access your tax info, it may happen automatically. If you miss the deadline, your payment can jump to the standard amount and unpaid interest might be added to your balance, which can get expensive. Set a calendar reminder a month before your deadline and log into studentaid.gov to check your status. Those 6 years of payments may count toward forgiveness, so it's worth keeping everything on track.
honestly my credit is trash (520). buy here pay here lot says they'll approve me. thoughts?

Buy-here-pay-here lots will approve almost anyone, but they often charge rates of 20 percent or more, overprice the cars, and some install trackers or kill switches and repossess quickly. Before you sign, try a local credit union, since some have programs for rebuilding credit. Another option is buying a cheap car outright with saved cash while you improve your score. If you do go with one of these lots, make sure they report payments to the credit bureaus so you at least rebuild credit.
honestly how much should a normal person spend on gambling a month

There's no universal number, but a good rule is that it should come from your fun money after savings and bills, and you should be fine losing all of it. For many people that's something like a night out's worth, often under 1 percent of income. If you're going over your limit, chasing losses, or borrowing to play, the amount matters less than the pattern, and that's the time to cut back or get help.
I owe $15k on cards and my score is in the 500s. Should I just declare bankruptcy and start over?

Bankruptcy is a serious step that stays on your report for 7 to 10 years, and for $15,000 there are often better options to try first. A nonprofit credit counseling agency can review your situation for free and may set up a debt management plan that lowers your interest rates into one monthly payment. If your income truly can't cover the debts, then a consultation with a bankruptcy attorney, many of whom offer free first meetings, is the right next move. Avoid for-profit debt settlement companies that tell you to stop paying your bills, since that can make things much worse.
Getting divorced. What insurance stuff do I need to change? My head is spinning.

Start with beneficiaries: update your life insurance and retirement accounts, because an ex-spouse left on a policy can still collect in many situations. Then line up your own health insurance, since you'll lose coverage under your spouse's plan. You'll usually have a special enrollment window or COBRA eligibility, so act quickly. Split your auto and home or renters policies once you've separated property. Your divorce decree may also require you to keep life insurance for child support, so have your attorney confirm exactly what you owe before changing anything.
Is it better to put a big down payment on a car or keep the cash invested?

It depends on the loan rate. If it's low, like under 4 percent, keeping cash invested can come out ahead over time, though investment returns aren't guaranteed. At higher rates, paying down the loan is a guaranteed return equal to that rate, which is hard to beat. Either way, put enough down to avoid being underwater, and never use your emergency fund for the down payment.
Worried. I'm 72, got a call from 'Amazon security' saying my account was hacked and I need to move my savings into a safe account they'll set up. They sound official.

This is a scam. Please don't move any money or share any information. Amazon, your bank and the government will never ask you to transfer savings into a 'safe account.' Hang up, call your bank using the number on the back of your card, and tell them what happened so they can watch your accounts. It's also a good idea to let a family member know and report it to the FTC.
Is it legit that my bank's CD is paying 5% while Chase pays 0.01% savings?

That can be legitimate. Big banks often pay almost nothing on standard savings while smaller banks and online banks compete on CD and high-yield rates. Just confirm the bank is FDIC-insured, stay under the $250k coverage limit, and know the early withdrawal penalty before you lock in. CDs at insured banks are among the safest places for money you won't need for a while.
Should I claim social security at 62 since I retired early?

Usually not if you can afford to wait, because benefits grow about 7% to 8% a year between 62 and 70, which is inflation-protected income you can't buy that cheaply anywhere else. Many early retirees spend down savings in their 60s so they can delay claiming, especially the higher earner in a couple. Claiming early makes more sense if your health is poor or you truly need the cash.
is student loan interest tax deductible

Yes, you can deduct up to $2,500 a year of student loan interest, and you don't need to itemize to take it. The deduction phases out at higher incomes, and the limits are adjusted periodically, so check the current year's thresholds in IRS Publication 970 or your tax software. Your servicer will send you a Form 1098-E showing how much interest you paid.
Should I quit my job to day trade full time? I've been profitable for 3 months.

Three months is far too short to know whether you have an edge or just caught a good market, so I wouldn't quit on that basis. A fair bar is a full year or more of consistent results, across different market conditions, tracked in a spreadsheet with every trade and fee included, plus enough savings to cover a year of expenses that you never touch for trading. Keep the paycheck and trade on the side while you build that track record. Losing your job's income and benefits while also having a bad trading stretch is the scenario that wipes people out.
Can I day trade in my Roth IRA to avoid taxes on short-term gains?

Technically you can trade in a Roth, but IRAs can't use real margin, so you'll be limited by settlement times, and most brokers restrict what options strategies you can run. The bigger problem is that losses in a Roth are permanent: you can't deduct them, and you can't simply put the money back beyond the annual contribution limit. Tax-free growth is the most valuable thing a Roth gives you, so most people are better off holding long-term investments there and keeping any speculative trading in a small taxable account.
Is the 50/30/20 rule realistic when I'm barely covering rent?

Not really, because when needs eat 70 or 80% of your income, forcing 50/30/20 just makes you feel like you're failing. Use the idea loosely: cover needs first, keep a small fixed amount for something you enjoy so you don't burn out, and save whatever you can, even 2 or 3%. The ratio matters less than having a plan you can actually follow.
Is the 50/30/20 rule realistic on $25k a year?

Often not, because on $25k your needs can easily take up 70 or 80 percent of your income, and that isn't a personal failure. Adjust the ratio to fit your reality, perhaps 80/15/5, and focus on covering essentials and saving something consistently, even if it's small. As your income rises or costs drop, you can shift toward the classic split.
how much of my portfolio should be individual stocks if I like researching companies

A common rule of thumb is to keep individual stocks to 5 to 10 percent of your portfolio and let index funds handle the rest. That lets you enjoy the research and learn from your picks without risking your retirement on them. Track your stock picks against an S&P 500 fund honestly for a few years, and the results will tell you whether to grow that slice or shrink it.
I'm 27 and want to retire at 40. Should I skip the 401k since I can't touch it until 59?

Don't skip it, because early retirees have several legal ways into retirement accounts. A Roth conversion ladder lets you move money to a Roth and withdraw the converted amounts five years later penalty-free, and substantially equal periodic payments (72t) are another option. Roth IRA contributions can also be withdrawn anytime. Max the tax-advantaged accounts first, then add a taxable brokerage account to cover the early years.
I received $250,000 after my wife passed. Everyone keeps giving me opinions and I just want to hide. What's the minimum I have to do?

I'm so sorry. The minimum is simple: put the money in an FDIC-insured high-yield savings account or a money market fund at a major brokerage, and then let it sit. Keep balances under FDIC limits per bank, or use Treasuries, and it will be safe and earning interest. Say no to anyone pushing you to decide quickly. In six months to a year, a fee-only fiduciary planner can help you make a longer plan.
My girlfriend I met online (we haven't met in person yet) is teaching me to trade on a platform where I've turned $3k into $40k. Now they say I need to pay a 20% tax before withdrawing. Normal?

This is not normal, and I'm sorry to say it matches a well-known romance investment scam often called pig butchering. The $40k balance is almost certainly fake, and the 'tax' is a way to take more money from you. A real platform deducts fees from your balance and doesn't make you send new money to withdraw. Don't send anything else, stop communicating with her about money, and report it to the FBI at ic3.gov and to your bank right away.
My 15 yo wants to buy GameStop with his birthday money lol. Should I let him?

It could be a cheap lesson, but you can make it a better one. Suggest he split it, with most going into an S&P 500 fund in a custodial account and a small part going into GameStop. Then have him track both for a year or two and see which one actually did better and which one stressed him out more. That comparison will teach him more than any lecture.
Is selling covered calls on my retirement account stocks a reasonable way to get extra income? I'm 58.

It can be. Covered calls are one of the more conservative option strategies, and many IRAs allow them. The trade-off is that you cap your upside: if a stock jumps past your strike, you either let the shares go or buy back the call at a loss. Stick to stocks you'd be fine selling at the strike price, and consider talking it over with a fee-only advisor, since you're close to retirement and a misstep has less time to recover.
Should I take out a personal loan to lend my mom money? My credit is better than hers.

That puts all the risk on you, because the lender will expect payment from you whether or not your mom pays you back. Personal loans often carry high interest, so if she falls behind you're stuck paying for her debt at a premium. Look first at whether she qualifies for help herself through a credit union, a hardship program with her creditors, or nonprofit credit counseling. Only borrow on her behalf if you could comfortably make every payment yourself with no help from her.
My buddy said to put all my tax refund into the lottery since it's 'free money' anyway. lol thoughts?

A refund isn't free money, it's your own paycheck you overpaid during the year, and the lottery has a terrible expected return. Use it to build an emergency fund, pay down high-interest credit card debt, or open a Roth IRA, which will actually grow. If you want to have a little fun, carve out $20 for tickets and put the rest to work. Long term, consider adjusting your W-4 so more money lands in each paycheck instead of the refund.
I have $15k left in a 529 and my kid didn't use it all. Can it go toward her loans?

Yes, within limits. You can use up to $10,000 per beneficiary over a lifetime from a 529 for qualified student loan payments, and you can use another $10,000 for each of her siblings. Under newer rules, unused 529 money can also be rolled into a Roth IRA for the beneficiary, up to $35,000 over her lifetime, as long as the account has been open at least 15 years and you stay within annual contribution limits. Check your state's tax treatment first, since some states don't count loan payments as qualified and may recapture past deductions.
Should I stop paying my student loans so I can afford rent?

Don't just stop paying. Missed federal loan payments can lead to default, damaged credit and even garnished wages. If you have federal loans, apply for an income-driven repayment plan, because at a low income your payment could drop to very little or even zero. Call your servicer or go to studentaid.gov today, since that protects your credit and keeps rent covered.
I want to start a lawn care side business this summer. I'd need to borrow about $5k for equipment. Is that dumb?

It isn't dumb, but I wouldn't borrow the whole $5k upfront. Start with a solid used mower and trimmer for under $1,500, land your first few clients, and buy upgrades out of revenue once you know the demand is there. Debt for a business that's still untested is the main way side hustles turn into money pits. Also budget for general liability insurance, which is fairly cheap and protects you if a rock flies through someone's window.
My car needs a $1,200 repair and I have $200. Do I put it on a credit card?

Before borrowing anything, get a second quote, because repair prices vary a lot and some items on the list may not be urgent. Ask the shop which repairs are safety-critical now and which can wait, and whether they offer an interest-free payment plan. If you do have to use a card, use the one with the lowest rate and make a concrete plan to pay it off in a few months, since carrying it long-term at 25 percent interest adds up. A credit union personal loan is often cheaper than a card if the balance will take a while to clear.
I'm a nurse, I don't have time to research stocks. Is it fine to just buy one index fund and forget it?

That's genuinely one of the smartest strategies there is, not a lazy compromise. A single total market fund, or a target-date fund that adjusts automatically as you age, gives you broad diversification with almost no maintenance. Automate your contributions, check in once a year, and spend your limited free time on anything but stock charts.
I'm 58, renting, never owned. Is it too late to buy?

Not too late, but the math is different at your age. A 30-year mortgage running into your late 80s needs a solid plan for retirement income, and putting a big chunk of savings into a down payment can leave you short on cash. If you want stability, buying something modest with a payment you could cover on retirement income can work well.
