Steer clear of anything that promises $2k with no skills or asks you to pay upfront, because when you're in a hurry those are almost always scams.
I found out a coworker with the same job makes 15k more than me. I'm furious. What do I do?

Use it calmly as data, not ammunition. Go to your manager with market research and your own accomplishments, and ask for an adjustment to bring you in line with the role's value. You don't need to name the coworker. If you suspect the gap is tied to gender, race, age or another protected characteristic and the company won't fix it, an employment lawyer or your local labor agency can tell you your rights.
I owe $15k on credit cards at 24%. Should I cash out my IRA to pay it off?

Usually not, because cashing out means income tax plus a 10% penalty, so you could lose 30% or more to pay a debt that has better solutions. Try a 0% balance transfer card, a lower-rate personal loan, or a free nonprofit credit counseling agency that can arrange a debt management plan. Pause extra retirement contributions beyond any employer match and send that money to the cards. The IRA should stay a last resort for true emergencies.
my kid is 16 and we have nothing saved. are we screwed?

Not at all, though the plan now looks different. Start with the FAFSA in her senior year, push hard on scholarships, and seriously consider starting at community college or an in-state public school, which can cut the cost dramatically. Put whatever you can save over the next two years into a 529 in a conservative option, or a high-yield savings account if your state gives no tax break, rather than chasing big returns. Use federal student loans, not private ones, if you need to borrow.
I'm a nurse and want to do private home care on the side for cash. Any issues?

There are a few to sort out first. Check your employer's moonlighting and conflict-of-interest policies, and make sure you're not picking up their patients privately. Your license makes you personally liable for the care you give, so carry your own professional liability insurance, because your employer's policy won't cover outside work. Cash income is still taxable, so keep records and report it, since an audit or license issue over unreported income isn't worth the risk.
I'm 41 and switching careers into UX. They offered junior pay. Should I push back because of my age and experience?

Push back on the basis of transferable skills, not age. Name specific things from your past career that make you productive faster, like stakeholder management, research or domain expertise in their industry. Junior bands can be rigid, so if base won't budge, ask for a six-month performance review with a defined path to the next level. Get that commitment in writing so it doesn't evaporate.
got an email saying i won an inheritance from a distant relative overseas, just need to pay $400 processing fee. lol obviously fake right

Yep, obviously fake. It's an advance-fee scam, and the $400 would only be the first of many 'fees' that keep coming. Real inheritances never require you to pay to receive them; the estate pays any costs. Delete it, don't reply, and never send gift cards or wire money to anyone who contacts you like this.
I've got 40k sitting in checking earning nothing. Inflation's like 3%. What do I do

Move most of it out of checking today, because it's quietly losing value. Put three to six months of expenses in a high-yield savings account or money market fund, which currently pay well above zero and stay fully accessible. Money you won't need for five years or more can go into a low-cost diversified index fund, ideally in a tax-advantaged account like an IRA or 401k.
I'm 24 and just got my first real job. How big should my emergency fund actually be?

A solid target is three to six months of essential expenses, meaning rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation and minimum debt payments, not your full lifestyle spending. Since you're just starting out, aim first for a starter cushion of about $1,000 to $2,000, then build toward the full amount over the next year or two. If your job feels shaky or you work in a volatile industry, lean toward the six-month end.
I'm 24, no business history, decent credit. Where do I even start getting funding for a mobile car detailing business?

Start small, because detailing doesn't need much capital, and a few thousand in savings or a microloan can cover equipment. Groups like Kiva, Accion Opportunity Fund and local CDFIs lend to first-timers with no business track record. Build a simple plan with your startup costs and pricing, and look for free SCORE mentoring to sharpen it before you apply.
honestly just tell me buy or rent. 31, single, make 85k, live in Denver, have 40k saved

With $40k saved and $85k income in Denver, you could likely buy a modest condo or starter home, but only buy if you expect to stay at least five years and can keep three to six months of expenses in savings after closing. If $40k would be your entire cushion, keep renting another year or two and build it up. Run your numbers through a rent-vs-buy calculator like the NYT one using actual Denver listings. That will tell you more than any general rule.
I'm 3 months behind on my federal loans and getting scary letters. I lost my job in January. What do I do

Call your servicer today. You haven't defaulted yet, which on most federal loans happens around 270 days past due, so there's still time to fix this. Ask about unemployment deferment or forbearance, which can pause your payments, and ask whether the past-due amount can be included. Also apply for an income-driven plan, since with no income your payment could be $0, and those months may count toward forgiveness. Get everything confirmed in writing, and keep checking StudentAid.gov to make sure the change actually went through.
Can I lie about smoking on my life insurance application? I only smoke at parties.

Don't. Misrepresentation on an application can let the insurer deny the claim entirely, especially within the first two years, which means your family could get nothing when they need it most. Many insurers test for nicotine anyway. Be honest about occasional use, since some companies are more lenient toward occasional cigar or social smokers, and an independent broker can steer you to them. If you quit for 12 months, you can usually reapply for nonsmoker rates.
Is a business line of credit better than a loan?

They serve different purposes, so it depends on what you need the money for. A line of credit is best for uneven cash flow, seasonal inventory or emergencies, since you only pay interest on what you draw. A term loan is better for one-time purchases like equipment or a renovation, where predictable payments over a set term make sense.
should i refinance my federal loans with a private lender to get a lower rate

Only do it if you're very confident you'll never need federal protections. Refinancing federal loans into a private loan permanently gives up income-driven repayment, Public Service Loan Forgiveness, generous deferment and forbearance options, and discharge if you become disabled. If you have a high, stable income, a solid emergency fund, and the rate drop is meaningful, it can make sense. If your job or income is at all uncertain, the federal safety net is usually worth more than a point or two of interest.
I'm 19 in college. Is dollar cost averaging $25 a week into BTC dumb?

That's actually one of the more sensible ways to do it. Small fixed amounts on a schedule take the emotion and timing out of it, and $25 a week won't sink you if prices crash. Just make sure you've got an emergency cushion and aren't carrying credit card debt, and consider putting some money into a Roth IRA with index funds too, since starting at 19 is a huge advantage there.
Should I just cash out my 401k to kill my $15k credit card debt? I'm 34.

Almost certainly not, because an early withdrawal usually costs you a 10% penalty plus income tax. That can eat 30% or more of the money, and you also lose decades of compound growth. You'd likely need to pull out over $20k to clear $15k, and that's a terrible trade. Look first at a balance transfer card, a fixed-rate personal loan at a lower rate, or a free session with a nonprofit credit counselor who can set up a debt management plan. Treat your retirement account as off-limits for this unless you're facing something truly dire.
Is it smart to quit my job now that my side hustle is making as much as my salary?

It can be, but don't make the jump until a few things are true. That income should hold steady for at least six to twelve months, not just one great quarter. You'll also want six months or more of expenses saved, plus a plan for health insurance, which can cost hundreds a month on your own. Factor in that self-employment tax and the loss of your employer's 401(k) match mean you need to earn more just to break even.
Should my emergency fund be in a CD for the higher rate?

Locking all of it in a CD can backfire, because early withdrawal penalties can eat your interest right when you need the money. A middle ground is to keep one or two months in high-yield savings and ladder the rest across short-term CDs that mature every few months, or use no-penalty CDs. Most people are better served by a plain high-yield savings account, since rates are usually close.
I found a YouTube guy who says you can use a self-directed IRA to buy a rental property and live in it part of the year. Sounds like a great hack?

That one is a trap: living in, vacationing at, or otherwise personally using property owned by your IRA is a prohibited transaction. The penalty is brutal, because the IRS can treat the entire IRA as distributed, meaning taxes and possibly a 10% penalty on the whole thing. Self-directed IRAs can hold real estate legitimately, but the rules on who can use it, manage it, and pay its expenses are strict. Talk to a CPA who specializes in them before you move a dollar.
Got married in December. Do we file jointly for the whole year?

Yes, your filing status depends on whether you're married on December 31, so you can file jointly for the entire year. For most couples, filing jointly gives a lower combined tax and access to more credits. Run a quick comparison in tax software if one of you has large medical bills or income-based student loan payments, as separate filing occasionally wins. Also update your W-4s at work for the new year so your withholding fits your combined income.
I'm 19, work part time, live with my parents. Is it even worth budgeting on like $600 a month?

Yes, and this is honestly the best time to build the habit because your costs are low and mistakes are cheap. Try saving a fixed chunk, even $150, the day you get paid, then spend the rest freely without guilt. Within a year you could have a solid emergency fund before rent and bills ever hit you.
difference between fico and vantagescore?

They're two competing scoring models that use similar ingredients but weigh them a bit differently, so your numbers can differ by 20 points or more. VantageScore is common on free credit apps. FICO is what most lenders actually use, especially for mortgages, which rely on older FICO versions. Treat the free score as a trend indicator, and check your actual FICO score through a card issuer that offers it if you're about to apply for a big loan.
Paid off a car loan early — will that hurt my credit?

Your score might dip slightly for a little while because an active installment account is closing, but it's minor and temporary. Being debt-free and saving on interest is worth far more than a few points. Just double-check that your loan doesn't carry a prepayment penalty, which is uncommon on auto loans but worth confirming.
Disabled, on SSI, can I save money without losing benefits?

Yes, but carefully. SSI generally caps countable resources at $2,000 for an individual, so going over that can pause your benefits. An ABLE account is the best tool here, because it lets you save much more without affecting SSI as long as your disability began before age 26 (rising to age 46 starting in 2026). Talk to a benefits counselor through your state's WIPA program before you make big moves, since the rules are tricky and a mistake can be costly.
Got a call from a company saying they can get my student loans forgiven for a one time fee of $799. They sounded legit and knew my loan balance. Should I pay?

Don't pay, and don't give them your FSA ID or any personal information. Everything they're offering, including consolidation, income-driven repayment, and forgiveness applications, is free through StudentAid.gov or your loan servicer. Scammers often get balance details from leaked or purchased data, so knowing your numbers doesn't prove they're legitimate. Hang up, log in to StudentAid.gov yourself, and report the call to the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
index or stocks. one word answer

Index, for nearly everyone. You get instant diversification, very low fees and returns that beat most stock pickers over the long run. If you enjoy picking stocks, keep it to a small slice of your money.
We're 58 and 60 with 12 years left on our mortgage. Should we use our savings to pay it off before retiring?

Going into retirement debt-free is a great feeling and can lower the income you need. Still, don't drain liquid savings to get there, because a paid-off house can't cover a medical bill or a car repair. If paying it off would leave you with a thin cushion, or would mean pulling taxable money out of retirement accounts, a gradual extra-payment plan is safer. A fee-only planner can model your income and taxes to find the right balance.
Need my refund ASAP. Should I do one of those refund advance loans?

Most refund advances are free, but they usually come bundled with paid tax prep or a prepaid card that has fees, and some offers are just high-cost loans. The free and fast route is to e-file and choose direct deposit, which typically gets your refund to you in under three weeks. If you claim the EITC or child tax credit, refunds are held until mid-to-late February by law, so plan around that. Steer clear of any offer with an interest rate or a big prep fee.
I'm 52 and want my side consulting income to boost retirement. Best account to use?

A Solo 401(k) is usually the strongest choice. As both employee and employer you can contribute a large share of your consulting profit, and at 52 you also get catch-up contributions. A SEP IRA is simpler but often allows less at moderate income levels. If you already max your 401k at your day job, the employee deferral limit is shared across plans, though the employer portion is separate. A CPA can run the exact numbers for your income mix.
is it bad that my emergency fund is like 2 years of expenses? feels like a lot sitting there

Unless your job or health situation is unusually uncertain, two years is probably more than you need, and the extra cash is losing ground to inflation. Keep six months or so in savings and consider investing the rest according to your goals, maybe after talking with a fee-only advisor. If having the big cushion genuinely helps you sleep, though, that peace of mind has real value too.
I got an email from 'Ledger support' saying my wallet is compromised and I need to verify my 24 words. It looks real.

It's a phishing scam. Do not enter your words anywhere. Ledger and every legitimate wallet company will never ask for your recovery phrase, for any reason. Delete the email, and if you've already typed your phrase anywhere, move your funds immediately to a new wallet with a freshly generated phrase.
I owe $15k in back taxes. A company on the radio says they can settle it for pennies on the dollar. Legit?

Be careful, as many of those firms charge big upfront fees for results you could get yourself, or never deliver. An Offer in Compromise does exist, but the IRS only accepts it when you truly can't pay, and most people end up on a payment plan, which you can set up for free at irs.gov. Before paying anyone, contact the Taxpayer Advocate Service or a Low Income Taxpayer Clinic, or hire a licensed CPA, enrolled agent, or tax attorney you can verify, who will charge reasonable fees.
should i put my student loans on a credit card to get the points

No. Most servicers don't accept credit cards at all, and payment processors that do will charge fees that usually wipe out any rewards. Worse, you'd be moving low-interest debt with federal protections onto a card that probably charges 20% or more. Stick with paying your servicer directly, and set up autopay, which usually gets you a 0.25% rate discount.
just tell me the fastest way to get rid of 6k debt

The fastest realistic route is to cut your expenses hard for a few months, pick up extra income, and send every spare dollar to the highest-rate card. Move the balance to a 0% transfer card if you qualify, so all of your payments go toward principal instead of interest. Sell stuff you don't use, put any windfalls straight toward the debt, and freeze the card so the balance stops growing. If you can find $600 or more a month, you'll be done in about 10 months.
rates are high. should i just rent forever?

Renting forever is a perfectly legitimate choice, and it beats buying when local rents are low compared with home prices or you might move within five years. The key is investing the difference you'd otherwise put into a down payment and maintenance, rather than spending it. Run the numbers with a rent-versus-buy calculator for your city. If you buy later, you can refinance if rates fall, but don't stretch just to avoid feeling left out.
Is it smart to do an adjustable-rate mortgage to get a lower payment now and refinance later?

That's a real gamble, because refinancing depends on future rates and your future credit, and neither is guaranteed. An ARM can make sense if you're confident you'll sell before the first rate adjustment. Even then, only take one if you could afford the payment at the full rate cap written into the loan. If you can only afford the house on the teaser rate, it's too much house.
Is whole life insurance a good investment? An agent at my church is pushing it hard for me and my wife.

For most families, whole life is an expensive way to combine insurance and investing, and you'll usually come out ahead buying a much cheaper term policy and investing the difference in retirement accounts or index funds. Whole life policies carry high fees and big agent commissions, and the cash value grows slowly, especially in the first decade. There are niche uses, like certain estate planning situations for very wealthy households, but that's rarely the typical couple. Before you sign anything, get a second opinion from a fee-only financial planner who doesn't earn a commission on the sale.
What happens to the 529 money if my kid doesn't go to college?

You have more options than most people realize. You can switch the beneficiary to a sibling, a cousin, or yourself. You can use it for trade school or apprenticeship programs that qualify, or keep it in case they go later. Under current rules, up to $35,000 over a lifetime can also be rolled into the child's Roth IRA, as long as the account has been open 15 years and you stay within annual contribution limits. If you do cash it out for non-qualified reasons, only the earnings get taxed plus a 10% penalty. Your original contributions come back to you.
I make $32k and have $8k in credit card debt. Am I doomed?

Not doomed, it's very manageable with a plan, though high interest will make it drag if you only pay minimums. Call each card company and ask for a lower rate, and look into a nonprofit credit counseling agency that can often negotiate rates down to single digits through a debt management plan. Then pay as much as you can toward the highest-interest card while paying minimums on the rest, and stop adding new charges. At around $300 a month at a reduced rate, you'd likely be done in under three years.
Is it smart to cancel my health insurance to save $150 a month? I'm healthy.

I'd keep coverage, because one ER visit or accident can cost thousands and is a leading cause of debt for people on tight budgets. Check healthcare.gov or your state marketplace, or apply for Medicaid, since at a low income you may qualify for a much cheaper or free plan with subsidies. Cutting the cost makes sense, but cutting the coverage entirely is a risk that's rarely worth it.
My brother-in-law made 50% on a high-yield fund last year. Should I follow him in?

One great year tells you little, and a fund up 50% is clearly taking big risks that can just as easily cut the other way. Ask for the fund's name, then look up its prospectus, fees, multi-year track record, and registration yourself. If it holds up and fits your goals, keep it to a small portion of your money rather than chasing last year's number.
I saw a TikTok saying you should use whole life insurance as a college savings plan instead of a 529. Legit?

For almost everyone, no. Whole life policies come with high fees and commissions, and in the early years the cash value grows slowly. The people pushing this are often the ones selling the policies. A 529 is cheaper, more transparent, and built for exactly this goal. If you need life insurance to protect your kids, buy inexpensive term coverage and keep investing separately.
Insurance agent wants to put my whole emergency fund into an annuity for 'guaranteed returns'. I'm 38. Good idea?

No, don't do that. Annuities typically have surrender charges that lock your money up for years, which defeats the whole purpose of an emergency fund being available instantly. At 38 you also lose decades of growth to fees and low guaranteed rates. Keep the emergency fund in a high-yield savings account, and if you want annuity advice later, get it from a fee-only fiduciary rather than someone paid on commission.
I'm 22, $2,300 on my card, making $16/hr. Am I screwed?

Not even close, because $2,300 is a very manageable balance and you're catching it early. If you can find $200 a month by trimming spending or picking up a few extra shifts, you'll have it gone in about a year, and faster if you can do more. Stop using the card for now, set autopay for the minimum as a safety net, and send extra payments every payday. Getting this cleared at 22 puts you way ahead of most people.
28 and my partner and I aren't married. Is it dumb to buy a house together?

It's not dumb, but unmarried couples don't get the legal protections married couples do if things go wrong. Before buying, decide how you'll hold title and what happens if one person contributed more or wants out. Put it in a written cohabitation or property agreement drafted by a real estate attorney. It feels unromantic, but it's far cheaper than a messy split later.
I'm 67, retired, and a man on Facebook has been helping me invest in a gold trading platform. The account shows I've made 40% but they want a 'release fee' before I can withdraw. Should I pay it?

Please don't pay that fee. A withdrawal or release fee on a platform you were introduced to through social media is one of the most common signs of an investment scam, and the 40% gain on the screen is almost certainly fake numbers designed to get more money out of you. Stop sending money, don't give them any more personal information, and call your bank today to flag the transfers. Then report it to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov and the FBI's IC3 site, and consider telling a family member or trusted friend so you're not handling this alone; you've done nothing to be ashamed of, these people are professionals at this.
Is renters insurance a scam? My landlord has insurance already.

It's not a scam. Your landlord's policy covers the building, not your belongings or your liability. If a fire destroys your stuff or a guest gets hurt in your apartment, you're on your own without renters insurance. It usually costs $10 to $25 a month, which makes it one of the best-value policies you can buy. Make sure you get replacement cost coverage, not actual cash value, so you aren't paid depreciated prices for your things.
lol is 'arbitrage trading' with 2% daily returns a thing

No. Real arbitrage opportunities are tiny, fleeting, and hoovered up by firms with huge infrastructure, so nobody is paying retail investors 2% a day for them. 'Arbitrage' is a favorite buzzword in Ponzi schemes because it sounds technical and riskless.
Won $40,000 at the casino. How much will I owe in taxes?

Casinos usually withhold 24% federally on a win that size, but that's just a prepayment, and your actual rate depends on your total income and could be higher. You'll also likely owe state tax unless you live in a state with no income tax. Set aside roughly 30 to 40% until you've talked with a tax preparer, so you don't get blindsided in April.
28, got 45k windfall, student loans at 5%, no emergency fund, no retirement savings. priority order?

Start with an emergency fund of three to six months of expenses in a high-yield savings account. Next, make sure you're getting any 401k employer match, then open and fund a Roth IRA for this year. At 5%, your loans sit in a gray area, so you can split what's left between extra loan payments and index funds based on how much the debt bothers you. Before prepaying federal loans, check whether you qualify for forgiveness programs.
mom needs 3k for rent. just send it or write something up?

For a parent covering rent, many people simply treat it as a gift, which avoids the awkwardness of chasing repayment later. If you do expect it back, a quick written note with the amount and a rough repayment plan protects the relationship more than it hurts it. Either way, decide in advance which one it is and tell her clearly, because unspoken expectations are where family money fights start.
My son wants to borrow from his 401k to invest in an 'AI arbitrage' platform paying 1.5% daily. He's 34. How do I talk him out of it?

Lead with the math instead of a lecture: 1.5% a day works out to roughly a 230-fold gain in a year, and no arbitrage, AI-driven or not, comes close to that. Real arbitrage profits are tiny and get competed away quickly. Ask him to look the platform up on the SEC and his state securities regulator sites and to try withdrawing a small amount first, since these schemes often stall at that point. Remind him that a 401k loan has to be repaid even if the money disappears, and leaving his job can make it due fast.
How much house can I afford on $85k a year?

As a rough guide, keeping total housing costs near 28 percent of gross income means about $2,000 a month including taxes and insurance. Depending on rates, taxes and your down payment, that often translates to a home somewhere around $250,000 to $320,000. Your other debts and your local tax and insurance costs can move that number a lot. Lenders may approve you for more, but approval is a ceiling, so base your budget on what still lets you save and keep an emergency fund.
A company called me saying my computer has a virus and they can fix it, plus sign me up for a 'crypto investment program' they run. They sound professional. Thoughts?

Hang up and don't let them access your computer; tech support cold calls are a classic scam, and bundling in an investment program is a second hook to take your money. Legitimate companies like Microsoft or Apple don't call you about viruses. If you already gave them remote access or payment info, disconnect from the internet, have a trusted local repair shop check the computer, change your passwords from another device, and call your bank.
Can I just put my kid's whole college fund in crypto? He's 3 so I have 15 years, it'll probably 10x by then.

I wouldn't bet a goal with a hard deadline on something that can drop 70% in a year and might not recover in time. Fifteen years is long enough for a diversified stock index fund, which is where most of that money should go. If you want crypto exposure, keep it to a small slice you could lose entirely without derailing his education. Most 529 plans won't hold crypto anyway, and that guardrail is probably a good thing here.
my cousin says i can turn $500 into $5k in a month with this forex signals group on telegram. legit?

Almost certainly not. Telegram forex signal groups make their money from subscription fees and broker referral kickbacks, not from winning trades, and a 10x return in a month is a claim no legitimate trader would make. Keep your $500, and if you're curious about currencies, read up on how forex actually works before risking a cent.
someone on tiktok says i can add a CPN to my credit apps instead of my SSN and get a fresh 800 score. legit??

No, that's a scam that can land you in serious legal trouble. CPNs sold online are usually stolen Social Security numbers, often taken from children, and using one on a credit application is federal fraud. If your credit is rough, a secured card, a credit-builder loan, or a free session with a nonprofit credit counselor will get you to a good score legitimately in a year or two.
I'm a nurse at a nonprofit hospital. Is PSLF real or is it a myth? I keep hearing nobody gets it.

It's real, and the program has forgiven billions of dollars after paperwork problems got cleaned up in the last few years. You need Direct Loans, full-time work for a qualifying employer like a nonprofit hospital, and 120 qualifying monthly payments, ideally on an income-driven plan so more of your balance is left to forgive. Use the PSLF Help Tool on studentaid.gov to certify your employment, and do it every year so you catch any errors early instead of a decade from now.
Is an HSA actually a retirement account? People keep saying that.

Sort of, and it's a great one if you have a qualifying high-deductible health plan. Contributions are tax-deductible, growth is tax-free, and withdrawals for medical costs are tax-free at any age, while after 65 you can withdraw for anything and just pay income tax, like a traditional IRA. To use it this way, invest the balance rather than leaving it in cash, and pay current medical bills out of pocket if you can afford to, keeping receipts for later reimbursement.
What's invoice factoring and should I do it? Clients pay me net 60.

Factoring means selling your unpaid invoices to a company that advances you most of the value now, typically 80-90%, and keeps a fee of roughly 1-5% per month until the client pays. It can work if slow-paying clients are your main cash problem, but those fees add up quickly, so compare it with a bank line of credit, which is usually cheaper. Also check whether the factor contacts your clients directly, and ask your clients whether they'd pay faster in exchange for a small early-payment discount.
Wife wants to retire at 45, I want to work till 60. We're 39. How do we not fight about this?

Put real numbers on both paths so the conversation is about trade-offs, not feelings: what spending each date supports and how much you'd need to save to get there. There are often middle options, like one of you going part-time first, or both downshifting at 50. A neutral fee-only planner can be surprisingly helpful as a referee who models the scenarios for you both.
is it true student loans get forgiven if you die?

Federal student loans are discharged if the borrower dies, and Parent PLUS loans are discharged if either the parent or the student dies. Private loans are a different story, since some lenders forgive them at death while others go after a cosigner or even the estate, depending on the contract. If you have private loans with a cosigner, it's worth checking your loan terms and considering a modest term life insurance policy so a family member isn't stuck with the bill.
just got evicted notice. 10 days. what do i do first

Contact local legal aid or a tenant rights organization today, because an eviction notice is usually not the same as an eviction order and you likely have more time and rights than the notice suggests. Call 211 to find emergency rental assistance, and tell your landlord in writing that you're applying for help, since some will pause if money is coming. Don't ignore any court papers, because missing a hearing can mean losing automatically.
Is it smart to max out my personal credit to fund my bakery so the business looks clean?

No, because maxing out your personal credit drops your score sharply and leaves you with no safety net if the bakery has a slow stretch. It also makes future business financing harder, since most small business lenders check personal credit anyway. Set up a business bank account, apply for a business credit card or SBA microloan, and keep personal and business finances separate the right way.
Thinking about cashing out my small 401k ($4,000) to pay bills. Good idea?

Usually not, because before age 59½ you'll typically owe a 10 percent penalty plus income tax, so that $4,000 could shrink to around $2,800 or less. Exhaust other options first, such as hardship plans with your creditors, local assistance programs, or a 401(k) loan if your plan offers one. If you're still considering it, a quick call with your plan administrator or a free VITA tax volunteer can show you the real after-tax number.
I'm 58 and close to retirement. Do I still need an emergency fund?

Yes, and many planners suggest retirees hold one to two years of expenses in cash so they never have to sell investments during a market drop. That cash buffer protects your portfolio while covering things like home repairs and health costs. A fee-only financial planner can help you set the right size based on your pensions, Social Security timing and withdrawal plan.
My grandma just left me $40k and I'm 22. My friends say put it all in crypto while I'm young. Thoughts?

Being young means you can take more risk, but that's an argument for a stock index fund, not for betting the whole amount on crypto. First set aside three to six months of expenses in a high-yield savings account and pay off any high-interest debt. Then put the bulk into a low-cost total market or S&P 500 index fund, ideally through a Roth IRA if you have earned income. If you still want crypto exposure, cap it at around 5% so a crash stings but doesn't wipe you out.
ugh just tell me which index fund to buy, i don't want a lecture

A total US stock market fund or an S&P 500 fund from Vanguard, Fidelity or Schwab with an expense ratio under 0.10 percent is a solid default. If you want global exposure, a target-date fund matching your retirement year handles stocks, bonds and rebalancing for you. Pick one and set up automatic contributions.
do student loans affect credit score

Yes, they work like any other installment loan. On-time payments build your credit history, and missed payments can drop your score significantly once they're reported. Federal loans usually aren't reported as delinquent until you're about 90 days late, but don't count on that cushion. Autopay is the simplest way to make sure they help your score instead of hurting it.
Is a big signing bonus as good as a higher salary?

Usually not, because a signing bonus is one-time while a salary bump compounds through future raises, bonuses, and 401(k) matches. Signing bonuses also often come with clawback clauses requiring repayment if you leave within a year or two, so read that fine print. They're great for covering a gap, like lost bonus from your old job, but push for base pay first.
My rate is 7.4% and I keep seeing ads for 6.5%. Is it worth refinancing a $320k loan?

Probably, but run the break-even before you get excited. A drop of about 0.9 points on $320k saves roughly $190 to $200 a month, so if closing costs come in around $6,000 you'd break even in about 30 months. If you plan to stay at least three or four years, that's a solid move. Get Loan Estimates from at least three lenders on the same day so you can compare them fairly.
Got a letter saying I inherited shares in a private oil venture and can claim 18% dividends if I pay a $2,500 transfer fee. Real?

This is almost certainly an advance-fee scam, since legitimate inheritances and share transfers don't require you to wire a fee to unlock them. Don't call any number in the letter and don't send money. If you think you might really have inherited something, contact the estate's probate attorney or the county probate court using contact details you find yourself. You can also report the letter to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov.
can i get a loan with a 520 score, i need 3k fast for car repairs

You can, but it's exactly the situation where predatory lenders find people, so steer clear of payday loans, title loans, and anything charging triple-digit APRs. Try a credit union first, because many offer small personal or emergency loans with more flexible approval, and a payday alternative loan caps rates at 28 percent. Ask the repair shop about a payment plan, and consider borrowing from family with a written agreement. If you do take a loan, make sure the payment truly fits your budget, because missing it would sink your score further.
Is renting really just throwing money away? My dad says it is.

Not really. Rent buys you housing and flexibility, while a big chunk of an early mortgage payment goes to interest, plus property taxes, insurance and maintenance, none of which build equity either. A fair comparison is the total unrecoverable cost of owning versus your rent, and in many expensive cities renting while investing the difference comes out ahead. Your dad's rule of thumb works best when you plan to stay put for many years.
Rent vs buy, 10 words or less.
Buy if staying five-plus years and it fits comfortably; otherwise rent.
529 or just a regular brokerage account? which one

For money you're confident will go toward education, a 529 usually wins because earnings grow tax-free and many states give you a deduction on contributions. A taxable brokerage account gives you more flexibility, but you'll owe taxes on gains and it can count more heavily against financial aid if it's in the child's name. Plenty of families split the difference: they fund the 529 up to a comfortable estimate of education costs and put extra savings in a brokerage account they control.
quick q: adjustable rate mortgage good idea rn?

An ARM can make sense if you're confident you'll sell or refinance before the fixed period ends, since the starting rate is often lower than a 30-year fixed. The risk is that when it adjusts your payment could rise significantly, and refinancing isn't guaranteed if rates climb or your income drops. If you plan to stay long-term or your budget is tight, a fixed rate is the safer bet, and you can always refinance if rates fall.
Is there a legit way to make money from casino bonuses / matched betting?

Matched betting can produce small, fairly reliable profits by using sportsbook promotions to cover both sides of a bet, and in the UK it's a known side hustle. It's tedious, the offers dry up, books often limit accounts that only take promos, and the tax rules differ by country. In the US, winnings are taxable and mistakes can lose real money. If you try it, start small, track everything and quit if it starts pulling you into regular betting.
Should I buy calls on a biotech before its FDA decision? Seems like easy money if it's approved.

It's not easy money, because the market already knows the decision is coming and prices that into the options. Implied volatility is usually sky-high before a binary event like an FDA ruling. After the news, volatility collapses, so your calls can lose value even if the drug is approved, unless the move is bigger than expected. A rejection usually sends both the stock and your calls toward zero. If you play it at all, size it as a lottery ticket you can fully lose.
I'm buying a house in 6 months. Anything I should NOT do with my credit right now?

Avoid opening new credit cards or loans, financing a car or furniture, and closing old accounts, since each can shift your score or your debt-to-income ratio right before underwriting. Keep balances low and pay everything on time, ideally on autopay. Don't co-sign for anyone either. Talking to a mortgage lender now for a pre-approval can tell you exactly where your score needs to be and what would help most.
my coworker says I should borrow against my house to invest and retire faster. smart?

That's a risky shortcut. Borrowing against your home to buy stocks means a market drop could leave you owing money while your investments are down, and your house is the collateral. Retiring early is about reducing risk over time, so paying down debt and investing from cash flow is the far safer route.
I'm 58 and was just laid off. I have about 4 months of savings. Should I start pulling from my 401k now to stretch it?

Hold off on touching the 401(k) for now, since early withdrawals can trigger taxes and possibly penalties, and your savings plus unemployment benefits should be your first line of defense. File for unemployment right away, trim expenses to the bare essentials, and look into whether you were laid off in the year you turn 55 or later, because that can allow penalty-free withdrawals from that employer's plan. Given the stakes this close to retirement, a one-time session with a fee-only financial planner is genuinely worth it to map out the next year.
Can I just stop paying my cards and let them go to collections? I heard they settle for less.

Sometimes they do, but deliberately defaulting will tank your credit score for up to seven years, rack up late fees, and can lead to lawsuits and wage garnishment. If a debt is forgiven in a settlement, the forgiven amount may also count as taxable income. If you truly can't keep up, call your issuers about hardship programs, or work with a nonprofit credit counselor on a debt management plan, which can lower your rates without wrecking your credit. Treat settlement as a last resort you pursue with professional guidance, not a strategy you stumble into by going silent.
do index funds ever lose money

Yes, they do, and sometimes sharply: the S&P 500 fell about 34 percent in early 2020 and roughly 50 percent in 2008 to 2009. Historically, though, broad US index funds have recovered and reached new highs, which is why they work best for money you won't need for at least five years. Keep short-term money in savings, not the stock market.
I make about 70k as a 1099 contractor. Do I really need to pay quarterly or can I just pay it all in April?

You should pay quarterly, because if you'll owe $1,000 or more, the IRS expects estimated payments in April, June, September and January. Paying it all at once in April triggers underpayment penalties, and a lump sum that big can be a shock to your budget. A simple safe harbor is paying 100 percent of last year's total tax split into four payments, which protects you from penalties even if you earn more this year.
We got $1.2 million from my father-in-law's estate. Do we really need an advisor or can we just buy VTI and chill?

A simple index approach like VTI can absolutely be the core, and plenty of disciplined people manage that themselves. At $1.2 million, though, the planning around it matters a lot: tax-efficient account placement, any inherited IRAs with withdrawal deadlines, estate planning, and making sure you aren't over-concentrated. Hire a flat-fee or hourly fiduciary for an initial plan instead of paying 1% a year forever, then manage it yourselves if you're comfortable.
My parents passed and left me their house plus about $120k cash. My siblings want to sell the house fast. I'm overwhelmed and don't know who to trust.

Feeling overwhelmed right now makes complete sense, and nothing has to be decided this week. Leave the cash in an insured account, and before anyone agrees to a sale, make sure the estate is being handled properly by the executor, ideally with an estate attorney involved. Inherited homes usually get a stepped-up cost basis, so selling soon often means little capital gains tax, but you should confirm that with a CPA. Paying a professional you hired yourself is the best way to know whose advice you can trust.
Health insurance before Medicare is freaking me out. 50, want to retire at 53.

That's a reasonable worry, and very solvable. ACA marketplace plans are subsidized based on your income, so managing taxable income in retirement, for example by drawing from cash or Roth funds, can sharply cut your premiums. Budget conservatively anyway, perhaps $10k to $25k a year for a couple including out-of-pocket costs, because subsidy rules can change and Medicare is still 12 years away.
How much should I set aside for taxes from my freelance graphic design gigs? I'm W-2 at my day job too.

Setting aside 25 to 30 percent of your freelance profit is a solid rule of thumb. That covers roughly 15.3 percent self-employment tax plus federal and state income tax at your marginal rate, and since your day job already uses up the lower brackets, the extra income lands at your higher rate. One simple fix is to raise your W-4 withholding at your day job to cover the freelance taxes, which can spare you from making quarterly estimated payments. If freelance income gets substantial, one session with a CPA to set this up correctly is worth the fee.
Can I get an SBA loan with a 590 credit score?

It's tough, since most SBA lenders want 640 to 680 or higher, though SBA microloans and CDFIs are more flexible and look harder at your plan and cash flow. Spend a few months improving your score by paying down card balances and fixing errors on your report, which can make a meaningful difference. Steer clear of lenders who say credit doesn't matter at all, because they often make up for it with brutal rates.
I'm 23 and just got my first real job. Should I build an emergency fund or start investing first?

Build a starter emergency fund of at least one month of expenses first, but if your employer offers a 401(k) match, contribute enough to get the full match at the same time, since that's an immediate return you shouldn't leave on the table. Once you have a few months of expenses saved, shift more toward investing. Investing without a cushion means a surprise bill could force you to sell at a bad time or rack up high-interest debt.
how much do i actually need to save? kid is 6

It depends on the type of school, but a common rule of thumb is to aim to cover about a third of projected costs from savings, with the rest from current income, aid, and modest loans. For an in-state public school, that might mean saving roughly $200 to $300 a month starting now, and more if you're targeting private schools. Plug your numbers into your 529 plan's college savings calculator to get a target, then adjust as you go.
My mom is in her 80s and asking to borrow money but I think someone is pressuring her. What do I do?

Trust your instinct, because elder financial exploitation is common and often involves someone close to the victim. Talk with her gently and privately about who's asking for money, and consider contacting Adult Protective Services or her bank, which can flag unusual activity. An elder law attorney can also advise on protections like a power of attorney.
Is it okay to borrow from my 401k to build an emergency fund?

That's generally a bad idea. A 401(k) loan pulls money out of the market, and if you leave or lose your job, the balance can come due quickly or be treated as a taxable withdrawal, which is exactly the scenario an emergency fund is meant to protect against. Build the fund from your paycheck instead, and if you need to free up cash, temporarily lower your contributions above the employer match rather than borrowing.
What's escrow and why did my payment go up $200?

Escrow is an account your servicer uses to pay your property taxes and homeowners insurance out of your monthly payment. When those bills rise, which often happens after a reassessment or insurance renewal, the servicer raises your payment and may add a catch-up for the shortfall. Read your annual escrow analysis to see what changed, and if your insurance spiked, shopping for a new policy or appealing your assessment can bring it back down.
My uncle swears by a trading bot that does 3% daily returns. He wants me to join with $10k. He's not a scammer, he's family.

Your uncle probably isn't the scammer; he's more likely a victim who hasn't been hit yet. A steady 3% a day compounds to absurd numbers, so no real bot does that. These platforms usually show fake gains and reward you for recruiting, which may be why he's bringing in family. Don't invest, and gently encourage him to try withdrawing his full balance now.
What's the difference between an index fund and an ETF? I'm confused.

An index fund is defined by its strategy: it tracks a market index instead of having a manager pick stocks. An ETF is a fund structure that trades on an exchange like a stock throughout the day. Many index funds are ETFs, like VOO, and others are mutual funds, like VFIAX, which trade once a day at the closing price. For a long-term investor, both versions of the same index work almost identically.
I got preapproved at 6.2% from my credit union but the dealer says they can beat it. Should I let them run my credit?

Sure, let them try, because a preapproval is your leverage and dealers sometimes access promotional manufacturer rates. Rate shopping within about two weeks counts as a single inquiry for scoring purposes. Just compare the full terms side by side, since a lower rate with a longer term or added products can still cost more. If their offer isn't clearly better, use your credit union loan.
ugh I missed the April deadline. am I screwed

You're not screwed, but file as soon as possible, because the failure-to-file penalty is much steeper than the failure-to-pay penalty. If you're owed a refund, there's generally no penalty at all and you have three years to claim it. If you owe, file now and pay what you can, then set up an installment agreement for the rest to keep interest and penalties from snowballing.
Should I give equity to an angel investor or take a loan? I'm building a SaaS app, 23 years old.

For a pre-revenue SaaS company, equity often makes more sense than debt because you won't have steady cash flow for loan payments and software can take a while to monetize. Equity is the more expensive option if you succeed, though, so raise only what you need to reach your next milestone and understand the terms, including valuation, dilution and any board seats. Have a startup attorney review the term sheet or SAFE before you sign, because mistakes made early follow you through every future round.
I'm 19 and want to be a millionaire by 25. What's the fastest realistic path?

Going from nothing to a million in six years is extremely rare, and chasing it with risky bets usually sets people back. The realistic fast lane is raising your income through in-demand skills, a trade, sales or a business, while investing steadily in index funds. Starting at 19 is a huge advantage, and consistent saving now can make you a millionaire well before retirement.
There's a crypto staking platform paying 2% per week, my friend has been withdrawing fine for 3 months. Safe to put in my savings?

Don't put your savings in. Successful withdrawals for a few months is exactly how Ponzi schemes win trust, because they pay early investors with new deposits until they collapse, as Celsius and many smaller platforms did. Two percent a week works out to over 100% a year, which no real yield supports, so your friend should probably think about getting their money out too.
My business partner and I want to borrow money but we never wrote anything down about who owns what. Problem?

Yes, sort that out before you borrow, because lenders will ask for an operating or partnership agreement and it protects you both if things go wrong. It should spell out ownership percentages, who guarantees debt, how decisions are made, and what happens if one of you leaves. A small business attorney can draft one for a few hundred to a couple thousand dollars, which is cheap insurance.
My grandparents want to give me $50k for a house. Anything I should watch out for?

That's a wonderful gift. Your lender will want a signed gift letter stating it's not a loan, and they'll want to see the money move from their account to yours. Your grandparents may need to file a gift tax return since the amount is over the annual exclusion, though they almost certainly won't owe tax. Have them check with a tax professional, and keep all documentation clean to avoid underwriting delays.
Is now a bad time to invest my inheritance? Everyone says a crash is coming.

Someone is always predicting a crash, and nobody reliably times them. Waiting for the perfect moment usually costs more than investing through some bad days. If the fear is real for you, invest in chunks over a few months, and keep money you'll need within five years out of stocks entirely.
should I file a claim for a $900 fender bender? my deductible is $500

Probably not. You'd only get $400 back, and an at-fault claim can raise your premium for three to five years, which can easily cost more than $400 in total. Get a repair quote and pay out of pocket if the other party wasn't involved or there were no injuries. If another driver or any injury was involved, notify your insurer anyway, because failing to report can jeopardize your coverage if they make a claim later.
ugh i hate negotiating. what's the minimum effort move

Reply to the offer email with one line: thank them, say you're excited, and ask whether there's any flexibility on the base salary. That single question often gets you a few thousand dollars with no number or haggling required. If they say no, you accept, and you've lost nothing.
My 16yo wants to trade options with birthday money. Is there a way to let him?

Minors can't open their own brokerage accounts, and most custodial accounts don't allow options trading at all, so options are mostly off the table. A better route is a custodial account where he picks a few stocks or ETFs, paired with a paper trading app to practice options with fake money. That way he learns how the mechanics and risks work without losing his birthday money while he figures it out.
My ex isn't contributing anything to our son's college fund and I'm doing it all alone. Should I open an account in my name or his?

Open a 529 with yourself as owner and your son as beneficiary. That way you control the money, it gets favorable financial aid treatment, and you can change the beneficiary if needed. Avoid putting it in his name through a UTMA, since he'd control it at adulthood and it would hurt his aid more. If your custody agreement or divorce decree mentions college costs, ask a family law attorney whether your ex owes a share.
do I have to pay taxes on venmo money from friends paying me back for dinner

No, reimbursements from friends for split dinners, rent or gifts aren't taxable income. Business payments are a different story, so if you're getting paid for services or sales, that's taxable whether or not you get a 1099-K. Mark personal transfers as friends and family where the app lets you, and keep a loose record in case questions come up.
Im 58 and worried negotiating will make me look 'difficult' and they'll pick someone younger

Negotiating professionally signals confidence and experience, not difficulty, and a calm, well-researched ask is unlikely to hurt you. Keep it collaborative by stating enthusiasm first, then your number and the specific value your experience brings. If you ever sense age is influencing pay or hiring decisions, document it and consider talking with an employment lawyer, since age discrimination is illegal for workers 40 and over.
Should I charge my brother-in-law interest on a $25,000 loan for his down payment?

At that size, charging at least the IRS Applicable Federal Rate keeps you clear of tax complications, and it makes the loan feel like a real obligation. Check with his lender too, because mortgage lenders often require a gift letter or count your loan as his debt. Hiding it from them could be mortgage fraud. Have a simple promissory note drafted, ideally reviewed by an attorney, and get the whole thing in writing before any money moves.
My nephew needs 15k bail money. Family's pressuring me. Is that a loan or what?

Bail paid directly to the court is generally returned once the case concludes, provided he shows up to every hearing, though fees or fines can be deducted from it. If he misses court, you can lose all of it, so the real question is how much you trust him to appear. Going through a bail bondsman is cheaper upfront, but the fee, usually around 10%, is not refundable. Talk to his defense attorney first, because they can sometimes argue for reduced bail or release without it.
What's a target date fund and is it actually good or lazy?

It's a single fund holding a diversified mix of stocks and bonds that automatically shifts more conservative as its target year approaches. Lazy in the best way: it handles diversification and rebalancing so you don't make emotional mistakes. Just check the expense ratio, since index-based versions often charge 0.1 percent or less while some charge far more.
Living alone on $1,700/month. Is it dumb to have a $90 gym membership?

At your income, $90 is over 5 percent of your take-home, so it's worth reconsidering unless you go often and it's keeping you healthy and sane. Budget gyms like Planet Fitness run $10 to $25, and running, bodyweight workouts or free YouTube routines cost nothing. If you love that gym and use it four times a week, trim somewhere else instead. If you've gone twice this month, cancel it.
Retire at 45 with a pension and $500k? Pension is $40k/yr, spend $55k.

That looks very doable, because the pension covers most of your spending and you'd only need about $15k a year from savings, a 3% withdrawal rate. Check whether the pension is adjusted for inflation, because if it isn't, its buying power will shrink a lot over 40 years and your portfolio will need to cover more over time. Also confirm what survivor and health benefits come with it before you lock in your election.
Need fast money for rent in 2 months, have $1500. Any investment that could triple it quick?

Nothing that can triple money in two months does so without a big chance of losing it, and losing your rent money is far worse than not growing it. Keep the $1,500 in a savings account, and look at extra shifts, selling unused stuff, or local rental assistance programs to cover the gap. Also talk to your landlord early, since many will work out a short payment plan if you ask before rent is late.
I moved 401k money into a check made out to me when I left my job and they withheld 20%. Did I screw up?

Not necessarily, but you're on a clock: you have 60 days to deposit the full original amount into an IRA or new 401k, including the 20% that was withheld, which you'll need to make up from other cash. If you deposit only what you received, the missing 20% counts as a taxable distribution and may be hit with a 10% penalty if you're under 59½. You'll get the withholding back as a credit at tax time. Next time, ask for a direct rollover so nothing is withheld, and loop in a tax preparer when you file.
Thinking of putting my whole FIRE stash into leveraged ETFs like TQQQ to get there 10 years faster. Thoughts?

Don't do this with money you're counting on. Leveraged ETFs reset daily and decay during choppy markets, and TQQQ lost roughly 80% in 2022, a drop that can take a decade or longer to recover from. One bad stretch could push your retirement out by ten years instead of pulling it in. If you want to speed things up, raising your savings rate is the lever that actually works, and a plain broad index fund does the compounding for you.
My 16 year old is winning skins on gambling sites for a video game and says it's harmless. Is it?

It's not harmless. Skin gambling sites are often unregulated, don't verify ages properly, and use the same reward patterns as casinos, which teenagers are especially vulnerable to. Talk with him calmly about how the odds and design work rather than banning it outright, check where the money comes from, and use parental controls or payment restrictions on his accounts. If he can't stop or is hiding it, a counselor familiar with gambling or gaming problems is worth contacting.
Rent is $2,100. Similar house would cost $2,900 a month all in. Buy or rent?

That $800 gap is meaningful, so it depends on what you'd do with it and how long you'll stay. If you'd reliably invest the $800 each month and might move within five years, renting likely wins. If you'll stay a decade and the $2,900 fits comfortably, equity and appreciation can tip it toward buying. Make sure the $2,900 includes maintenance, then plug both scenarios into a rent-vs-buy calculator.
Investor wants 40% of my company for $50k. Seems like a lot? I'm desperate though.

That values your company at $125k, and 40% is a heavy stake that can limit your control and scare off future investors. Desperation is the worst position to negotiate from, so before you agree, look at alternatives like a microloan or revenue-based financing, or counter with a smaller stake or a convertible note. Either way, have a startup attorney review the term sheet, because details like board seats and liquidation preferences can matter as much as the percentage.
I'm 68 and just inherited $300,000 from my sister. A broker wants me to buy an annuity with all of it. Good idea?

Be cautious about putting all of it into one product, especially on a salesperson's recommendation, because many annuities carry high commissions, surrender charges that lock up your money for years, and fees that eat into returns. A simple income annuity can make sense for part of a retirement plan, but rarely for everything, and you'll want liquid savings for health costs and emergencies. Before you sign anything, get a second opinion from a fee-only fiduciary advisor who doesn't earn commissions, and ask the broker in writing exactly what they're paid on the sale.
Is renters insurance actually worth it?

Usually yes, because it's often around $15–25 a month and covers far more than people expect. It pays to replace your belongings after theft or fire, covers liability if someone gets hurt in your place or you accidentally flood the unit below, and can pay for a hotel if your apartment becomes unlivable. That liability piece alone can save you from a five-figure bill. Pick replacement-cost coverage rather than actual cash value so a claim pays what it costs to buy new stuff.
Crypto trading as a side hustle? I've got $10k saved and want to turn it into income.

I'd steer you away from that. Short-term crypto trading isn't a side hustle, it's speculation, and most active traders lose money compared with just holding. If that $10k is your savings or emergency fund, putting it at risk to chase income is how people end up worse off. Keep it in a high-yield savings account and look for a side hustle that trades your time and skills for money. If you're curious about crypto, a small amount you can fully afford to lose is the way to explore it.
dealer asked what monthly payment i want. what do i say

Don't give them a number. Saying a payment target lets them stretch the term or add fees to hit it while the total price climbs. Tell them you're negotiating the out-the-door price of the car and that you already have financing lined up. Once the price is settled, you can see whether their financing beats your preapproval.
Friend offered to cosign my business loan. Any downside for her?

Yes, a big one, because a cosigner is fully on the hook if you can't pay, and the loan will appear on her credit and affect her ability to borrow. Make sure she understands she could owe the whole balance, not just a share. Put a written agreement between you two covering what happens if things go wrong, and only accept if you're confident in the repayment plan.
Recruiter says the offer is 'final, non-negotiable.' Is it actually?

Sometimes it really is, especially at large companies with rigid salary bands or for entry-level roles, but it costs little to ask one polite question about other levers. Try asking whether there's any room on a signing bonus, start date, remote days, or a six-month compensation review. If they say no across the board, decide based on whether the offer works for you as is, not on trying to force movement.
roth ira or traditional ira. which one. 26, making 52k

At 26 and $52k, the Roth is usually the better pick because you're likely in a lower tax bracket now than you will be later, and all qualified withdrawals in retirement come out tax-free. You can also pull your contributions (not earnings) back out anytime without penalty, which gives you a little flexibility. Open one at a low-cost brokerage like Fidelity, Schwab, or Vanguard and put the money in a broad index fund or target-date fund.
what's total comp and why does everyone say look at it instead of salary

Total compensation is everything the job pays you: base salary, bonuses, equity, retirement match, health insurance and other benefits. Two offers with the same base can differ by thousands once you factor in, say, a 6 percent 401(k) match versus none, or cheap versus expensive health premiums. Ask for the full benefits summary in writing so you can compare offers fairly.
honest question: are any get rich quick things actually real?

Almost none are repeatable. The rare big wins, like early crypto buyers or lottery winners, were luck, and for every one of them thousands of people lost money doing the same thing. What does work is boring but powerful: raise your income, spend less than you earn, and invest consistently in diversified low-cost funds for years. Anyone selling a shortcut is usually getting rich from you.
honestly can I lie a little on my life insurance application about smoking? I only smoke socially lol

Don't. Misrepresenting tobacco use is insurance fraud, and if you die within the contestability period, usually two years, the insurer can investigate and deny the claim entirely, leaving your family with nothing. Many insurers also test for nicotine, so they may catch it anyway. Be honest. Some companies have better rates for occasional cigar or social use, and if you quit for 12 months you can often ask to be reclassified at nonsmoker rates.
28, making $55k, no retirement savings, $12k credit card debt at 24%. Where do I start?

First, contribute enough to your 401(k) to get any employer match, because that's free money. Then put every extra dollar toward the 24% credit card debt, since paying it off is a guaranteed 24% return. Keep a small emergency fund of $1,000 to $2,000 so a surprise expense doesn't go back on the card. Once the debt is gone, push your retirement savings toward 15%.
Can I contribute to an IRA if I already have a 401k at work?

Yes, anyone with earned income can contribute to an IRA regardless of a workplace plan. The catch is that deducting traditional IRA contributions phases out at certain incomes when you're covered at work, and Roth eligibility has its own income limits. If you qualify, a Roth IRA alongside your 401k is a great way to get tax diversification.
is daily fantasy sports gambling or investing

It's gambling, though there's more skill involved than a slot machine. The top players are professionals using models and big data, which means casual players are usually the ones funding their winnings. Treat it as paid entertainment with a firm budget, not as a way to grow money.
Single mom, two kids, $2,100/month take home. Groceries are killing me, like $700 a month. Tips?

Plan meals for the week around cheap staples like rice, beans, eggs, oats, frozen vegetables and whole chickens, and shop with a list only after checking what's already in the pantry. Store brands and discount grocers like Aldi or Lidl can cut a bill by 20 to 30 percent on their own. With your income and two kids, you very likely qualify for SNAP and WIC if they're young, plus free or reduced school meals, so apply for all three, since that could take hundreds off your grocery costs each month. Local food banks are there for exactly this situation too, and using them is completely fine.
is a 40 year mortgage a good way to get a lower payment

It lowers the payment a bit, but you'll pay dramatically more interest and build equity very slowly. That can leave you stuck if prices dip and you need to sell. If you need a 40-year term to make the numbers work, that's usually a sign the house is too expensive for your budget. A cheaper home on a 30-year loan is almost always the safer move.
honestly should i pay off my credit card first or build an emergency fund

Do both in stages: build a starter fund of around $1,000 first, then throw everything extra at the credit card, then go back to building the full emergency fund. Without that small cushion, the next flat tire goes right back on the card and you're stuck in a loop. Once the high-interest debt is gone, the money you were paying toward it can fill your emergency fund fast.
How are day trading profits taxed in the US?

Profits on positions held one year or less are short-term capital gains, taxed at your ordinary income rate, which is often much higher than long-term rates. Watch the wash sale rule as well: if you sell at a loss and buy a substantially identical security within 30 days before or after, you can't deduct that loss yet. Active traders can rack up messy tax situations quickly, so it's worth working with a CPA who handles trader taxes.
should my emergency fund be in a different bank than my checking

It's a good idea for many people. A separate bank, especially an online one paying a higher rate, adds a day or two of friction that stops impulse spending while still getting you money quickly in a real emergency. Just make sure both accounts are FDIC- or NCUA-insured and link them so transfers are easy when you actually need the cash.
I'm 61, retiring next year. Should I take Social Security at 62 right away?

If you're healthy and can cover expenses from savings, waiting usually pays off. Claiming at 62 permanently cuts your benefit by about 30% compared with full retirement age. Delaying to 70 increases it about 8% a year beyond that age and gives you strong, inflation-adjusted longevity insurance. Claiming early can make sense if you have health issues, need the cash, or are the lower earner in a couple, so run your specific numbers or talk to a fee-only planner.
Friend says I should make my nephew sign a note and hold his car title as collateral for $6k. Overkill?

It's not overkill if $6,000 matters to you. A signed note plus collateral makes the loan clear and gives you a fallback. For the lien to actually hold, you generally need to file it through your state's motor vehicle agency, not just keep the title in a drawer. Also ask yourself honestly whether you'd ever repossess your nephew's car. If you wouldn't, the collateral is mostly symbolic.
Is it ok to not tell my employer about my side business?

Usually yes, since your free time is generally your own. Check your employee handbook and contract first, though. Many have moonlighting, conflict-of-interest or IP clauses, and breaking them can cost you your job or even the rights to what you build. If your side work competes with your employer, uses their clients, or touches their equipment or hours, disclose it or don't do it.
I lent my daughter money for college and now she says it was a gift. No paperwork. Can I do anything?

Without paperwork it's a he-said-she-said situation, and small claims court against your own daughter rarely ends well even when you win. Look for texts, emails or bank memos that show it was meant as a loan, since that's your strongest evidence. Honestly, a calm conversation about a modest repayment plan will probably do more than legal action. Before deciding, think about what preserving the relationship is worth to you.
is it dumb to try saving when i barely make enough to cover bills

Not dumb at all, but the goal right now is a small cushion, not a big savings number. Even $10 or $20 a paycheck moved automatically into a separate account adds up to a few hundred dollars over a year, which can be the difference between a flat tire being an annoyance and a crisis. Aim for a starter buffer of around $500 before worrying about anything bigger. If $10 is truly impossible, focus first on cutting one recurring cost so the room exists.
Just tell me the fastest way to be debt free. No lectures.

Pick the avalanche method: make every minimum payment, then throw every spare dollar at the highest-rate loan until it's gone, and roll that payment into the next one. Raises, tax refunds and side income all go straight to the debt. Keep a small emergency fund so a surprise bill doesn't force you onto a credit card, and keep any free employer match. That's the fastest path that won't blow up on you.
My loans went into default years ago. Is it too late to fix it?

It's not too late. Federal loans offer a couple of routes out of default. Loan rehabilitation means making 9 affordable, income-based payments within 10 months, and afterward the default notation comes off your credit report. Consolidation is faster but doesn't remove the default record. Programs like Fresh Start have also helped some defaulted borrowers, so check StudentAid.gov or call the Default Resolution Group to see what's currently available. Once you're back in good standing, you regain access to income-driven plans.
is 'theta gang' actually profitable long term

Selling options can be profitable on average because implied volatility tends to run a bit higher than what actually happens, so sellers collect a small edge over time. The catch is that you make many small gains and occasionally take a large loss, and a few bad trades without proper sizing can wipe out years of premium. It works best with defined-risk spreads or fully secured positions, small position sizes and the discipline to keep doing it through drawdowns.
How much car can I afford making $55k a year?

A solid guideline is to keep the total car payment under about 10 to 15 percent of your take-home pay. For you, that's roughly $350 to $500 a month. Put at least 10 to 20 percent down and keep the term at 60 months or less, which points to a car somewhere around $18,000 to $25,000. Budget separately for insurance, gas and maintenance, which can add a few hundred dollars a month on their own.
My in-laws want me to lend them money and keep it secret from my wife. Should I?

No. Hiding a financial decision from your spouse, especially one involving her family, can do real damage to your marriage regardless of the amount. If the money comes from shared finances, she has a right to know. Tell her about the request and decide together, and if the in-laws object to her knowing, treat that as a red flag.
impatient. just tell me the one stock that will double this year

Nobody knows that, and anyone who claims to is guessing or selling something. Even professional fund managers mostly fail to beat a simple index fund over time. If you want growth with real odds behind it, a low-cost total market or S&P 500 index fund is the honest answer, even if it's not the exciting one.
should i take a 401k loan to pay off my credit cards lol

It's tempting but usually not the move. If you leave or lose your job, many plans want the balance repaid quickly, and anything you can't repay can turn into a taxable distribution with a possible 10% penalty, plus the borrowed money misses out on market growth. Try a balance transfer card or a nonprofit credit counseling debt management plan first, and treat the 401k as a last resort, ideally after talking it through with a fee-only financial planner.
Where should I keep my emergency fund?

A high-yield savings account at an FDIC-insured bank or NCUA-insured credit union is the best default, because it's safe, liquid and currently pays far more than a typical big-bank savings account. Keep it separate from your checking account so you aren't tempted to dip into it for everyday spending. A money market fund at a major brokerage is a reasonable alternative if you're comfortable with a slightly less direct setup.
lol can I claim my dog as a dependent? he's basically my kid

Sadly, no. Pets don't qualify as dependents, no matter how much they run the household. The one narrow exception is a certified service animal, whose care costs can count as a medical expense if you itemize. Expenses for fostering animals through a registered nonprofit may also be deductible as charitable contributions. For the average beloved dog, though, the IRS isn't sympathetic.
Wife and I are 38, $1.4M, spend $55k/yr, two kids. Are we done?

Your withdrawal rate would be under 4%, which is solid. With kids, though, I'd stress-test for college costs, family health insurance, and spending that will likely climb as they get older. If you can show a sustainable plan at around 3.5%, roughly $49k on these assets, or keep some flexible income, you're in strong shape. Given the stakes and the kids, it's worth paying a flat-fee planner to check your assumptions before you both quit.
Got approved for level 4 options at my broker. Does that mean I'm ready for spreads and naked selling?

Approval means the broker let you trade those strategies, not that you're ready for them; approval is often based mostly on what you reported on a form. Start with defined-risk spreads, where your maximum loss is known upfront, and learn how assignment and early exercise work before going further. Hold off on naked selling until you've traded spreads through some volatile markets and fully understand margin requirements.
quick q: roth or traditional 401k for a 24 year old making 55k

Roth is usually the stronger pick for you. You're probably in a low bracket now, and decades of tax-free growth is hard to beat. If your employer matches, contribute at least enough to get the full match, because that's free money in either account. Some people split contributions between the two to hedge against future tax rates, which is a perfectly reasonable middle ground.
Pretty anxious here. I'm 29, put $10k into a total market index fund and it dropped $1,200 this month. Did I mess up?

You didn't mess up, because drops like this are a normal part of owning stocks and the market has recovered from every decline in its history given enough time. A 12 percent dip is uncomfortable, but with decades until retirement it barely matters, and buying while prices are lower helps you. The worst thing you could do is sell now and lock in the loss. If the swings keep you up at night, make sure you have an emergency fund in cash and consider checking your account less often.
inherited 250k. dont know anything about money. where do i even start

Start by doing nothing dramatic: put it in a high-yield savings account or money market fund for a few months while you get your bearings, since there's no penalty for waiting. Use that time to list your debts, build an emergency fund, and figure out your goals, like a house, retirement or paying off loans. With this amount, a session with a fee-only fiduciary financial planner who charges a flat or hourly rate rather than commissions is well worth it. Steer clear of anyone who pitches you a specific product in the first meeting.
is a 529 actually better than just a regular savings account for my kid's college
